item.title: AI Cyber Panic, Ken Griffin’s Bubble Warning, The Fall of France?
item.description: Chamath estimates 90% of AI spending is concentrated in 1% of companies, with 80% from unprofitable VC-backed businesses, leaving genuine demand diffusion the key test. France’s 10-year yield has exceeded 5%; Chamath says bond pressure toward 8% could force a reset, while Jason sees no reasonable endgame.
item.content:encoded:
All-In · Chamath Palihapitiya、Jason Calacanis、David Sacks、David Friedberg、Nikesh Arora · 2026-10-23 · 103 min · 原语言 EN

Chamath estimates 90% of AI spending is concentrated in 1% of companies, with 80% from unprofitable VC-backed businesses, leaving genuine demand diffusion the key test. France’s 10-year yield has exceeded 5%; Chamath says bond pressure toward 8% could force a reset, while Jason sees no reasonable endgame.

TL;DR

  • Chamath sees AI’s bubble risk in concentrated, venture-funded demand rather than in the technology’s usefulness. His estimate puts 90% of AI spending in 1% of companies, with 80% of that coming from unprofitable VC-backed businesses. He describes VC-funded startups circulating spending, showing revenue traction, then raising again from the same investors. “AI has a diffusion problem”; Jason counters that startups’ rush toward the cheapest, fastest competitive advantage is an encouraging adoption signal.
  • Open models could redirect AI spending toward infrastructure, but compute scarcity limits enterprise independence. Nikesh Arora says Palo Alto Networks prefers open weights for customization and auditability, yet cannot easily procure globally resilient inference outside hyperscalers. His likely destination is rented bare metal running open models: buyers remain “a taker of terms,” while profit pools might shift from chips and memory toward available compute.
  • Arora expects AI-discovered vulnerabilities to arrive faster than enterprises can clear their accumulated technical debt. Jason describes PHP exploits rated 9.2/10 affecting software used across roughly 70% of websites; Arora explains how persistent compute unlocked an attack previously considered impractical. More defensive compute alone cannot fix fragmented infrastructure, making the operational priority “how quickly can I find them and how quickly can I eject them?”
  • Banking agents expose an unresolved boundary between user authorization and defective software. Arora and Chamath put responsibility primarily on users who hand over credentials, while Friedberg sees potential provider liability when an agent disregards bank access restrictions. Arora preserves a crucial exception: a “rogue agent” that fails to behave as advertised creates a product-liability issue.
  • France becomes the episode’s sovereign-risk warning, with disagreement over the relative roles of government provision and immigration. Jason reports French 10-year yields above 5%; Chamath ultimately calls for bond vigilantes to push them toward 8% and force a reset. Chamath warns that political actors can capture power during a reset; Jason, doubting AI abundance would be persuasive to France, concludes, “I don’t see a reasonable endgame.”
  • Friedberg’s fiscal proposals include winding down federal student lending, changing housing finance, and transitioning defined-benefit retirement promises into individually owned investments over a decade. David Sacks supplies the more specific proposal to reduce federal home-loan underwriting, warning of a possible 10–20% hit to middle-class net worth. Chamath supports making student debt dischargeable; the retirement transition would still remove guaranteed income.
  • The closing dispute is whether AI-led growth reaches voters without more direct measures on affordability. David Friedberg calls the US economy “entirely and completely levered to and correlated with the AI trade,” while Jason wants equal attention to housing and lower-paid workers. Jason proposes $1 annual minimum-wage increases toward $15; Friedberg argues for tax relief and credits instead, rejecting government intervention in labor prices.

Digest

1. AI’s bubble question is about who pays the bills

  • Jason introduces Ken Griffin’s warning that AI is “almost certainly a bubble,” alongside Griffin’s longer-term optimism: major economic transformations commonly bring bubbles. The immediate concern is businesses examining Anthropic and OpenAI bills and asking where productivity appears. Jason reports Thursday declines of 10% for CoreWeave, 6% for Meta, and 5% for AMD and SpaceX, while noting recent volatility and a generally upward trend.
  • Chamath’s estimate puts 90% of AI spending in 1% of companies, with 80% of that spending coming from unprofitable VC-backed businesses. His causal chain runs from LP capital to venture funds, startups, token purchases, revenue growth, and subsequent fundraising. The danger is “a bunch of money-losing entities just spinning a bunch of money around,” supporting valuations before demand broadens.
  • An unpublished Ramp chart and a call with its chief economist broadly support Chamath’s estimate, according to his researcher. Jason flags Ramp’s concentration in startup financial services; Chamath says its economist also accesses broader data. Chamath contrasts today’s circularity with early AWS adoption: startups initially dominated EC2 and S3 usage, but Amazon’s retail business was roughly break-even on free cash flow.
  • Jason’s pushback — worth keeping: startups adopting a technology aggressively can reveal genuine economic advantage. They seek the “cheapest, best, fastest edge,” unlike slower enterprises. His examples include cloud computing and WeWork as cost-saving advantages, and initially underpriced Facebook advertising, into which startups poured venture dollars because it worked. Concentrated early adoption therefore can be a leading indicator of diffusion rather than evidence that demand lacks substance.

2. Open weights attract enterprises, but infrastructure remains scarce

  • Chamath reads rising GPU-compute spending in Ramp’s chart as evidence that heavy users are moving toward open models. He also reports changed enterprise buying patterns following Alex Karp’s comments about data sovereignty. One unnamed major US bank told his team it had reduced AWS and GCP spending and built six independent, ground-up data centers: “It’s back to the future.”
  • Arora says Palo Alto Networks prefers open-source, open-weight models because it can modify weights, train them, and interrogate their chain of thought. His enterprise requirements are “explainability, auditability, and verifiability.” In regulated financial services or healthcare, telling a boss that an unexplained result came from an AI model will not suffice; he sees open weights as necessary for that scrutiny.
  • Independence becomes harder at production scale. Arora needs global inference with 99.9% reliability, not a startup’s single 10-megawatt deployment that can tolerate several hours offline. He says Jensen cannot supply chips until 2028, while land, power, and buildings also constrain supply. Having closed Palo Alto’s data centers six or eight years earlier, he now finds rebuilding them an impractical negotiating threat.
  • Arora expects a hybrid outcome: hyperscalers or adjacent providers supply bare metal while enterprises run open models. The “profit pool” could move from NVIDIA and memory suppliers toward owners of available compute. He acknowledges slow enterprise diffusion but calls demand “insatiable”: even if every company committed immediately, he argues, there would not be enough compute to serve them all.

3. The PHP panic turns neglected maintenance into an emergency

  • Jason describes two critical exploits nicknamed “PHP2Shell,” discovered using AI in August and rated 9.2/10. He says PHP powers about 70% of websites, including WordPress and Wikipedia. Developers had coordinated an October 22 patch, but information leaked beforehand; PHP advanced the release to October 21. How the information escaped remained unknown during the recording.
  • The release coincided with increased hacking activity, according to Jason’s account of AWS and Cloudflare reports. He describes millions of attempts, precautionary shutdowns across European government websites, systems taken offline at Wikipedia, and NSA/FBI warnings. His question is whether such emergencies will recur every ten days. Arora’s answer is sharper: “I think 10 days is too long.”
  • Arora’s concrete example is a CIO whose websites run different PHP generations. Current versions can accept the patch; older ones require taking sites down and rebuilding them. The organization had tolerated those older versions because upgrading never seemed important enough. AI has changed the urgency of paying technical debt, rather than creating all the underlying weaknesses.
  • There are two defenses in Arora’s account: patch the vulnerable application itself, or deploy a “virtual patch” through a perimeter product such as Palo Alto’s or Cloudflare’s. The latter blocks the recognized attack before it reaches the server. But publication also informs attackers: they inspect what changed, reverse-engineer the vulnerability, and target organizations that have not yet patched.

4. Defensive compute needs coordinated systems to become useful

  • Arora says powerful models can find vulnerabilities and chain several into an attack path when given sufficient compute and persistence. The PHP problem, he explains, had been identified years earlier but seemed too difficult to exploit because of the coordination required. Persistent computation found a workable path. Once disclosed or reverse-engineered, that discovery became usable by many more attackers.
  • Jason asks whether well-funded defenders can simply outcompute hackers. Arora says that is not true today because infrastructure lacks the necessary orchestration. A company with 5,000 websites may still have IT staff cataloging them individually rather than operating from a unified inventory. Without that baseline preparedness, defenders cannot dispatch coordinated agents to patch systems merely because more compute is available.
  • Continuous penetration testing helps, Arora says, but each stronger model may discover additional entry points. His alternative starting assumption is that breaches will happen: “The question becomes less about how I got breached” and more about detection and ejection. Aggregating signals and data makes anomalous behavior visible, allowing superior defensive compute to operate against an intruder rather than an unknown inventory of vulnerabilities.

5. Banking agents blur identity and divide liability

  • Friedberg separates suspicious browser activity from conventional application access through verified APIs and intermediaries such as Plaid. Arora likewise distinguishes two problems: unauthorized access possibly connected to the PHP vulnerability, and personal agents logging in with their users’ credentials. Banks cannot readily distinguish the latter from users themselves. CAPTCHA is an incomplete boundary because AI can solve it or hand the challenge back to a person.
  • Jason asks whether banks are exaggerating danger to prevent agents from routing customers toward better rates and cheaper services. Arora considers that too much strategic credit. His explanation is liability and support costs: a customer says $50,000 disappeared, while the bank must reconstruct actions performed by software holding valid credentials. Repeated requests for explanations could become expensive even before reimbursing disputed transactions.
  • Friedberg’s initial liability view places responsibility on an agent provider if its software ignores a bank’s prohibition on agent access. If the software warns the user and receives an explicit override, he thinks responsibility shifts to the user. Jason supplies an e-commerce parallel: his Grok shopping agent can prepare an Amazon cart, address, and payment choice, but “I won’t hit the buy button.”
  • Arora’s default is user responsibility: “There’s a word in agent, it’s called agency.” Chamath calls that the only scalable arrangement. Jason pushes back on agents that find unauthorized workarounds to satisfy instructions, prompting Arora’s exception: a “rogue agent” that behaves contrary to its advertised purpose creates a product-liability problem for its maker. Their agreement on authorization does not erase that distinction.

6. Removing model guardrails produces the sharpest AI disagreement

  • Jason describes incubated company Obliteration AI as supplying models without built-in constraints for white hats and corporations, with customers responsible for controls and liability. He frames the product as infrastructure for serious testing rather than unrestricted public distribution. Arora asks what this adds beyond taking an open-weight model and training it internally; Jason’s answer centers on serving infrastructure and efficiency.
  • Chamath finds this “unbelievably scary,” calling it an underappreciated risk vector that concerns him more than alignment. Arora argues governance depends on the weakest link: restrictions elsewhere accomplish little if another provider supplies raw capability without guardrails. His analogy is handing a nuclear bomb to anybody who can afford it. Jason maintains that qualified defenders also need powerful tools to strengthen their systems.
  • Arora separately rejects Jason’s theory that frontier labs cause the security problem by withholding their strongest defensive capabilities. He sees researchers struggling to package powerful systems under compute constraints; even his access to recent publicly available models remains rate-limited. Their commercial motive is more basic than a deliberate attack on cybersecurity incumbents: “They just need money, bro,” including money ultimately owed to Jensen.

7. Security spending and management incentives have to change together

  • Chamath explains why technical debt persists: engineers prefer the next product to maintenance, while privately deployed software drifts into many versions with different upgrade schedules. Arora adds the incentive problem: CIOs are rewarded for keeping costs low and systems available. Upgrades cost money, introduce downtime risk, and generate complaints, so the behavior that preserves today’s service can accumulate tomorrow’s security exposure.
  • Arora puts cybersecurity spending at roughly 4–10% of IT budgets. Cloud-oriented businesses can sit around 4–5% because hyperscalers handle infrastructure security; financial services and the federal government are nearer 8–10%. He says customer calls increasingly ask how to stop getting “punched in the face every morning.” Jason expects the transition to raise both security’s importance and its claim on scarce AI talent.
  • Beyond existing defenses, Arora says enterprises still need security systems for AI itself: discovering agents, inspecting their actions, and controlling information leakage. He cites a researcher finding that a shared Muse conversation could expose private information. Yet he also sees opportunity: as finance, HR, and marketing all seek AI expertise, “the CIOs could become the next CEOs.”
  • Asked how he would respond to Bernie Sanders demanding an AI stop, Arora answers, “Why don’t you start? I’m right behind you.” He argues AI’s builders have overemphasized alarming capabilities and created a “race to the bottom” in public messaging. Jason sees the political consequence: predictions of lost jobs and catastrophic risk give populists on both the left and right an attractive campaign issue.

8. France’s unrest is becoming a financing problem

  • Jason reports more than half a million participants, damage to over 3,000 businesses, more than 1,000 injured police, and 2,500 arrests. He describes protests originating in dilapidated schools before becoming broader unrest and looting, including destruction of Limoges’ 143-year-old city hall. His account also includes spillovers into Italy, Spain, and Albania, along with French curfews and conflicting government explanations of the violence.
  • The market figures sharpen the discussion: Jason says France’s 10-year yield exceeded 5%, its highest since 2002, while the US equivalent slipped below 5%. He cites a possible flight from European into US debt. Polymarket prices mentioned on the show imply an 18% chance of a French emergency declaration by year-end and 91% odds of a Moody’s or S&P downgrade by October 31.
  • Chamath condemns the violence as domestic terrorism and argues the government created a “tinderbox” by failing to confront it. Economically, France’s proposed €50 billion austerity package would need to grow, he says, making additional education investment harder even if school conditions were the central grievance. He predicts the government will lose the coming presidential election and face a complicated bureaucratic and economic reset.

9. The hosts disagree over what France’s social contract proves

  • Friedberg resists Jason’s comparison with BLM and January 6, which he sees as tied to more specific political events. France’s complaints seem broader: schools, healthcare, jobs, and Palestine. His diagnosis is a cycle in which citizens demand more state provision, services disappoint, and the disappointment creates demands for still more spending. “The more the government tries to provide to the people, the more the people are let down.”
  • Friedberg calculates US public spending at $12 trillion against $33 trillion of GDP, or roughly 36%, including $7.4 trillion federal and $4.6 trillion state/local spending. He puts both countries near 120% debt/GDP, with deficits of 5.4% in France and 6.2% in the US. Growth of roughly 0.5% versus 2.3%, he argues, explains why France could reach the fiscal cliff first.
  • Chamath’s challenge is that France and Italy already provide roughly free healthcare and education, yet still face unrest. Jason cites French university fees around €300 annually against approximately €12,000 in state cost. Friedberg disputes that low prices mean the problems are solved: weeks-long medical waits and classrooms of 60 students can leave people dissatisfied despite formally available services.
  • A later chart puts French tax revenue at 46% of GDP versus 22% for the US. Jason challenges its persuasiveness: many Americans want the healthcare and education associated with countries above the US on that list. Chamath rejects the claim that most want to live there; Friedberg argues the comparison must include employment and advancement alongside public services.

10. Proposed affordability reforms would redistribute gains and losses

  • On education, Friedberg would end the federal student-loan program while creating a way to discharge existing debt, potentially through bankruptcy. Chamath is “extremely sympathetic” to cancellation and says the debt should always have been dischargeable. Friedberg insists relief must accompany termination of new federal lending, otherwise the price-support mechanism remains. He expects institutions and tuition to adjust over roughly ten years.
  • On housing, Friedberg argues for changing housing loans that inflate home costs. David Sacks later makes the more specific proposal to reduce underwriting in the federal home-loan system, warning that this could cut middle-class net worth by 10–20%. His premise is that financing has supported existing homeowners’ asset values while excluding younger buyers. Maintaining those values preserves current owners’ solvency and sense of wealth, but broader access requires existing middle-class, upper-class, and wealthy owners to accept a hit.
  • Healthcare is Friedberg’s least complete proposal: “Healthcare’s the hardest.” He would put more responsibility on employers purchasing insurance, expecting competition to pressure prices and services. He names HIPAA and state/local housing regulation as barriers in their respective markets. These are multi-year changes in his framing, not immediate fixes; healthcare’s complexity remains explicit even as he argues for reducing government intervention.

11. Retirement reform would replace guarantees with ownership

  • Friedberg proposes making defined-benefit retirement programs, including Social Security, illegal and moving them into defined-contribution accounts over a decade. Each year, 10% of an individual’s promised amount would transfer into an IRA-like or Trump account, with investment allocations chosen according to age and preference. He acknowledges the objection: people lose guaranteed income. Jason points to Australian superannuation, and David Sacks adds Norway as an example.
  • Jason connects the ownership thesis to Elon Musk’s stated plan to give every American child one SpaceX share, then worth roughly $150–170, describing the gift as about $10 billion. He imagines wider participation by wealthy donors and separate accounts for education and retirement. The important feature in Jason’s argument is holding productive assets over time: “forcing people to hold onto it makes them part of capitalism.”

12. Immigration arguments split economic selection from cultural assimilation

  • Jason places much of the blame on immigration and failed integration, while also assigning responsibility to native French society for not integrating newcomers. In the subsequent exchange, a speaker cites annual immigration of 1.5% of the population and argues that inflows should be weighed against growth, employment, and needed skills. Another participant argues for selecting immigrants who can support themselves and share civic principles; the transcript’s speaker labels for these comments are unclear.
  • The latter speaker distinguishes shared civic values from cultural assimilation, naming women’s equality, individual rights, respect for others’ rights, and civil law taking precedence over religious authority. The discussion presents this as a proposed screening criterion, not a claim that ethnicity or first language should determine eligibility.
  • Jason says there were reports that Chinese and Jewish businesses were targeted while Muslim businesses were avoided. Friedberg presents an interview expressing resentment that Chinese immigrants had become prosperous. Jason—not Chamath—says the targeting reminded him of a “bottom-up” version of Kristallnacht. This is his interpretation of alleged ethnic targeting and envy, rather than an established explanation for all the unrest.
  • Friedberg’s most personal example comes from his family’s restaurant: his nurse mother made desserts to save money, and he and his brothers polished silverware and worked from childhood while the family remained financially stretched. That experience underlies his anger at small businesses being destroyed. Both he and Jason argue owners should be able to defend their property with firearms, invoking Korean shopkeepers during the LA riots.

13. Bond vigilantes offer a reset that Chamath also fears

  • Chamath argues bond investors can force a structural bargain by making French debt unfinanceable. When Friedberg asks whether 6–7% yields would suffice, Chamath answers, “I think you need to take France to, like, 8% and just break them.” His desired result is to put pensions, immigration, service quality, and other commitments on the negotiating table before the underlying social tensions compound further.
  • Yet Chamath also describes why forced resets fail: political actors accrue power, assign blame, and preserve influence rather than repair institutions. “In the middle of a reset, what happens is you just give away all your rights.” AI abundance might offer another route, but Jason doubts distressed French citizens would trust promises from Silicon Valley oligarchs. His admission remains unresolved: “I don’t see a reasonable endgame.”
  • David Sacks distinguishes violent social collapse from debt-driven economic restructuring, citing Argentina, Brazil, and Greece. The latter still entails protests, inflation, and lost wealth, but might avoid a deeper social breakdown. Sacks argues US leaders should reduce annual federal spending from roughly $7.5 trillion toward $4 trillion “in a way that doesn’t destroy the economy,” using deliberate reforms rather than waiting for a financing crisis.

14. AI-led growth and voter reassurance are different political tasks

  • Jason turns France’s discontent into a warning about US political communication ahead of November 3. Trump, he argues, should discuss housing as frequently as data centers and visibly address lower-paid workers alongside technology and large businesses. He credits the administration’s economic activity but says voters hear attention to crypto and infrastructure while their own housing, wages, and healthcare remain unresolved.
  • David Friedberg’s defense is that the AI buildout carries an outsized share of economic growth and benefits workers beyond the largest technology companies. He points to skilled-labor wages, investment in local communities, and pressure to build data centers behind the meter while lowering electricity costs. His categorical framing: “The US economy is entirely and completely levered to and correlated with the AI trade.”
  • Jason accepts the growth argument but maintains that its political transmission is weak. He wants explicit commitments to affordable housing and the bottom half of the income distribution, not reassurance that a “golden age” has arrived. The disagreement concerns whether the administration has connected those benefits convincingly to everyday life, alongside the substantive question of what additional policies workers need.

15. Minimum-wage disagreement survives agreement on helping workers

  • Jason proposes adding $1 annually to the federal minimum wage for seven years toward $15, a destination he dates to 2032. He estimates the change would reach roughly 10–15 million people and argues their extra income would be spent back into businesses. His case combines spending velocity with social cohesion: the president should visibly ask employers to do better for their lowest-paid workers.
  • Friedberg invokes California’s AB 1228 and its $20 fast-food wage, citing 18,000 lost jobs. He explains the mechanism through a consumer who can afford a $4 burger but not an $8 one: employers cannot indefinitely pay wages unsupported by customer demand. In his account, closures hurt both willing workers and consumers, and even smaller mandated increases can push marginal transactions beyond viability.
  • Jason rejects the comparison with an abrupt move to $20, says the California policy added about 25 cents per meal, and argues displaced workers found more productive jobs without changing the overall unemployment rate. He challenges Friedberg to reconcile that objection with their usual argument that automation releases labor for better work. Friedberg maintains that Jason is still trying to determine the market’s correct price.
  • David Sacks’s alternative is lower taxes, credits, and other incentives that increase disposable income without setting labor prices. Jason endorses a zero tax rate up to $150,000 and urges presidential support. That agreement does not settle the original dispute: Sacks says intervention has adverse consequences, while Jason closes by noting the country already has a minimum wage, so the question remains what its level should be.
