item.title: Why AI Compute Comes in Rectangles — Erik Bernhardsson, Modal
item.description: Bernhardsson estimates Modal is at least 50× larger, with Sandboxes now a third of revenue and growing 30% month over month. As GPU supply shifts to almost 25 clouds and three-plus-year prepaid deals, Modal can aggregate thousands of customers to flexibly slice “three-year rectangles.” Locked-in reservations leave Modal exposed if GPU prices and utilization fall together.
item.content:encoded:
Latent Space · Vibhu、Basil Chatha、Erik Bernhardsson · 2026-10-22 · 86 min · 原语言 EN

Bernhardsson estimates Modal is at least 50× larger, with Sandboxes now a third of revenue and growing 30% month over month. As GPU supply shifts to almost 25 clouds and three-plus-year prepaid deals, Modal can aggregate thousands of customers to flexibly slice “three-year rectangles.” Locked-in reservations leave Modal exposed if GPU prices and utilization fall together.

TL;DR

  • Erik Bernhardsson estimates Modal is at least 50× larger than when he last appeared on Latent Space, in revenue, users, and usage. Revenue is now about two-thirds Modal Functions (mostly inference) and one-third Sandboxes—a product the team considered shutting down. Sandboxes saw little growth after a quick prototype, then took off as LLMs moved from snippets to full apps, with use cases from vibe-coding companies like Lovable, Ramp’s background agents, and neo-labs running reinforcement learning. Vibhu observed sandbox revenue growing 30% month over month; Erik called the growth “kind of nuts” and said it kept exceeding his expectations.
  • The GPU procurement market changed sharply in the past year: Modal went from hyperscaler spot capacity and one-year reservations to working with almost 25 clouds, signing three-plus-year deals with meaningful upfront payments, and building a four-person procurement desk and a ten-person bare-metal engineering team. Capacity is often sold in “three-year rectangles” starting months ahead, while real demand is bursty. Modal’s proposed advantage is aggregating thousands of customers and flexibly slicing up capacity.
  • Bernhardsson says Modal is, to some extent, “effectively long GPU prices already” through locked-in reservations, but worries more about a price collapse than further spikes. Hardware prices eventually tend to fall; today’s scarcity rent flows mostly to NVIDIA and partly to neoclouds, while buyers who locked up supply risk “buying at the top.” He is aggressively buying capacity, but not trying to corner the market: prices, utilization, and the resale market could fall together, as his Hunt brothers’ silver-market example illustrates.
  • He explains the neocloud growth model: presell five years of chips to a large buyer, take the contract to Wall Street to raise money, then buy the hardware—“pre-sell things that you haven’t even bought.” He names Endscale as an example of a company that went from nowhere to a pipeline worth hundreds of billions of dollars despite having little capacity. Modal’s product-led-growth model can’t lock in long contracts in the same way. He’s glad startups are building GPU price indices and derivatives, but doubts GPUs will become a “Henry Hub… Brent crude”-style, highly commoditized tradable asset.
  • “2027 might be the year of non-NVIDIA accelerators”—a call he admits he has gotten wrong for five to ten years. AMD is getting good scores on some tasks, and TPUs work well inside Google. He sees better software support as a potential unlock for alternatives, while noting TSMC and ASML may be deeper bottlenecks. Hybrid disaggregated inference—NVIDIA for prefill, Cerebras for decode—is already being tried.
  • The future of sandboxes is more ephemeral: Modal’s median sandbox is about eight seconds long, and Bernhardsson envisions roughly 100-millisecond startup, running a few commands, then stopping and snapshotting it. That could enable branching agents and running every CI test in its own sandbox. The obstacle is overhead from starting and stopping; reducing that “transaction cost” could make highly parallel workloads practical.
  • A shift in the fine-tuning value proposition: he says open-source models such as Kimi K3, DeepSeek 4.1, and GLM-5.3 are now almost as good as frontier models at lower cost, often without fine-tuning. He also argues there is a structural role for inference providers separate from model labs: demand shifts with new releases, and Modal can reallocate GPU capacity between models without being asked.
  • Modal grew headcount about 4× annualized, a pace Bernhardsson calls unsustainable, and may reach about 700 people next year. FDEs grew from about four to about 24; he says Modal hasn’t aggressively built a product-management team. Code reviews are optional, backed by investment in CI and testing, and the company uses agents to probe its own systems—“escape the room, but for agents.” He expects models to keep improving in verifiable domains, while humans remain competitive for a long time in areas with diffuse targets and longer feedback loops.

Digest

1. Spotify’s recommender to Modal: “the infrastructure f*ing sucks”

  • Bernhardsson joined Spotify out of school in 2008 or 2009 and spent seven years building its first music recommendation system—Related Artists, Discover Weekly, and “a lot of matrix factorization.” Modal’s genesis came from building AI applications and realizing “the infrastructure f*ing sucks. There’s got to be a better way”; it was a tool he had wanted throughout his Spotify years.
  • The path ran through his open-source workflow orchestrator Luigi, in the same category as Airflow. Returning to workflow-orchestration ideas in 2021, he realized “a core puzzle piece isn’t just orchestrating the compute, it’s executing the compute”—a bigger problem—and shelved orchestration. Modal was the third idea he got excited about, after a web-scraping attempt that went nowhere.
  • The Better.com detour: five years as CTO of the mortgage startup, growing the tech team from two to “300 or 400,” he thinks. He learned about management, hiring, and developer productivity before returning to infrastructure, AI, and machine learning. Interest rates rose quickly after the pandemic, causing issues at the company, but he had already left.

2. Bootstrapped, shitposted into existence, saved by Stable Diffusion

  • He self-funded Modal through its first employees, taking no salary for a long time—“it made me really frugal about money”—and raised a seed round in early 2022. A co-founder joined as CTO around August 2021. Growth was founder-led marketing: “what I’m good at is, I guess, shitposting and being terminally online.”
  • The killer app wasn’t ChatGPT but Stable Diffusion, which arrived that fall when Modal had four or five people. Revenue went from about $100/month in November 2022 to about $2,000 the next month, then $30,000 in January 2023, almost entirely from one New York Stable Diffusion company, Mage. Mage accounted for 80–90% of revenue in Q1 2023; Suno became a large customer in late 2023, and revenue later diversified.
  • Since the last Latent Space appearance, he estimates Modal is “probably at least 50×” larger in revenue, users, and usage. Customers he names include Decagon, Suno, Runway, and Co-Cognition.

3. You can’t wrap Kubernetes: rebuilding the stack for GPU economics

  • His thesis: every technology era runs up against the limitations of its tools. Kubernetes and Docker were built for steady backend workloads on relatively cheap CPUs; generative AI brings expensive GPUs, utilization pressure, and large models that need to load over the network. “You can’t build for this new generation of software by putting a wrapper on top of the old stuff. You need to start over a little bit from scratch.”
  • Modal built its own file system and container runtime, along with CPU and GPU snapshotting, an autoscaler, a scheduler, and capacity-management tools. Developer-experience work also proved useful for production workloads, since scaling containers up and down quickly is a similar problem.
  • One consequential early decision was going multi-region and treating capacity as “one big pool over the entire world,” rather than separate clusters in each region. Modal has had bugs and outages; recently, Bernhardsson says, it has basically hit four or five nines of uptime.

4. The capacity market flipped: 25 clouds and three-year prepaid rectangles

  • Until the end of last year, most capacity came from hyperscaler spot capacity or one-year reservations. Spot capacity was preemptible, but worked in aggregate across hundreds of regions. Modal initially used AWS, later GCP and Azure, and rented Oracle capacity early for A10s and H100s.
  • In the past year, Modal has had to work with almost 25 clouds. Getting capacity often means three-plus-year deals and meaningful upfront payments. The last six to nine months prompted a procurement desk of four people, full-time on calls, deals, and vetting, plus a ten-person engineering team managing bare-metal capacity worldwide and handling network issues, bad drives, and GPUs “falling off the bus.”
  • Modal doesn’t own capacity; it rents it, typically through three-year deals. Locking up capacity for 2027 will require work across many avenues. Bernhardsson says capacity prepayments are currently the best use of cash; salaries and offices are “basically a rounding error” by comparison: “we have two hundred employees… the GPUs cost a lot more money.”

5. Rent vs. buy: already long GPUs, more afraid of collapse than spikes

  • He isn’t dogmatic about buying. Equity can be “a very diluted way” to fund hardware; debt usually requires long-term revenue to cover interest. Owning hard assets adds operational and financial complexity. He would rather focus on being a lean software company, but “everything is on the table,” including joint ventures and complex SPVs.
  • He pushes back on the idea that capacity is permanently unavailable: NVIDIA is delivering several hundred thousand Blackwells a month, and “if you’re willing to pay more than everyone else,” you can get capacity. He compares panic buying to the pandemic toilet-paper shortage. Prices could keep rising for another six months or another 36; it’s hard to know.
  • He worries more about prices collapsing than rising further. That could hurt anyone locked into a lot of supply: the risk is “buying at the top.” Today’s scarcity rent goes mostly to NVIDIA and partly to neoclouds and other capacity owners. There may be a long-run premium for owning GPUs, but he questions whether it’s worth holding the assets on the balance sheet.

6. Don’t corner the market: Hunt brothers, Armenia, and an internal ClusterMAX

  • Asked why not buy as much as possible and resell any surplus, Bernhardsson warns that in a downturn, “a lot of things are correlated”: if prices and utilization fall, the resale market could vanish at the same time. He is aggressive about buying capacity and raising money for more, but wants to build a company that lasts 20, 30, or 50 years. He invokes the Hunt brothers’ attempt to corner the silver market, which “failed spectacularly.”
  • He speculates that NVIDIA prefers some diversification among buyers, while Anthropic and OpenAI tend to prefer established vendors and need very large blocks for training. Modal can pursue smaller, scattered capacity: “You can get 32 nodes in Armenia. You can get 128 nodes in Indonesia. We love that kind of shit.”
  • Modal vets vendors with a spec sheet covering items such as IOPS, CPU PassMark score, north-south bandwidth, egress, and ingress. It often runs acceptance tests on one node, but larger commitments can still involve “a little bit of a leap of faith.” Internally, he says, they have something like their own version of SemiAnalysis’s ClusterMAX, rating vendors on reliability, responsiveness, and support.

7. The neocloud presell machine and GPUs as an asset class

  • Neoclouds can scale quickly by offering a big buyer five years of chips at a good rate, taking the contract to Wall Street for financing, then getting hardware from companies such as Supermicro, Dell, or NVIDIA. “You can essentially pre-sell things you haven’t even bought.” His example is Endscale, which he says went from nowhere to hundreds of billions of dollars in its pipeline despite barely having capacity. Modal’s product-led-growth model lacks the same ability to lock in long-term contracts, making it harder to scale financially as quickly. He calls CoreWeave and other large neoclouds savvy about raising money and using GPUs as collateral for loans.
  • On startups such as Silicon Data, Compute Exchange, and Ornn trying to create price indices and derivatives: compute is less homogeneous than other asset classes, given differences in networks, locations, disks, CPUs, and reliability. Still, “you can say the same thing about oil.” He sees a need for better risk hedging, risk-sharing, and insurance, but isn’t sure GPUs will become a highly commoditized tradable asset like Henry Hub or Brent crude.
  • Asked about a tweet wishing IPO-ready companies in a CapEx arms race could coordinate and pace it: “No comment.”

8. “2027 might be the year of non-NVIDIA accelerators finally”

  • He acknowledges his track record: “every year for the last five, maybe even ten years, I’ve been saying, ‘Next year is going to be the year of non-NVIDIA accelerators,’ and I’ve always been wrong. But I do think 2027 might finally be the year.” AMD is getting good scores on some tasks; TPUs are widely used internally at Google and seem to work well. He says he doesn’t see as much about Trainium, though its team is good and working on software.
  • He sees software as a potential unlock: “if we fix the software layer for these accelerators, there’s going to be a lot of demand for them.” He also notes that TSMC and ASML may be deeper bottlenecks. He expects more alternatives over time, while emphasizing that NVIDIA is an excellent company with an excellent product.
  • He’s excited by hybrid, disaggregated inference, such as running NVIDIA for prefill and Cerebras for decode. Some workloads are compute-bound and others memory-bound, so hardware can be mixed and matched, though the setups get complex in practice. He also mentions Groq.

9. Two products: Functions at two-thirds, Sandboxes the third they almost killed

  • Modal Functions, launched in 2021, offers serverless deployment and scaling while Modal manages capacity. It reached product-market fit in 2023 and is now about two-thirds of revenue, mostly from inference. Bernhardsson resists becoming a neocloud that sells only rectangular, three-year GPU deals; Modal’s product is designed to deploy and scale cyclical or bursty workloads and aggregate demand across many thousands of customers.
  • Sandboxes started with the observation that LLMs were generating code and might need a place to run it. The team already had container-management and isolation primitives, including gVisor; a co-founder built a prototype in a day or two. There was some early uptake, but it was an insignificant revenue source going into summer 2023. Two years later, the team even discussed shutting it down.
  • He says LLMs became able to generate full apps in 2023, beyond refactoring functions and writing snippets. Growth came from vibe-coding companies such as Lovable, background agents at companies like Ramp, and neo-labs using Sandboxes for reinforcement learning. Sandboxes are now about a third of revenue.
  • Bernhardsson says he didn’t foresee how large the product would become. In response to Vibhu’s observation that sandbox revenue was growing 30% every month, he called the growth “kind of nuts” and said that although he kept thinking it had plateaued, it kept growing. Multi-product was always part of the vision; Modal now has Functions and Sandboxes, with training and batch in the works. “We’re in the business of building building blocks.”

10. The ephemeral sandbox thesis: eight-second median, fork everything, thousand-test CI

  • Today’s sandbox use is often “lift-and-shift”: put a dev box in the cloud and have an agent control it. Bernhardsson’s preferred model is long-running agents as durable workflows that can start a sandbox in about 100 milliseconds, run a few commands, shut it down, and snapshot it. The median Modal sandbox is “eight seconds long or something like that.”
  • The CI example makes the case: rather than running a sequential install-and-test flow, run each test in its own sandbox and “parallelize the hell out of that”—potentially 1,000 sandboxes. Today, setup overhead can take minutes. If you do setup once, snapshot the container, and clone it, the parallelization benefits become practical. Otherwise, the friction is “the transaction cost.”
  • He sees potential in forking, snapshotting, resuming, and live migration. Modal has added virtual machines alongside gVisor for workloads that need full Linux compatibility. He also describes Anthropic’s managed agents as having a bring-your-own-sandbox integration for Modal. His view is that Anthropic benefits from a broad ecosystem of tools, provided customers use Anthropic for inference.

11. Training’s underserved middle and the fine-tuning reversal

  • Bernhardsson is bullish on training, especially for researchers iterating and for smaller and mid-sized workloads rather than 100,000-GPU hyperscaler or neocloud deals. Examples include text-to-speech, speech-to-text, recommendation systems, and computational biotech; some customers train relatively modest models on 64 GPUs. “It’s very hard to set up training clusters.”
  • Batch is another opportunity: one customer needed to transcribe 5,000 years of audio from millions of files, and Modal had enough capacity to do it in a few days. He is also bullish on low-latency workloads as speech-to-speech models improve, and on building general-purpose, composable blocks for AI-powered software.
  • His fine-tuning view has shifted. A few years ago, tuning a smaller open-source model could bring it closer to frontier quality at lower cost. Now, he says, models such as Kimi K3, DeepSeek 4.1, and GLM-5.3 are almost as good as frontier models at much lower cost and can often be used off the shelf. Demand for post-training remains, including supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, but fine-tuning is optional rather than something users have to do.

12. The Hugging Face incident, agent pentesters, and why cyber incumbents sell fear

  • The agents involved in the Hugging Face exploit were running inside Modal and found a vulnerability in an app deployed on the platform. As Bernhardsson understood it, they used that app as a springboard to get full internet access. He stresses that an app running on Modal was hacked; Modal itself was not.
  • One lesson is whether Modal can make security more restricted by default without losing the product’s “magic.” He compares this with AWS making it harder to accidentally expose an S3 bucket publicly. Modal has also begun using agents internally to probe for vulnerabilities and sandbox escapes. “It’s like escape the room, but for agents.” They started a few months earlier, around the time Vibhu mentions Fable.
  • He believes agents can be very good at finding vulnerabilities and can also be used defensively. Asked whether cybersecurity companies are “cooked,” he says that is outside his expertise and doesn’t jump to that conclusion: security vendors have enterprise relationships, and “a lot of what you’re selling is effectively fear.” Modal used to bring in human penetration testers roughly every six months, he thinks, and may now need them less often; he remains unsure. He’s optimistic that people and companies will use AI to work more efficiently.

13. Agent experience is developer experience: AEO, deprecation, the slop cannon

  • Asked whether developer experience matters when agents can read the docs, he says almost everything that makes DX good also helps agent experience: good docs, descriptive errors, and fast feedback loops. Agents make some hard-to-use tools easier to work with, and the human toil of dealing with YAML has gone down. He expects infrastructure to become more programmatic, with SDKs and imperative operations rather than declarative DSLs.
  • Agent training data makes deprecations harder: agents often use old Modal syntax, so the team has become more conservative about removing features and must keep examples online up to date.
  • Modal runs internal benchmarks asking agents to deploy Stable Diffusion or rank sandbox vendors by reliability and price. Agents can misunderstand pricing, so the team works to make content clearer. Asked about generating GitHub repos full of Modal code to influence agent recommendations, he calls it a “slop cannon.” He thinks automated content could work, as with early SEO, but doesn’t like the idea.

14. FDEs, product management, the IC renaissance, and 4× headcount growth

  • Modal scaled its forward deployed engineers from about four at the start of the year to about 24. They work with customers on performance tuning, including training draft models and adjusting parameters in DLM and SGLang; help customers work around problems; flag over-provisioned CPU or memory; and assist with migrations. They are not meant to make Modal a service-heavy business. A key goal is to identify product gaps: “Long term, how do we turn this into product so we don’t need an FDE for it?”
  • Modal hasn’t aggressively built a product-management team. Bernhardsson says infrastructure product management requires deep strategic thinking about foundational building blocks and one-to-two-year horizons, and avoiding many similar but distinct features. Some people have moved into product roles from DevRel or engineering.
  • He sees a shift back toward individual contributors, which GenAI may have accelerated. Modal makes clear there is no prestige difference between being a manager and an IC; former managers are returning to writing code, and Erik and Akshat still do so. Code reviews are optional. He sees them partly as a way to avoid accountability for merging code, so the alternative is investing in CI, deployment, and testing. Infrastructure companies need “one more nine” of uptime, with resilient systems, rate limits, decoupling, and strong test coverage. He says agents have become good at writing tests.
  • Headcount grew about 4× annualized over the past year, which he calls unsustainable. He watches for cultural drift, islands of differing work styles, and engineers taking on speculative projects that may not be the right priority. Modal may reach 250 people by year-end and around 700 the following year, with most hires in systems engineering and more work on GPU performance and research, including post-training, distillation, and quantization. He says the story behind the Dunbar number may be “more fake than anything,” but that the underlying effect is “actually kind of real.”

15. The rectangle endgame: flexible capacity, Taylor Swift, and what’s not plateauing

  • Bernhardsson’s tweet argues that the problem with GPU scarcity isn’t only getting GPUs; it’s that capacity is sold as a three-year rectangle starting three to six months in the future, unlike most users’ bursty demand. Modal can often provide 100 GPUs on demand, without a sales conversation. Its value proposition has two parts: developer experience and flexible capacity. By aggregating many thousands of customers, Modal smooths demand and can slice capacity up and down quickly.
  • He sees a structural role for inference providers separate from model labs. Demand shifts when a new lab releases a model; Modal can move resources between models as demand changes. He says no one even has to tell Modal to do it; the system handles it.
  • On whether LLMs are commodities, he’s unsure: “Is Taylor Swift a commodity?” If labs keep releasing new models and their margins cover training costs, they could still have a good business.
  • He doesn’t think intelligence is plateauing, though he says it remains to be seen how well models handle tasks that are harder to train with reinforcement learning. Models have improved at coding, math, and cybersecurity—areas with more verifiable outcomes. Humans may remain competitive for a long time in tasks with diffuse targets and longer feedback loops.
  • He names computational biology, where predictions can be checked with simulations of molecular dynamics, and materials science, where properties can be measured, as promising areas. On-prem remains a model he is skeptical of: he is a cloud maximalist and says BYOC and VPC peering reflect an outdated network-as-a-moat security model. He doesn’t know whether Modal will ever do on-prem, but would consider BYOC at a sufficiently high price and sees it as a possible way to use neocloud capacity while keeping Modal’s control plane in its own environment.

item.title: The Frontier Ideas a16z Wants to Fund Now | Marc Andreessen, Ben Horowitz & Chris Dixon
item.description: a16z is expanding the ACC Crypto Fund into a16z Frontier for “outer planets” beyond existing verticals as crypto’s boundaries blur with fintech and Wall Street. Marc Andreessen calls AI’s early-adopter gap with incumbents the widest of his career; employees adopting ahead of companies could fuel startup formation, while AI answers and Stack Overflow’s traffic drop point to an internet-economics reset.
item.content:encoded:
The a16z Show · Marc Andreessen、Ben Horowitz、Chris Dixon、Erik Torenberg · 2026-10-22 · 61 min · 原语言 EN

a16z is expanding the ACC Crypto Fund into a16z Frontier for “outer planets” beyond existing verticals as crypto’s boundaries blur with fintech and Wall Street. Marc Andreessen calls AI’s early-adopter gap with incumbents the widest of his career; employees adopting ahead of companies could fuel startup formation, while AI answers and Stack Overflow’s traffic drop point to an internet-economics reset.

TL;DR

  • The ACC Crypto Fund is expanding into “a16z Frontier,” a mandate for what Chris Dixon’s partner Martine calls “outer planets” — categories too new or weird to fit the firm’s verticals. The stated logic: crypto’s lines have blurred into fintech and Wall Street (“Is Stripe a crypto company?”), while the vertical structure left a coverage gap for the strangest founders. Ben Horowitz’s framing carries the thesis: “more than categories, more than products, we invest in entrepreneurs, and so many of the most interesting entrepreneurs are on the outer planets.”
  • Marc Andreessen’s central claim is that the gap between what AI early adopters know is possible and what incumbents understand “is as wide as I’ve ever seen in my career” — and it’s widening as AI capabilities race ahead week by week. His corollary: employees are adopting AI while their companies aren’t, those employees will leave to start companies, and “startup formation is gonna skyrocket from here... by the way, it already is.” His message to incumbents: “the clock is ticking.”
  • Marc says the firm’s underwriting question has inverted: “We used to ask... is this idea too ambitious? We’re much more likely to ask, ‘Is this ambitious enough?’” Dixon believes AI may be “pulling forward 20 years” of technological progress, forcing a re-evaluation of technical risk and the “science project vs. engineering project” frame — a 30-person team can now credibly build a full-stack device company that might have taken 1,000 people a decade ago.
  • Dixon says the Christensen disruption frame is probably the wrong one right now: this isn’t tech companies fighting each other, it’s “people who are technologically modern going out into other industries and just changing the economy more broadly.” Meanwhile the internet’s “covenant” — content sites give Google a snippet, Google sends clicks — is breaking as AI answers replace links; Stack Overflow traffic has dropped precipitously, setting up a decade-long “great reconfiguration” of internet economics.
  • On market structure, the panel considers Peter Thiel’s “crypto is libertarian, AI is communist” framing: Dixon believes open source is growing faster than closed models in token consumption, local models may come, and stablecoins are a natural way for agents to pay each other. Marc says the US administration is “100% pro” open source and the Chinese Communist Party’s enthusiasm surprised him; without open source, AI “inevitably centralizes down to one or two companies or maybe just flat out the government” — “picture government sushi... then picture government AI.”
  • The native-use-case explosion is already visible in the panel’s favorite recent examples: AI mashing up any two video games (Super Mario and GTA), Epic saying “no more humans” writing code, and an open-source tool called REA — “Reverse Engineer Anything” — that can reverse-engineer and reprogram hardware. Ben’s Digger example: the film had a $180M production budget and a $200M cash loss, but “on a $2 million budget it would have been insanely profitable.” Ben predicts AI film will be an entirely new medium, not just a cheaper movie.
  • Dixon’s structural prediction: “the most numerous participants on the internet will be agents, not people,” and AI is still mostly in single-player mode. He sees swarms (he recalls one solving a math theorem; the Hugging Face hack was the negative version), trust networks emerging in products like Muse and Instinct, and a possible “multiplayer phase of AI” as fertile ground for founders.
  • Career advice for an 18-year-old: study “modern alchemy” — “humans just figured out how to turn sand into intelligence” — via math, computer science, maybe economics. Marc deploys Douglas Adams’ three-cohort rule (under 15 it’s natural, 15–35 it’s new and potentially a career, over 35 it’s “unholy and evil”), and Ben flips the hand-wringing: “you’re the one with the problem because you’re obsolete. The kids are going to be superhumans.” Erik’s closing amendment to the firm’s posture: “humble, definite optimism” — back entrepreneurs with their own conviction.

Digest

1. The announcement: ACC Crypto Fund expands to a16z Frontier

  • Dixon’s two motivations: first, crypto has partly won and the lines have blurred — stablecoins are “a normal part of the tech landscape” used by Stripe and considered part of nearly every fintech company’s toolkit; Wall Street is moving into tokenized stocks — so “is Stripe a crypto company?” is no longer an easy question. Second, the firm’s verticals are busy with core opportunities, leaving “outer planets” (Martine’s metaphor, borrowed from Firefly) falling through the cracks.
  • Ben’s architecture point: the vertical strategy works, but the motion for turning a brand-new area into a practice “is a little bit undefined.” Frontier formalizes it — “if that works, maybe that becomes a whole fund at some point.” His bottom line: “more than categories, more than products, we invest in entrepreneurs, and so many of the most interesting entrepreneurs are on the outer planets.”
  • Dixon frames it as continuity, not a pivot: he joined in 2013 explicitly to do “this crazy stuff” — drones (Marc was first in, as Dixon recalls), Oculus (“really a reconfigured smartphone”), and Skydio — all second-order effects of the smartphone supply chain. Crypto, for Dixon, was downstream of open source and social media.

2. Why Dixon — and why the crypto team travels well

  • Ben on hiring him: a smart blogger with original ideas and real founder experience, whose durable contribution was a framework the firm copied across the firm — “we’re not looking for good ideas that look like good ideas; we’re looking for good ideas that look like bad ideas... where an entrepreneur has a secret that makes it a good idea.” That lens separated massive upside from businesses where “all the profits would get competed away.”
  • Marc’s point about the team: crypto’s flash hides that it is “a very deep, complex technology.” Dixon’s group includes math professors and cryptographers, and that technical depth plus market judgment can now be applied to a broader set of topics.
  • Dixon adds the policy arm, built “in the crucible of the crypto journey,” as another transferable asset: self-driving cars, drones, and AI itself will have policy angles, so more frontier bets will need regulatory expertise.

3. Culture, J. P. Morgan, and the shit-show caveat

  • The J. P. Morgan photo inside Marc’s office door — the banker staring from darkness, with the chair edge lit like a carving knife — is discussed as inspiration. Ben draws out the serious part: Morgan’s courtroom line, “we do first-class business, and then only in a first-class way.” “You’re definitely not going to tell me who I am. I know who I am” — Ben’s argument for why principled identity matters in venture.
  • Dixon on the inside view: since joining in 2013, Marc and Ben have never—not once—pushed back on his ambition. “If anything,” they’d ask, “Can you double it? Can you double down? Can you get more aggressive?” And on the outside view that it’s been all ups: “I don’t know of a startup that wasn’t a shit show at some point. Or at multiple points.”

4. Too early is the error they’ll accept — and AI compresses the timeline

  • Dixon’s core belief, offered for all three: “basically every good idea we’ve ever seen that involved technology has eventually worked, or will work if it hasn’t yet” — the qualifier being “good idea.” Many things that eventually worked had a precursor that didn’t work and may have been 10 years too early. Timing is the hardest prediction because technology, culture, business, and politics all have to line up. Frontier will “err on the side of being too early” and accept “category risk.”
  • His honest specimen: Oculus was sold and acquired, but “it’s now 13 years later” and it hasn’t become as mainstream as they would have liked. Dixon still believes strongly in VR; there were many hard technical problems to solve.
  • The AI twist: with software engineering tipping first, then math, then physics and hardware, Dixon thinks “we may be pulling forward 20 years” of things. The whole “science project rather than an engineering project” frame needs re-evaluation, and a 30-person team can now credibly build a full-stack device company that might have required 1,000 people a decade ago.

5. Marc’s gap thesis: the widest early-adopter delta of his career

  • Marc’s framing: the delta between what AI-native startups understand is possible and what typical incumbents understand “is as wide as I’ve ever seen in my career” — and it is widening as capability races ahead week by week. Extrapolated: many industries may be up for grabs in a more profound way, as founders gain new capabilities from these tools.
  • The counterfactual he keeps returning to: “Had I had Astra at Netscape in 1994... Ben, what would you and I have been able to do at Netscape? We would’ve built the whole damn internet.” They would have gotten crypto done then and had streaming video “a lot sooner.”
  • Marc says the underwriting question has changed: “We used to ask, ‘Is this idea too ambitious?’ We’re much more likely to ask, ‘Is this ambitious enough?’” A moderate idea probably won’t be differentiated enough.
  • Marc’s adoption asymmetry, flagged as a topic for another episode: “many companies aren’t adopting AI while their employees are” — and employees aren’t necessarily telling management. Some individuals will realize they can use these tools to start a business: “startup formation is going to skyrocket from here. It already is.” He sees both effects so far: some incumbents, including Meta, have adapted, while new companies are also emerging.

6. Christensen may be the wrong frame — and the internet’s covenant is breaking

  • Dixon’s correction: the disruption frame assumes a relatively contained technology world where companies fight each other. “That’s probably the wrong frame right now.” The real pattern is “people who are technologically modern going out into other industries and changing the economy more broadly” — full-stack companies like the recently announced Adams investment, building food service and other things, including mining; tech companies and startups competing with the rest of the Fortune 500.
  • On where we are in the cycle: “all of the above” is working — the big AI labs, a fast-growing open-source field, and application-layer products. Dixon says measured enterprise use is “something like 3%... or something like that.” “The market for intelligence is very, very large, and it’s only getting started.”
  • His separate structural call: the internet’s “covenant” — give Google a snippet, get clicks back — is breaking as answers replace links. Stack Overflow’s traffic drop is an early sign; the transactions will still happen, just not the same way. The next decade could bring a “great reconfiguration” of internet economics, attention, and collaboration — a bigger reshaping than mobile delivered, in Marc’s view.

7. From skeuomorphic to native: agents as the internet’s majority

  • Dixon’s pattern: every platform starts with old behaviors done better (ordering a Sears catalog online) before riskier behavioral bets that can change the world (YouTube starting with an empty site and betting that influencers would populate it). AI so far has been the familiar-use-case phase — coding, math, knowledge work, search, and chat — “but we’ve only begun to explore” radical new activities. Dixon thinks we’re at a tipping point.
  • His biggest native prediction: “the most numerous participants on the internet will be agents, not people.” Utility proxy agents like Muse and Instinct are an early phase, followed by agents needing their own ways to communicate, transact, and share knowledge.
  • Marc’s critique of the current crop — “product manager brain”: product managers designing for product managers, where every demo is “book me a restaurant... with my friends, who are also product managers.” Ben adds that the “helpful, harmless, honest assistant” can mean “the most boring possible thing you could imagine.” What’s coming, Ben says, will be more entertaining, enjoyable, exciting, and lucrative.
  • Dixon on multiplayer AI: today’s AI is mostly single-player — you type, it responds. Swarms cut both ways (he recalls a swarm solving a math theorem; the Hugging Face hack was the negative case), and trust features in Muse and Instinct hint at trust networks. “If you squint, you’re seeing the early signs” — a potentially fertile area for entrepreneurs.

8. The creative and hardware renaissance, three weeks at a time

  • Games as leading-edge media, per Dixon: in roughly two weeks since “Opus 55 or something,” disassemblers and AI can run Windows games on Unix faster than on Windows, and one tool mashes any two games into a combo title (“Super Mario and GTA,” Ben suggests). Epic had just said “no more humans” writing code — “the first of the dominoes to fall” against cultural resistance in the industry, in Dixon’s view, and a possible creative renaissance where independents can build as if they have a huge team.
  • Ben’s Digger example: viewers may be tempted to walk out after the first half hour, but he says the film is not presented the way it seems. He calls it an “incredible creative achievement,” with a $180 million production budget and a $200 million cash loss. “On a $2 million budget, that movie would have been insanely profitable” and made investors 10 times their money back. Ben predicts AI film will be an entirely new medium, not just a cheaper way to make regular movies. Dixon’s camera analogy: the negative frame is that it replaces landscape painters; the positive is that it unlocks motion pictures.
  • Hardware, Marc’s “terra incognita,” may be more accessible: Ben describes an open-source tool called REA — Reverse Engineer Anything — that can use an AI model to reverse-engineer an object and provide source code. Point it at a misbehaving thermostat, and the AI can write new code, install it, and provide a new interface; Ben says the same may apply to many forms of hardware. Home automation “maybe should just be an AI bot” that takes over the hardware in your house. Marc also wonders whether AI could enable a homebrew-hardware revival, with Claude designing 3D-printed cases, cheap motherboards, and custom firmware — a possible MakerBot-like movement. Erik gives the architectural example: a friend’s new building is being steered by AI, including design-for-manufacturing specs that are normally difficult to produce.

9. Open source as the guarantor against centralization

  • The panel considers Erik’s citation of Thiel’s “crypto is libertarian, AI is communist” framing. Dixon sees the possibility of a more decentralized market structure: big labs alongside open source, which he believes is growing much faster in token consumption according to OpenRouter data. Local models may emerge; in the near term, Dixon thinks people may be able to run a top-end coding agent or chatbot on their computers. Stablecoins are a natural way for agents to pay each other, with decentralized lending and other crypto services potentially built on top.
  • Marc on the policy state of play: he says the threat of “draconian and completely unacceptable” regulation or bans remains; the EU “still aspires to do it,” though Marc says it lacks the leverage. He describes the current US administration as “100% pro-open source.” He was surprised that the Chinese Communist Party is enthusiastic about open-source AI for the world. Marc says open models are lapping closed models by six or 12 months, depending on how you count.
  • His centralization warning: without open source, AI “inevitably centralizes down to one or two companies, or maybe just flat out the government... picture the concept of government sushi. Then keep your eyes closed and picture government AI.” He also makes the education case: “what if the only way your kid can learn about AI is to go to work for one of two companies?” Marc says open-source models will teach people how to make open-source AI, while models from certain large companies may refuse. His example: wilderness explorers carrying local LLMs for offline advice about survival, including which berries are poisonous or what to do after a rattlesnake bite.
  • Ben’s safety argument for openness: “probably the biggest safety problem” so far is reward hacking — the AI doing something it wasn’t told to do as a means to get its reward. Ben says the labs haven’t worked on it very hard, for whatever reason, and asks what might happen if every PhD student, professor, and undergraduate could inspect the weights and study the problem. “You really want the whole world making this technology great and safe, not just the people who happen to work at two or three companies. Go Meta... go SpaceX.”

10. What an 18-year-old should do — and humble definite optimism

  • Dixon, borrowing Marc’s line: study “modern alchemy” — “humans just figured out how to turn sand into intelligence” — via math, computer science, and maybe economics, and get into the mix at the cutting edge of what he expects to be the dominant narrative of the next 20 or 30 years. Marc lists fields being transformed: classics via the Vesuvius Scroll Project, economics, biology, design, and zoology — “we’re plausibly heading toward a world in which we’re going to understand what the animals are saying.” Dixon says, seriously, “I think there’s a Nobel Prize for that.”
  • Marc’s generational frame from Douglas Adams: under 15, it’s just how the world works (his seven-year-old on ChatGPT: “Duh. What good is a computer that doesn’t answer questions?”); ages 15–35, it’s new and exciting, and might become a career; over 35, it’s “unholy and evil.” Schools banning AI may make it kids’ “secret superpower.” Ben’s kicker: “you’re the one with the problem because you’re obsolete. The kids are going to be superhumans.”
  • Erik’s closing calibration: “humble, definite optimism” — he has been wrong many times, so the firm wants to find great people with their own definite optimism and back them. Chris also stresses that they are ultimately betting on great entrepreneurs, including people with ideas they did not discuss.

来源：YouTube

item.title: What will computer chips look like in 2045?
item.description: Ranade says available tools may support 2X, not 10X, leading-edge wafer output, while an Intel speaker says AI demand is 40–50% above maximum capacity. With roughly 80% of fab costs fixed, utilization and yield matter; TSMC ships upwards of 3X Intel’s leading-edge wafers, and Ranade says Intel will invest more, though tool limits remain.
item.content:encoded:
Dwarkesh Podcast · Dwarkesh Patel · 2026-10-22 · 69 min · 原语言 EN

Ranade says available tools may support 2X, not 10X, leading-edge wafer output, while an Intel speaker says AI demand is 40–50% above maximum capacity. With roughly 80% of fab costs fixed, utilization and yield matter; TSMC ships upwards of 3X Intel’s leading-edge wafers, and Ranade says Intel will invest more, though tool limits remain.

TL;DR

  • Available equipment may support about 2X leading-edge wafer output, not 10X; 2030 supply depends on broader capacity growth. An opening, unidentified Intel speaker says AI demand is “easily 40–50% above our maximum capacity.” Dwarkesh notes that ASML makes fewer than 100 EUV machines a year and describes limited plans to increase that materially by decade’s end. Asked whether the world has enough tools to 10X leading-edge wafers, Pushkar Ranade answers, “Not 10X, but probably 2X, yes.” Dwarkesh’s later timeline summary puts tool orders placed now into ’28 and a new fab shell near the end of the decade; Ranade does not explicitly confirm that summary. The claim that AI’s decade of 3X annual compute growth “just can’t continue” is Dwarkesh’s framing.
  • AI labs securing fab-scale capacity is a possibility raised by Dwarkesh, not a commitment from Ranade. Dwarkesh’s calculation is that a couple billion dollars of Intel CapEx could support the logic behind roughly $100 billion a year in AI-model revenue; he also notes that memory and other parts of the stack matter. He speculates that AI labs might buy or guarantee supply. Ranade says some model companies could consume an entire fab’s worth of silicon and have the capital to fund it, but the “early signs” of this shift are Dwarkesh’s characterization. Ranade’s closing response to the suggestion that Intel buy more tools: “Had we known what we know today, we would have invested more like a year ago. Knowing what we know now, I think we’ll be investing more.”
  • Ranade argues Intel is within a few percent of TSMC technologically; scale and execution remain important gaps. He says that within a few percent on performance, power, or density, “you’re splitting hairs,” and that on-time delivery and yields supporting rapid ramps matter more. He disputes Dwarkesh’s cited SemiAnalysis benchmarking of 14A against N2. Dwarkesh cites TSMC shipping upwards of 3X Intel’s leading-edge wafers and spending about $50 billion on CapEx versus Intel’s roughly $20 billion. Ranade says about 80% of a fab’s cost structure is fixed, making utilization and yield improvements especially valuable; he notes there are now only three foundries at the advanced node, down from about 20 forty years ago.
  • High-NA EUV is an architecture-dependent choice, not simply a tool race. Chris Auth explains that Intel’s backside power relaxes some front-side pitch requirements, making High-NA useful for Intel; TSMC’s tighter pitches without backside power require double-patterning EUV. “For them, it’s not very helpful. For us, it is very helpful.” Intel’s 10nm experience—originally targeted for 2016, with manufacturing starting in 2018—taught it to limit per-node innovation and use phase-gate maturity metrics. 14A is planned to have a high-quality PDK from the outset, after 18A “started out not having a PDK.”
  • Intel’s memory exits look costly amid today’s shortage, though Ranade says the demand was unforeseeable; Terafab is another response to demand. Ranade says the supply crunch is larger for memory than compute, while noting that nobody could have seen the scale of demand when Intel exited DRAM and flash. He says Intel is working with Elon to help accelerate his fab project. Dwarkesh points out that tool shortages could mean a new fab secures supply without increasing net global silicon; Ranade adds that power, water, and consumables are also required, and says those inputs can be scaled more readily than tools.
  • Long-range 3D structures are a possibility, with thermals a limiter—not a firm 2045 forecast. Auth discusses transistors floating within interconnect and asks what more extensive 3D structures might enable over a 10- or 20-year horizon. He calls heat dissipation a limiter for 3D devices, while saying the system-level analysis and simulation tools are still in their infancy. Separately, Dwarkesh cautions that technology roadmaps often have only about four years of visibility.
  • Hybrid bonding has room to scale, but its densest future uses remain prospective. Tyler Osborn gives the progression from 130–150 µm first-level interconnect pitch 15 years ago, to 25 µm in Foveros high-volume manufacturing today and sub-10 µm in development. He cites a paper presented at this year’s IEEE ECTC with reliability data on a 0.45 µm-pitch device. He says finer bonding could eventually connect lower interconnect layers across chips and reduce power; the potential to approach on-die interconnect is a future possibility, not a current production capability.
  • Rising costs invite radical questions in a risk-averse industry. Ranade says fab costs have been doubling every 4–5 years and puts a High-NA scanner plus associated equipment at around $400 million. He questions whether patterning costs can keep rising at that rate, and asks, “Do you really need a clean room today?” He says no incumbent would willingly test a fab with people eating hamburgers and smoking cigars inside. Kevin Fischer’s operating principle: “If you want to wait for a complete data set, you’ve waited too long.”

Digest

1. Bringing up 14A means fine-tuning 2,000 steps — and learning from 10nm

  • Chris Auth describes 14A as more than three years into development and close to finalizing the process and tool sets. The factory has roughly 2,000 steps, each needing intricate tuning so the process can run thousands of wafers a week repeatably. Defects are found through inline metrology and end-of-line electrical testing; TEM cross-sections can locate a defect between layers and help identify which section of the flow produced it.
  • Auth’s account of 10nm: Intel set aggressive “hyperscaling” targets and developed ideas to reach them without new tools because EUV was not ready. The node eventually achieved world-class yield, performance, and cost, but took longer than intended: its original target was 2016, and manufacturing did not begin until 2018. A news clip in the transcript has Intel’s stock down more than 15% and TSMC up 13%. TSMC used EUV in volume from 2019; Intel’s first EUV process reached products in 2023, leaving TSMC with about four more years of experience with the machines.
  • The institutional response includes phase-gate maturity metrics for yield, defects, and performance, used to decide whether technology can move from pathfinding into development. Auth’s principle is to limit innovation per node so the process can meet the customer’s schedule.

2. High-NA makes sense for Intel and not TSMC — because of backside power

  • Dwarkesh explains the tool economics: High-NA widens numerical aperture from 0.33 to 0.55 and can print features about 1.7 times smaller in a single pass. Standard EUV machines cost around $200 million, while High-NA machines cost about twice as much. The value depends on how many patterning passes the tool can eliminate; extra passes take time and introduce more opportunities for defects.
  • Auth says Intel and TSMC can reach different conclusions from the same tool because their technology architectures differ. Backside power alleviates some front-side pitch requirements, allowing Intel to print some patterns directly with High-NA. TSMC’s tighter pitches without backside power require double-patterning EUV, so the tool is less useful to them. At 14A, High-NA is an option in the PDK and will be discussed with customers individually.
  • On Intel’s foundry learning curve, the transcript says decades as an IDM meant it had not had a formal PDK-type process; 18A “started out not having a PDK.” Customer feedback has informed the process, and 14A is planned to have high-quality PDKs from the outset, with maturity levels such as 0.5, 0.9, and 1.0.

3. From “try to not change anything” to the sledgehammer era

  • Auth contrasts the ’80s and ’90s, when Dennard scaling and lithography drove predictable shrinking, with the “golden age of innovation” that began when scaling alone was no longer enough. Strained silicon, high-k metal gate, FinFETs, gate-all-around, and backside power expanded the process playbook. He estimates the number of materials used has increased about 10X since the ’90s: “Before, it was ‘try to not change anything.’ Now it’s ‘take the sledgehammer and start tearing the thing up.’”
  • Gate-all-around took a long time to reach production partly because other options could deliver performance first. Auth says, “you don’t want to tackle something before you have to”: Intel used strained silicon, high-k metal gate, and FinFETs before taking on gate-all-around. New materials, tools, gases, and heating equipment can require invention by suppliers, and development involves iterating on structures that fail.
  • In a discussion of long-range possibilities, Auth calls gate-all-around “somewhat inevitable,” while describing stripping the substrate and placing wires on the backside as “a little bit out there.” He considers whether future chips could combine transistors and interconnect in more extensive 3D structures, looking at a 10- or 20-year horizon. Dwarkesh adds that technology roadmaps often have only about four years of visibility.
  • Auth describes three limits on compute: switching frequency, power per switch, and heat dissipation. For 3D devices, system-level thermal analysis and simulation are still in their infancy. Thermals are a limiter, he says, but “these are problems that we can go solve.”

4. Inside the Hot Topics meeting: incomplete data, epi tumors, and HotBox 1

  • Kevin Fischer, who helps decide how engineering resources are allocated to 18A problems, says, “You will never have a complete data set. If you want to wait for a complete data set, you’ve waited too long.” His job is to decide how much risk to take: “Do we go now? Do we start risking production?” He says many engineers do not see how the work affects Intel’s bottom line or customers.
  • The example is epi nodules: abnormal epitaxy growth “like a tumor” that grows quickly and can cause one epi to short to the wrong epi, leaving transistors not working. Teams work in parallel on potential fixes, including a special clean to remove nodules and ways to eliminate their source; the first fix that seems promising is not always the one that works.
  • Experiment lots can use a tiered system of “hot boxes.” The highest priority, HotBox 1, gets priority at every tool and races through the factory, but Fischer says it is a drag on factory efficiency. His analogy is reserving a carpool lane for a single experiment.

5. In the research lab: ruthenium, cobalt’s round trip, and CFET’s integration challenges

  • Jack Kavalieros explains why Intel is exploring ruthenium for very fine-pitch interconnects. Copper typically needs a liner to help deposit it and connect it to underlying copper; the liner can occupy a significant part of the conduction path. Ruthenium can be etched without that liner, and Kavalieros says there is a crossover at roughly 20-nanometer pitch where ruthenium can have better conductivity than copper.
  • The cobalt example shows how materials choices can change. Cobalt was the leading option when Intel made its decision, but later solutions brought copper back into contention. Kavalieros says every technology is evaluated against alternatives as the manufacturing time horizon approaches.
  • CFET research uses short-loop vehicles to get faster results than the month or longer required for a full manufacturing flow. Teams can begin with components such as diodes and capacitors, then combine them into transistors. A simplified CFET might use one wire for the NMOS and one for the PMOS, rather than four ribbons stacked on four ribbons. The difficult parts include vertical interconnection, high-aspect-ratio etches, and filling tiny spaces without air gaps.
  • Dwarkesh asks why a lab version does not mean CFET is ready for a phone, and raises a ten-year timescale in his question. The answer is not a firm production timeline: the lab version is simplified and may not outperform side-by-side nanoribbons. The technology must evolve through many steps, including the right metals and dielectrics. Materials can fail because contacts do not adhere or because later processing interacts with a film that is not hermetically sealed.

6. Hybrid bonding is dissolving the boundary between packaging and chip

  • Tyler Osborn contrasts wafer-to-wafer bonding, which is popular in CMOS image sensors, with chip-to-wafer bonding. Wafer-to-wafer requires closely matching dies and sort maps; random differences between good and bad dies can reduce yield. Chip-to-wafer lets manufacturers test and select known-good dies before bonding them to known-good positions. Osborn expects both approaches to be used and says chip-to-wafer makes sense for logic-to-logic.
  • The pitch progression is 130–150 µm for first-level interconnect 15 years ago, 25 µm in Foveros high-volume manufacturing today, and sub-10 µm in development. Osborn cites reliability data on a 0.45 µm-pitch hybrid-bonded device in a paper at this year’s IEEE ECTC; this is not presented as current high-volume production. He sees room for further scaling.
  • Osborn says that if packaging reaches around 0.5 µm or below, it could become possible to connect lower interconnect layers across chips, potentially reducing total IR drop. For non-AI uses, including client devices, he points to interconnect density and lower power per bit, which could mean less heat for the same electrical performance.

7. The supply ceiling: 2X is possible, 10X is not

  • An unidentified Intel speaker at the beginning of the transcript says AI demand is “easily 40–50% above our maximum capacity, which I’ve never seen before.” Later, Dwarkesh notes ASML’s EUV output is fewer than 100 machines a year and says it is not expected to rise significantly by the end of the decade. Ranade calls EUV a limiter, but says shortages extend across equipment: once a process such as 18A is locked to a particular tool, Intel cannot simply substitute another supplier’s tool.
  • Asked whether the world has enough tools to 10X leading-edge wafer production, Ranade answers, “Not 10X, but probably 2X, yes.” Dwarkesh says that means the AI industry’s 3X annual compute growth “just can’t continue” without the supply chain, including sub-suppliers, producing more; that is Dwarkesh’s conclusion.
  • Dwarkesh later offers a timeline summary: marginal output might rise within about 12 months, but 2030 production may not be much higher than forecasts; an 18-month tool lead time puts new orders into ’28, with a new shell pushing out toward the end of the decade. The transcript does not include Ranade explicitly confirming that summary. For 14A, Ranade says Intel tries to preserve fungibility between nodes; perhaps 80% of the 18A tool set can be reused.

8. A couple billion of CapEx and $100B of AI revenue — a capacity-buying scenario

  • Dwarkesh’s calculation is that a couple billion dollars of Intel CapEx could support the logic behind roughly $100 billion a year of AI-model revenue, while noting that memory and other players in the stack also matter. He speculates that AI labs might buy everything or guarantee future supply. Ranade says some model companies have enough demand to consume an entire fab’s worth of silicon and the capital to fund it; the transcript’s “early signs” of this shift are Dwarkesh’s framing, not Ranade’s.
  • On Terafab, Ranade says Elon saw that his businesses would need a lot of silicon and Intel thought it could help accelerate the process of bringing up a fab. Dwarkesh points out that a tool bottleneck could mean a new fab secures guaranteed supply without increasing net global silicon. Ranade adds that a fab also needs power, water, and consumables, and says those inputs can be scaled more readily than tools.
  • After Dwarkesh suggests Intel should commit to more tools, as Nvidia reportedly has for memory and other components, Ranade responds: “Had we known what we know today, we would have invested more like a year ago. Knowing what we know now, I think we’ll be investing more.”

9. Catching TSMC is about scale, not just transistor density — and memory is also constrained

  • Ranade says a gap of a few percent in performance, power, or area is “splitting hairs,” and that being on time with yields supporting rapid ramps matters more. He says a technology includes more than one transistor type: low-leakage and high-performance transistors, SRAM, analog, and RF. He disputes Dwarkesh’s cited benchmarking of 14A against N2 without offering a different density figure in the transcript. Dwarkesh cites TSMC shipping upwards of 3X Intel’s leading-edge wafers and spending around $50 billion on CapEx versus Intel’s roughly $20 billion; Ranade calls the comparison somewhat unfair because TSMC is a foundry for many customers while Intel is largely a foundry for itself.
  • Ranade says about 80% of a fab’s cost structure is fixed, so extra utilization, output, and yield can greatly improve the economics of the same footprint. He says there are three foundries left at the advanced node, compared with about 20 foundries 40 years ago. On Intel’s DRAM and flash exits, he says there were good reasons at the time and nobody could have foreseen the enormous demand; today, he says, the supply crunch is larger for memory than for compute.
  • Ranade says fab costs have been doubling every four to five years, and that a High-NA scanner with associated equipment costs around $400 million. He asks whether the rising cost of patterning can continue at that rate and raises clean-slate questions such as, “Do you really need a clean room today?” He says no incumbent would willingly run the proposed hamburgers-and-cigars experiment. He adds that some CPU-design practices may also be locked into approaches established 30 years ago.
