item.title: 20VC: Trillion or Bust: The New VC Game | Coreweave Sell-Off Creates Panic | Town at $1B, Anduril at $90B: Revenue Multiples Out of Control | General Atlantic Eyes IPO & Modal Raises $750M at $15.75B
item.description: Fund-scale return targets narrow venture: $50–100M seed valuations and $300–500K allocations can make an $18B winner immaterial. CoreWeave must fill capacity and fund buildout; Modal topped $1B run rate after raising $750M at $15.75B, amid unresolved inference competition. Town at $1B and Anduril at $90B highlight entry-price risk, with Anduril’s roughly 40x revenue demanding substantial execution.
item.content:encoded:
20VC · Harry Stebbings · 2026-10-22 · 61 min · 原语言 EN

Fund-scale return targets narrow venture: $50–100M seed valuations and $300–500K allocations can make an $18B winner immaterial. CoreWeave must fill capacity and fund buildout; Modal topped $1B run rate after raising $750M at $15.75B, amid unresolved inference competition. Town at $1B and Anduril at $90B highlight entry-price risk, with Anduril’s roughly 40x revenue demanding substantial execution.

TL;DR

  • Mega-fund return targets are narrowing what gets funded while making seed ownership harder to monetize. Harry cites a profitable $20M ARR company growing 600–700% that attracts little interest; Jason’s explanation is “billion-dollar positions or nothing” for large funds. Meanwhile, $50–100M seed valuations and $300–500K allocations can leave even an $18B winner immaterial to a fund. Rory’s objection: an industry historically producing 10–20 decacorns per decade cannot support everyone pursuing only enormous outcomes.
  • CoreWeave’s sell-off tests whether AI demand can outrun infrastructure spending, rather than whether demand is growing at all. Rory describes a leveraged business that must keep filling capacity while financing the next buildout; Harry’s proposed “generational buying opportunity” therefore requires more than confidence in AI adoption. Jason prefers Nvidia’s differentiated assets, but Rory challenges that hierarchy with the returns he cites: Nvidia up 18% versus Micron up 350%.
  • Anthropic’s reported slowdown leaves room for a huge valuation, but its revenue deserves less predictability than conventional SaaS. Harry cites $16.8B of Q3 revenue, 45% sequential growth, an 85% gross margin and adjusted profitability, alongside a rumored IPO valuation falling from $2T to $1.5T. Rory can construct a roughly 12–13x forward-revenue case; Jason warns developers switch providers and Anthropic could lose market share while still growing substantially. “There’s only so much ARR in the ARR here.”
  • The panel’s strongest software call is that production readiness has become more important than generating another feature. Jason argues models get developers most of the way there, while testing and fixing can consume the next three days. He broadens “code review” into “build to prod,” encompassing verification, testing and deployment. Rory agrees these are compelling markets, while warning that their exceptional growth comes with repeated foundation-model competition.
  • Modal’s $750M raise at $15.75B exposes an inference opportunity the panel admits it underestimated. Its run rate exceeds $1B, against Rory’s recollection of less than $100M around mid-to-late last year. He contrasts roughly $5–6B across leading independent inference providers with more than $100–110B at OpenAI and Anthropic combined. The opportunity is cheaper, sufficiently capable tokens; the unresolved question is whether competition eventually overwhelms today’s growth and improving margins.
  • Town at $1B and Anduril at $90B force a distinction between exceptional companies and attractive entry prices. Jason calls Town an early venture bet with limited data, dressed in a billion-dollar valuation; Anduril’s roughly 40x revenue demands substantial execution. Rory agrees growth might justify the prices, but expects little help from broader public-market multiple expansion. His warning is straightforward: “amazing companies just priced wrong.”
  • Cash-generating software can reward founders even when it fails the venture industry’s outcome requirements. Jason revises his former enthusiasm for raising one round and stopping: “none and done” may preserve more freedom to distribute profits. The panel questions the exact $370M profit claim for 37signals but accepts the broader wealth-creation point. Bending Spoons offers another ownership model, although Rory challenges whether software assets can endure like Berkshire’s See’s Candy.
  • A venture firm IPO creates an obligation to keep growing assets, while returning LP liquidity could fuel another funding cycle. Rory estimates roughly $800M–$1B of annual fee income is needed for a meaningful public listing and warns that the structure can change investment culture. Harry expects SpaceX distributions and prospective Anthropic/OpenAI IPOs to recycle money into venture. Harvard’s reported 27.1% return illustrates the rewards—and resulting FOMO—of exposure to the few dominant private assets.

Digest

1. Billion-dollar positions are narrowing the venture market

  • Harry’s opening puzzle is a profitable company at $20M ARR, growing 600–700%, that encounters “crickets” from VCs. Jason describes a comparable agentic company planning to stop after a $3M seed. Rory accepts that strong businesses struggle, but challenges the diagnosis: investors also fund previously implausible projects, including data centers in space and quantum computing. Capital is willing to take risk when the perceived upside is enormous.
  • Jason’s explanation is fund arithmetic: firms raising $5–10B every 18 months need billion-dollar positions, sometimes much larger ones. A $2B exit cannot deliver that without unusually high ownership. “It’s billion-dollar positions or nothing.” Rory objects that the industry historically produced 10–20 decacorns per decade, whereas current expectations appear to assume 90 this year; there cannot be enough giant outcomes for everyone.
  • For merely excellent companies, Jason’s prescription is to meet 100 investors. A less fashionable growth fund may fund the best opportunity it has seen that quarter, even when the marquee partnerships decline. What changed is that top-decile metrics once practically guaranteed a term sheet; now founders must search much more widely.
  • Seed reverses Rory’s initial intuition: Jason says $50–100M entry valuations, lower ownership and lost pro rata make 5x net harder. Harry’s $300–500K allocation in a company reaching $18B still “doesn’t move the fucking needle.” Rory agrees the next five years look inverted, citing SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI rising from roughly $400B combined to $4–5T over three years.

2. CoreWeave needs demand to outrun its next construction bill

  • Rory reports a roughly 15–20% decline the previous week; bond prices rose, implying lower default risk. Neoclouds amplify changes in sentiment because they underwrite rapid growth with large capital expenditures and debt. Recalling figures from memory, he sketches something like a $7B runway, $10–20B of CapEx and $35–40B of debt. Grow too slowly and customers are unhappy; build too quickly before demand softens and there is no software-style option to hunker down.
  • Harry, a shareholder, asks whether a roughly 25% decline creates a “generational buying opportunity.” Rory’s qualification matters: filling existing capacity is insufficient when another $20B of spending requires demand to rise substantially every year. He would track OpenAI and Anthropic’s combined growth to remove market-share transfers, then compare that demand trajectory with CoreWeave’s investment plans.
  • Jason calls CoreWeave and Oracle “B-tier” relative to Nvidia. CoreWeave, he says, depends on Nvidia and lacks unique silicon and software; Oracle cannot sell enough enterprise software and is renting excess capacity. He calls them more sensitive to shocks, while saying B-tier assets “should trade at a premium.” Rory rejects quality ranking as a complete investment rule, citing Nvidia up 18%, Nebius up 50% and Micron up 350% over the year he references. Yet when Jason asks about putting 20% of personal assets into those riskier names, Rory admits: “I wouldn’t dare.”

3. Anthropic can slow sharply without becoming a weak business

  • Harry reports Q3 revenue of $16.8B, up 45% from Q2, an 85% gross margin and adjusted profitability; the rumored IPO valuation shifts from $2T to $1.5T. Rory sees deceleration from an unsustainable starting point after three years of 10x growth. His illustrative continuation of roughly $5B in quarterly revenue additions produces around $105–110B the following year and a 12–13x forward-revenue valuation. “I’m not saying they will.”
  • Jason’s concern is post-IPO volatility: “developers are not loyal,” and provider shares have moved dramatically. Anthropic’s revenue market share could be down 10% from where it is today by the end of next year while its absolute business remains excellent. “There’s only so much ARR in the ARR here.” Rory adds the next risk: companies defending share through price cuts, especially if aggregate end-user demand slows.
  • On OpenAI’s supposed $1.4T financing, Rory declines Harry’s strategic-anchoring interpretation. “When you need money, you take money.” His simpler explanation is compute spending and an unfinished IPO: raise above the last round, but leave enough upside for new investors. Jason relays Chamath’s suggestion to raise what Anthropic needs at $1.5T and move on, noting that a $2T price could stress its capital needs.

4. Application routers reveal what customers will pay for intelligence

  • Jason dismisses the significance attached to Replit switching its default to OpenAI. Replit already routes among models; his explanation is comparable output at a 30–40% better price. Unlike users manually configuring routing, Replit, Lovable, Base44 and v0 have a strong incentive to optimize quality against cost, because they cannot simply pass every expense through to customers.
  • Those applications are useful laboratories, Jason argues, because SMB users seeking a roughly $25-a-month product and enterprise customers alike are cost-sensitive. He says the default could change again, mentioning Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5. His narrower inference about Kimi is that Replit is not seeing sufficient benefits to route everything through it. Rory agrees: at roughly billion-dollar revenue scale, these applications can run an economically meaningful comparison of intelligence against price.

5. “Build to prod” is becoming the critical software bottleneck

  • Claude Code Review threatens specialists because coding sits at Anthropic’s core, Jason says, but independent products retain benefits—including having one model check another’s work. He mentions Greptile’s $75M raise and CodeRabbit as examples in the category. His example captures the remaining workload: an engineer builds Harry’s feature from a phone during dinner, then spends “the whole next three fucking days testing it and fixing it.” Generating the feature does not finish the job; Jason says review and processing can take an order of magnitude longer than building.
  • Rory’s “Icarus moment” framing preserves the trade-off: the fastest-growing applications sit closest to foundation models precisely because those models unlock their capabilities. Coding, code review and legal startups therefore face a fresh competitive scare every six months. Investors cannot demand extraordinary growth while also expecting complete insulation from the technology producing it. “You can’t have it both ways.”
  • Jason initially calls code review software’s most important category, explicitly separating importance from the largest eventual fortunes, then broadens it: “build to prod.” Code may work in development without being production-ready. Rory agrees that testing, memory management, sandboxes and deployment create related opportunities. “Coding is the mother lode of LLM value”; the unresolved work is getting that output into reliable production.

6. Modal reveals an inference opportunity the panel underestimated

  • Harry describes Modal’s $750M Series D, led by Accel at $15.75B, with run rate exceeding $1B. Rory recalls revenue around $60M or below $100M in mid-to-late last year: the acceleration is “stunning.” Jason prefers its developer-facing value creation to simply supplying GPU racks, although he acknowledges seemingly limitless competition.
  • Rory estimates four or five leading inference providers together generate roughly $5–6B of run-rate revenue, versus more than $100–110B for OpenAI and Anthropic. His economic example returns to Replit: why buy a comparable token while supporting a model provider’s 70% gross margin if an inference supplier can deliver it at a 30% margin? Harry and Jason acknowledge underestimating how much revenue could accrue outside the leading labs.
  • The valuation debate remains open. Neoclouds might ask why they finance infrastructure while another layer captures developer economics, then enter that business themselves. Against that threat, Rory says extraordinary growth “covers a multitude of sins.” Harry puts Fireworks’ margins in the mid-30s and says they will be hitting 50% “pretty soon.” Jason says even mid-30s margins can work publicly, with consequences for the eventual multiple.

7. Town and Anduril test how far future growth can justify today’s price

  • In the mock investment committee, Jason passes on Town’s $108M Series B at $1B. He sees a smart team from Plaid but insufficient data: essentially a conventional early venture bet at a radically larger price. “A billion’s the new 100 million.” If the partnership wants this as one of ten bets over the next year, he would let it proceed.
  • Jason’s comparison of Town needing $500M of inference with Instinct needing $5B turns toward future financing obligations. Rory wants the clip revisited in two years: a billion dollars remains real money, however casually investors discuss it. Jason instead keeps asking whether they can get back into Modal.
  • Anduril at $90B is the sharper valuation test. Jason calls it generational, with contracts and depth, but questions roughly 40x revenue given its margins. Rory contrasts a mature $2B-revenue defense contractor worth perhaps $8B with one doubling toward $4B, $8B and eventually $20B. The latter might justify the price, but investors are “leaning in a lot into the future.”
  • Jason’s broader concern is whether AI companies inherit their categories’ depressed public multiples once growth slows—even to 60–70%. He cites Braze at around 6x revenue in one comparison, versus Monday.com and HubSpot at 2x and Klaviyo at 2.2x; he separately notes Braze had been trading at roughly 3x revenue. Rory agrees investors can own “amazing companies just priced wrong,” and doubts broad US market multiple expansion will rescue them.

8. Bending Spoons tests the Berkshire model in software

  • Harry introduces Berkshire’s reported $330M purchase of additional Bending Spoons shares. Jason sees “the Berkshire version of software”: select a handful of enduring assets from thousands of opportunities, improve them and hold them. He contrasts earlier, challenged acquisitions such as Evernote and Vimeo with what he considers better-quality assets such as Miro and Airtable.
  • Rory’s objection is durability. See’s Candy from the 1960s resembles today’s product; software cannot be assumed to remain similarly stable. He calls it “conceptually the same idea as Berkshire Hathaway, but perhaps in an industry where the idea doesn’t apply.” Jason accepts the distinction but argues this may be as close as software gets to that ownership model.

9. Bootstrapping gives founders more freedom to keep the cash

  • Harry cites $370M in 37signals profits since 2020. Jason questions the precision: the figure appears inferred from $37M of profit sharing at 10%. His own rough guess is about $60M a year, with perhaps $40M reaching the bottom line; he calculates that as $240M over six years. Nevertheless, both accept the central point: unfashionable software can make its owners extraordinarily wealthy.
  • Jason changes his earlier view that raising one small round and stopping is an ideal outcome. Using Zapier’s approximately $300M revenue as an illustration, he asks what founders might keep if they had raised nothing. “None and done” may be preferable because dividends become harder with venture investors. He says 37signals took money from Bezos or others, while allowing that they presumably worked out their arrangements.
  • Harry proposes buying investors out. Rory explains the constraint: repurchasing a 30% stake at six times cash flow absorbs roughly two entire years of company cash, creating risk if financed with debt. Jason says such deals happen but can be expensive and deliver mediocre investor outcomes. Rory’s broader conclusion: “not everything has to be through the lens of venture.”

10. Public venture firms must keep growing assets as LP liquidity returns

  • On General Atlantic’s prospective IPO, Rory estimates a meaningful listing needs roughly $800M–$1B of fee income. Public investors value management fees much more than carry, with firms trading around 4–5x revenue in his framing. Only the largest venture and growth platforms seem plausible candidates. He separately warns that public ownership can make a partnership more institutional and risk-averse.
  • Harry questions whether already enormous firms would change that much. Rory’s clearer distinction is the obligation to expand assets and launch products. A publicly listed version of old Benchmark, raising $450M every three years, would face pressure for growth funds and crossover strategies. Jason agrees that managers could no longer simply enjoy substantial personal income without growing.
  • Harvard’s reported 27.1% return brings its endowment to $68B, helped by a SpaceX stake worth roughly $2.2B. Harry expects SpaceX distributions and hoped-for Anthropic/OpenAI IPOs to recycle cash into venture, with OpenAI potentially in Q1/Q2. Jason resists declaring a peak boom: he cites 2021 university venture/PE returns averaging 36.6%, 41% for the top quartile and 62% at Cambridge. “This is no 2021 yet.”

11. Jason predicts Tesla’s latest spectacle precedes consolidation

  • Jason calls the new Roadster Tesla’s last major standalone celebration before an eventual merger with SpaceX over the next “X months.” He categorically predicts Chinese dominance in electric vehicles and autonomy, and an end to people driving themselves within a few years. Harry focuses on marketing: spectacular demonstrations sustain the “Elon premium” and can give the valuation another 12 months of life.
  • The discussed idea of placing a SpaceX share in every child’s Trump account combines distribution with shareholder affinity. Rory cites roughly $10B in aggregate value. Jason argues direct ownership could soften hostility toward extraordinary wealth creation: “It’s that much harder to hate someone when you’re a shareholder.” Harry’s counterexample is his own unhappiness holding CoreWeave; Rory notes he did not receive those shares free.

来源：Podcast

item.title: Peter Thiel: The Real Danger of AI Isn't What You Think
item.description: Thiel expects AI to lift productivity and lower inflation, but sees weak evidence that suppliers can sustain monopoly profits as leadership shifts from DeepMind to OpenAI and perhaps Anthropic. Even a better median outcome could bring wage gains of 3% with “plus or minus 10% or something like that,” while Thiel opposes pausing development amid China competition. He warns that AI catastrophe fears could empower a “softly totalitarian one-world government,” leaving oversight and the path to progress unresolved.
item.content:encoded:
The Builders · Walter Isaacson、Peter Thiel · 2026-10-22 · 58 min · 原语言 EN

Thiel expects AI to lift productivity and lower inflation, but sees weak evidence that suppliers can sustain monopoly profits as leadership shifts from DeepMind to OpenAI and perhaps Anthropic. Even a better median outcome could bring wage gains of 3% with “plus or minus 10% or something like that,” while Thiel opposes pausing development amid China competition. He warns that AI catastrophe fears could empower a “softly totalitarian one-world government,” leaving oversight and the path to progress unresolved.

TL;DR

  • Thiel expects AI to raise productivity and lower inflation, but sees weaker evidence that its suppliers can defend monopoly profits. AI pitches are “incredibly weak on the monopoly story,” while leadership has shifted from DeepMind to OpenAI and perhaps Anthropic. His description is a “fight to the death,” making sector growth and durable investor returns different questions.
  • He remains firmly against an AI pause, even when leading companies themselves warn about danger. Thiel “broadly” backs David Sacks and Trump’s China argument: “you have to develop the AI technology to control the AI technology.” Asked about a 5–10% chance of everyone dying, he says that “sounds way too high,” questions probability intuitions, and insists, “We need to hit the accelerator as hard as possible.”
  • A better median outcome would not eliminate AI’s distribution problem or its political backlash. Thiel’s illustrative 3% wage increase comes with “plus or minus 10% or something like that”—disruption a risk-averse society may reject. Isaacson’s globalization comparison forces a concession that growth can be badly uneven; Thiel nevertheless thinks AI is bigger than the internet and could improve per-capita GDP more smoothly.
  • Thiel’s alternative existential risk is a global authority empowered by fear of AI catastrophe. He concedes that AI, climate and nuclear risks are serious, but fears a “softly totalitarian one-world government” with no outside left. His “Antichrist or Armageddon” framing seeks a “moderate third way,” not dismissal of safety; he calls existing nuclear arrangements “definitely more good than bad.”
  • He credits effective altruists with spotting AI early while questioning the incentives behind alarmist messaging. Their big insight was “AI is around the corner”; he cites Anthropic, built in “6, 7 years,” and speculates about a value “probably close to $2 trillion at the IPO.” Danger warnings can also motivate staff by portraying their employer as history’s most important company.
  • Thiel prefers inventive founders to inert bureaucracies, but Isaacson keeps pressing the moral trade-off. Post-Jobs Apple is Thiel’s example of shareholder success without new invention; “good over evil,” but “evil’s better than bad,” is his provocative distinction between moral failure and incompetence. He says a moral compass ranks highly, yet emphasizes a “transcendent sense of purpose” when choosing builders.
  • The promised payoff is renewed progress in physical life, while consciousness and relationships remain reasons to preserve humanity. Thiel hopes AI can help restart broader science: “could we at least cure dementia?” Survival is extremely important but not the only goal, he says, while maintaining, “I don’t think AI is conscious or ever will be.”

Digest

1. AI’s safety movement spotted the inflection early

  • Thiel traces OpenAI to an “anti-Google” concern: technology too important and dangerous to sit inside one company. He thinks Musk exited around 2018; around 2020, seven people left to create Anthropic, wanting to take the risks still more seriously.
  • His steelman of effective altruism is not that its apocalypse scenarios are correct, but that its adherents recognized “AI is around the corner.” He calls parts of the movement cult-like, yet cites Anthropic: built in “6, 7 years” and, he speculates, worth “probably close to $2 trillion at the IPO.” He thinks that would probably rank sixth or seventh globally by market cap.
  • The consequential middle case is neither China-style surveillance nor Nick Bostrom’s godlike intelligence, but AI “like a human being”: outputs indistinguishable from a person’s. That Turing-test threshold alone raises the central economic question—whether AI complements people or substitutes for them.

2. AI’s growth may be broad while its profits remain contested

  • The macroeconomic forecast comes with “nobody really knows”: Thiel expects a large productivity boost and a “fairly disinflationary force.” Unless a few companies capture the gains exceptionally narrowly, he would expect the median person to be better off. His historical intuition is that displacement frees people for more productive work.
  • Isaacson asks whether four or five companies will capture the market. Thiel’s investment test is “tell me why you have a monopoly,” and AI pitches are “incredibly weak on the monopoly story.” He describes leadership shifting from DeepMind to OpenAI and perhaps Anthropic, despite Altman’s preemptive chip procurement and data-center construction. Google, Meta and Grok still feel close; he is not sure China is far behind.
  • Competition does not eliminate anxiety. Thiel illustrates the problem with an expected 3% wage increase, “plus or minus 10% or something like that”: even a better median outcome can bring volatility that a risk-averse society hates. The gains are unknown; the disruption is easier to identify.
  • Isaacson’s pushback is globalization: it produced growth but left people behind. Thiel concedes that history and AI’s distribution risk, while distinguishing labor arbitrage—cheap T-shirts when Chinese wages are 5% of U.S. levels—from successful technology’s “doing more with less.” He thinks AI is bigger than the internet and could improve per-capita GDP more smoothly, rather than relying on arbitrages that shrink as globalization succeeds.

3. China and stagnation keep Thiel against a pause

  • Thiel “broadly” agrees with Sacks and Trump that competition with China argues against pausing. Companies’ own warnings make that position less comfortable to defend, but do not change it: “We need to hit the accelerator as hard as possible.” His mechanism is that “you have to develop the AI technology to control the AI technology”; falling behind could expose America to Chinese weapons or cyberattacks.
  • Asked about a 5–10% chance of everyone dying, Thiel says that “sounds way too high” and does not think it will happen. Maybe even a tiny amount above zero is too high, he adds; probability intuitions are poor. Isaacson removes China from the thought experiment to isolate AI’s risk. Thiel rejects the premise with the Mrs. Lincoln “how did you like the play” analogy.
  • The domestic argument is stagnation. Thiel defines the middle class through expecting one’s children to do better; that expectation has frayed for millennials and, to some extent, Gen Z. He does not know whether AI can restore it, but says outlawing both internet and AI would leave “virtually no growth”—a Europe- or Japan-like zero-sum society with “a loser for every winner.”
  • On oversight, Thiel thinks companies know more than government and have internal controls. Regulation requests might exploit government’s ignorance and slowness, easing companies off the hook. They can also motivate employees: Amodei’s danger warnings tell staff they work at “the greatest, most important company in the history of the world.” Thiel reads Trump’s refusal to add regulation as leaving responsibility with companies.

4. Fear of catastrophe can authorize an irreversible world state

  • For Thiel, “Antichrist” is a literary-biblical image of a tyrant ruling the whole world. Isaacson reads back his warning: “The Antichrist wouldn’t seize power by creating an AI apocalypse, but by convincing everyone that the apocalypse was coming.” The mechanism is fear creating support for exceptionally powerful global authorities.
  • He explicitly concedes serious existential risks involving climate change, nuclear weapons and AI. His additional concern is a “softly totalitarian one-world government.” The Soviet Union could decay and collapse because an outside remained; a world-sized North Korea might endure. Such a “catastrophic singularity” might not be reversible.
  • Isaacson pushes back that Oppenheimer’s warning led to Acheson–Lilienthal and nuclear controls that have “kind of worked.” Thiel agrees partially and notes the short historical test, but calls the nuclear arrangements “definitely more good than bad.” His objection is not that every global authority must be harmful; some versions could be good.
  • The target is Eliezer Yudkowsky’s If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies: detailed technical catastrophe scenarios, but a global-regulation remedy whose institutional design Thiel finds “incredibly fuzzy, incredibly vague.” “One world or none” makes world government the obvious answer, he argues; “Antichrist or Armageddon” treats both outcomes as unacceptable and demands a “moderate third way.”

5. Founder power trades governance risk for invention

  • Isaacson asks whether billionaires have too much economic and political power, with too few moral guardrails. Thiel grants the critique for argument’s sake, then asks for the alternative. He claims a “bimodal distribution”: charismatic, potentially dangerous founders who create new things, or MBA-led bureaucracies whose boards never want to act. “Super lame bureaucracy” is his counterfactual.
  • Apple is Isaacson’s test. Thiel says, “in my telling it did nothing new after Jobs,” citing “by far the lowest dollar spend on R&D” and “by far the largest on share buybacks.” Cook, the “zero charisma efficient operator,” scaled the phone business over roughly 15 years. Both leadership styles can serve shareholders, Thiel allows, but he judges Jobs and Musk better for society than Cook.
  • Asked what he seeks in a builder, Thiel ranks a moral compass “pretty high” and says he dislikes investing where it is “simply a business.” What attracts him is a “transcendent sense of purpose,” rather than a “short-term coin-operated business.”

6. Imitation makes the builders’ motives central to AI

  • Drawing on René Girard, Thiel treats imitation as essential to human culture but potentially destructive when “two apes reach for the same banana.” The trap is sterile status competition. His counterexample is Musk’s sustained, unconventional Mars vision: it opened an avenue that might otherwise never have existed. He adds that Girard himself thought escaping imitation was outside human power.
  • Isaacson turns the “imitation game” back on AI. Thiel’s Girardian question is not what AI will do, but what motivates its builders. His honest non-answer is that motives are “hard to figure out,” despite endless reflection. Nevertheless, he scores Musk, Amodei, Altman and Zuckerberg “far more good than bad across the board.”
  • Thiel disclaims a “pro-evil argument,” then ranks “good over evil,” but “evil’s better than bad,” with bad meaning incompetent. His analogy contrasts Marlowe’s fraudulent Faust, damned, with Goethe’s devil-assisted Faust, saved after doing more good than evil. Isaacson presses whether Thiel would personally prefer an evil but effective builder. Thiel answers that he is making “a broad social observation” about society’s preference amid pervasive incompetence.

7. Progress must improve physical life without losing human experience

  • The concrete destination is more progress in atoms, not only bits. Thiel dates the slowdown to the 1970s and recalls nuclear engineering already being passé when he studied at Stanford in the late 1980s. His hope is that AI helps restart broader science and engineering: “could we at least cure dementia? Could we at least cure Alzheimer’s or something like that?”
  • Isaacson revisits Thiel’s hesitation when Ross Douthat asked whether humanity should endure. Thiel calls survival an “extremely important goal,” not the only one: he heard a Luddite argument for leaving things unchanged. His goal is survival and flourishing, invoking the Enlightenment’s “relief of man’s estate,” although he admits “Silicon Valley is always quite bad at the meaning of technology.”
  • On consciousness, Thiel says, “I don’t think AI is conscious or ever will be.” A computer would not experience a beautiful sunset as a person does. He is unsure this should be the single argument for human survival, but losing that experience would be a “very big loss.”
  • His second anchor is relational life: families, companies and wider society, not just an isolated mind. AI might change those relationships; “in theory it should improve” them by freeing people from robotic labor and allowing more time together. Replacing every human with computers would lose both consciousness and those relationships.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/peter-thiel-real-danger-ai-isn-t-what-you-think

item.title: Arvind Krishna & Nikesh Arora: Quantum Threat, Open vs Frontier AI, AI Cyber Warfare & SaaS Collapse
item.description: Krishna's 2028, 2029 or 2033 quantum timeline makes cryptographic migration a current spending decision: stolen encrypted data could be decrypted later. He expects open-weight models to capture 75%–90% of tokens, with optimized owned-GPU costs of $1–$2 per million versus $20–$50 externally. Enterprises may consolidate 500–5,000 software vendors into 5–10 platforms, but reliable transaction systems will be harder to replace.
item.content:encoded:
All-In · Arvind Krishna、Nikesh Arora · 2026-10-21 · 40 min · 原语言 EN

Krishna's 2028, 2029 or 2033 quantum timeline makes cryptographic migration a current spending decision: stolen encrypted data could be decrypted later. He expects open-weight models to capture 75%–90% of tokens, with optimized owned-GPU costs of $1–$2 per million versus $20–$50 externally. Enterprises may consolidate 500–5,000 software vendors into 5–10 platforms, but reliable transaction systems will be harder to replace.

TL;DR

  • Krishna’s quantum timeline makes cryptographic migration a current spending decision. He puts the debate over a working quantum computer at 2028, 2029 or 2033, uses 2030 as a midpoint, and says it would break current cryptography. An encrypted drive stolen today could be kept for five years and then broken; Arora warns companies waiting until 2029–30 that “we’re already late.”
  • Krishna expects open-weight models to capture 75%–90% of token use. His economics: roughly $20–$50 per million tokens versus $1–$2 on owned GPUs after optimization, for a model doing 95% of the work. Cost, intellectual property and control lead him to expect enterprises to say, “I need to run the models myself.”
  • Arora sees frontier intelligence earning its price in emergencies, while routine security needs cheaper models. Endpoint inspection costs roughly $20–$40 annually; a breach can threaten billions, justifying frontier models and agent swarms. For ordinary tasks, “you don’t need a Ferrari for every task.” He favors open-weight models trained on proprietary data for many business uses, with managed weights offering auditability and explainability.
  • AI improves vulnerability discovery without removing the attacker’s structural advantage. Arora says Mythos hallucinated 30% of the time, but attackers need only one real vulnerability while defenders must find and patch them all. Krishna says agents write roughly half his organization’s code and improve it through evaluations, while “we’re only finding the bugs we know how to find.”
  • Compute access—not simply a have-and-have-not divide—is a key concern. Arora says he does not expect a straightforward have-and-have-not scenario, but worries that compute access may concentrate around two major countries because of cost and supply constraints. Krishna says that if 30 states restrict data centers, the remaining 20 could be “rubbing their hands together with glee.”
  • Vertical integration offers profit flexibility and can lock customers in through context. IBM’s 65-year mainframe history illustrates retaining value across a stack; Arora sees personal agents accumulating memory, APIs and connectivity that make switching harder. The commercial unit could become “cost per action,” with distribution a major battleground.
  • The host flags uncertain software terminal values; Krishna expects consolidation amid fragmented spending. The host expects major SaaS disruption as AI changes product-market fit. Krishna sees enterprises with 500–5,000 vendors moving toward 5–10 core platforms; consolidation could take “six months or six years.” He says highly reliable transaction systems will be harder to replace easily with AI-generated software. On M&A valuations, he says they were attractive at the start of the year, but less so a month ago.

Digest

1. Quantum migration must precede the machine

  • Krishna says the debate is whether a working quantum computer arrives in 2028, 2029 or 2033; using 2030 as a midpoint, he says it will break current cryptography. DARPA’s Quantum Benchmarking Initiative has narrowed roughly 200 companies to about 13. An encrypted drive stolen today could be kept for five years and then broken.
  • His milestones are demonstrating error correction or mitigation on working hardware—not a simulation—and then scaling gate operations. He expects claims “next year,” with one or two making progress by 2027. Gate operations are near 10,000 today; adding a zero annually could reach 10 million by 2029. Physical qubits alone can mislead: 10,000 physical qubits might mean about 200 logical qubits after error correction.
  • Post-quantum cryptography is understood and the code exists, Krishna says, although its assurance rests on complexity assumptions rather than theorem-level proof. Arora urges replacing the IT stack with quantum-safe infrastructure now and using post-quantum keys around traffic as an interim measure. He guesses that 50% of the few hundred million dollars of IT spending people in the room have earmarked for this year is on infrastructure that is not quantum-secure.
  • The host raises the possibility that AI could find a classical arithmetic route to cracking codes, perhaps through prime-number theory. Krishna says AI could discover a quantum algorithm, but running it efficiently requires quantum hardware; otherwise it could be slower by a factor of 1,000 or 10,000. He concedes a different classical route is possible. Timing decides practicality: taking 10 years to crack one key is “not a practical answer.”

2. Experiment with frontier models, then price the task

  • Arora says his 20,000-person organization has only discovered AI in the last 12–18 months, and it is not fully integrated. In this experimentation phase, he wants teams to “Use the best model you can find, the simplest way to use it” to validate possible efficiency, revenue and product-development benefits. Making adoption harder slows that learning.
  • Routine endpoint defense has different economics from a breach response. Arora says machine learning inspects hundreds of megabytes of traffic per endpoint, running on endpoint compute and a 20–40 MB payload, for roughly $20–$40 per year. Sending all that traffic through token-priced frontier models is not practical. His alternative is a compressed, task-specific small language model trained until it reaches 99.9% accuracy: “you don’t need a Ferrari for every task.”
  • If a breach threatens billions, Arora says customers will authorize whatever model is needed to stop it, including swarms of agents and a state-of-the-art LLM. He expects frontier models to be used in one-off cases where the business value justifies the cost. For many business uses, including defense models in peacetime, he expects open-weight models trained on proprietary data; managing the weights can provide auditability, explainability and an open system for explaining outcomes.
  • Krishna compares roughly $20 per million tokens for “generation minus one,” or $50 at the extreme, with $1–$2 using owned GPUs and about a week of optimization. His example is a Chinese open-weight Kimi K2 model with something like 800 billion parameters, which he says could do 95% of the work at much lower cost. He adds that captured, registered and audited chains of thought could give away intellectual property. He sees little danger in running Chinese models in an isolated environment, distinguishes that from cloud hosting, and expects comparable Western open-weight models within a year or two; he puts the capability gap at 6–12 months.
  • Those economics and control concerns lead Krishna to put 75%–90% of token use in open-weight models. He jokes that developers are lazy and will use the most expensive answer unless checked. Arora says moving to a cheaper model for production may be fine if experimentation has already proven it works, but he is skeptical of doing so for production use except in a small number of cases.

3. AI defense needs coordination and verification

  • The host asks whether model providers might encroach on cybersecurity businesses and raises questions about ZDR, data retention and synthetic data. Arora says many coding-agent users do not have ZDR and are comfortable with cloud-based code training models. Teaching a model what good code looks like can also help it recognize bad code. Mythos hallucinated 30% of the time, he says, but attackers need only one vulnerability while defenders must find and patch them all.
  • The host proposes that trusted partners pool vulnerabilities, develop patches and distribute them broadly. Krishna answers with three lessons from warfare: powerful alliances, making defense less costly relative to attack, and technological superiority. The goal, he says, is to find and patch vulnerabilities and make it very expensive for attackers to find a way through.
  • Krishna says coding agents write probably half the code in his environment and that it is better than before because agents evaluate it and fix what they can find before release. But “we’re only finding the bugs we know how to find.” Full verification is currently computationally infeasible; limited inputs might make verification possible, while arbitrary inputs remain difficult.
  • Krishna also guesses that people in the room would judge roughly 60%–80% of models’ vulnerability findings real and 20%–40% hallucinations. He says models are good at identifying vulnerabilities, but he would not use Claude Code to patch one without retesting it.

4. Regulation can move investment without stopping development

  • Arora says nobody is slowing down the push for better, faster models. He argues that companies remain responsible for products they release; claiming an agent wrote the software does not remove corporate responsibility. He says existing regulations can hold companies accountable, and that there may already be too many.
  • The host recounts a senior congressman’s prediction of data-center bans in all 50 states by the fourth quarter, while noting that this is unlikely. Krishna says AI regulation and data-center politics are driven by populism, balanced against concern for long-term economic advantage. He says all 50 states banning data centers has no chance, but 30 is possible; the other 20 would be “rubbing their hands together with glee.”
  • On global access, Arora says he does not expect a simple have-and-have-not scenario and believes protection can be made affordable. His larger concern is that computing development and access may not be evenly distributed: compute is expensive and difficult to obtain at scale, particularly away from the two major countries advancing it. He cites possible access constraints for a European company, whether from economics or supply.
  • Krishna frames the shift as another labor-capital trade-off, saying capital-intensive adopters tended to win in the previous seven or eight cycles. The host, not Krishna, argues that societies should accept job displacement if it can lead to better jobs, rather than insisting every existing job must be protected.

5. Vertical stacks retain profits and accumulate context

  • Krishna’s IBM example spans 65 years of mainframes. The company once sourced sand, made wafers and chips, and built the metal around the machine; today, manufacturing is the part it does not do in-house, while chip and engineering design, resilience and most software remain internal. The host’s Nvidia comparison adds the argument that controlling a stack lets a company move profits between layers when competitors commoditize one.
  • Arora reframes open versus closed models as open versus closed stacks. Reasoning, memory and context become increasingly intertwined; an open router that only moves reasoning tokens may become impractical. A personal agent containing someone’s context, APIs and connectivity creates switching friction. He expects applications to integrate software, reasoning, memory and context, with pricing tending toward “cost per action.”
  • Arora says distribution will also be a major contest in enterprise and consumer markets. He expects cutting-edge labs to push the MCP concept hard in the next three months; he says they tried it nine months earlier without success, but Facebook has shown how it can work. He expects APIs and says every iPhone app will have to become headless.

6. Software consolidation meets uncertain terminal values

  • Arora’s cybersecurity case starts with customers having to buy and bundle 40 solutions they may not understand. His Fidelity experience offers an analogy: 23 systems collectively performed what would now be called CRM, before the work consolidated into platforms. He wants best-in-class security capabilities integrated so customers need not assemble them themselves. The host—not Arora—says cybersecurity valuations have improved amid AI enthusiasm and expects that to rationalize over time.
  • The host says it is difficult to understand software’s terminal value over the next 5–8 years as AI changes product-market fit, and predicts major SaaS disruption. Asked about M&A valuations, Krishna says they were attractive at the beginning of the year, but not so much a month ago, and that he will wait to see how the next few months go.
  • Krishna sees enterprises using 500–5,000 software vendors and asks whether they could replace 490 with smaller AI capabilities, returning to 5–10 core platforms. If software value falls, he says, companies cannot afford separate distribution for every product. He expects consolidation, whether it takes six months or six years.
  • Krishna distinguishes interaction-heavy software, which AI can replace more readily, from systems that need reliability of 10⁻¹⁵, such as database lookups in retail banking or closing the books. He says those will be difficult to replace easily with AI-generated software. The host says a digital twin would be needed for years before switching and that there would then be no cost advantage; Krishna agrees.

来源：YouTube

item.title: MARKET UPDATE: What Breaks First — Bitcoin, AI, or the Bond Market?
item.description: CoreWeave’s 2032 bonds at 79 cents, CDS at 16 points upfront, and projected 2026 $32 billion free-cash-flow burn signal financing risk. Jonah expects neocloud distress to spur consolidation, not broader AI contagion, though defaults could disrupt chip orders and weaken supplier pricing. Avi sees Bitcoin’s Nasdaq-sell-off resilience as bullish; Jonah flags a possible AI cryptographic threat within six-to-twelve months.
item.content:encoded:
1000x · Avi Felman、Jonah Van Bourg · 2026-10-21 · 45 min · 原语言 EN

CoreWeave’s 2032 bonds at 79 cents, CDS at 16 points upfront, and projected 2026 $32 billion free-cash-flow burn signal financing risk. Jonah expects neocloud distress to spur consolidation, not broader AI contagion, though defaults could disrupt chip orders and weaken supplier pricing. Avi sees Bitcoin’s Nasdaq-sell-off resilience as bullish; Jonah flags a possible AI cryptographic threat within six-to-twelve months.

TL;DR

  • Avi’s trading framework is to add to demonstrated winners; Jonah adds that deal access itself should be scrutinized. “Losers average losers” means doubling down becomes especially dangerous when the information behind a losing trade has changed. Jonah’s venture experience illustrates how better networks brought better deals, while earlier failures had discouraged him from investing.
  • Jonah treats CoreWeave’s debt sell-off as a genuine financing warning. He cites 2032 bonds at 79 cents on the dollar, CDS at 16 points upfront, and projected 2026 free-cash-flow burn of $32 billion. Unlike a sentiment scare, a credit squeeze can force borrowers into damaging decisions: “This is a credit-originated problem.”
  • The hosts agree that neocloud distress need not derail the broader AI trade; Jonah expects consolidation. His shale analogy is falling output prices meeting exhausted financing, followed by stronger operators buying distressed capacity. He calls it a “microcredit bubble”: creditors absorb losses and effectively subsidize hyperscalers’ acquisitions.
  • Jonah favors buying certain AI inputs during sharp sell-offs. He likes copper, NVIDIA, and Intel, while avoiding neocloud equity and debt; defaults could disrupt chip orders before hyperscalers assume them, potentially with weaker supplier pricing. His longer-term demand argument includes an edge-computing market of “$100 billion or $500 billion.”
  • Jonah doubts compute futures will become a major exchange-traded market. Rapid obsolescence, fragmented hardware, bespoke delivery, and incumbents’ interest in opaque pricing obstruct an enduring benchmark. He expects bilateral or brokered contracts instead, while conceding, “I could be wildly wrong. Don could be right.”
  • Avi reads Bitcoin’s resilience during the Nasdaq sell-off as bullish. His rule is that bad news failing to push an asset lower often precedes an advance. He also remains bullish on ZRO after its move from $2.30 to $2, citing his earlier discussion with Brent and Helena.
  • Jonah’s separate Bitcoin concern is an AI-driven cryptographic breakthrough. He worries future open-source models spawning “fifty million sub-agents” could create a six-to-twelve-month threat that Bitcoin developers are unprepared to address. Avi says quantum is the more plausible, though more distant, risk, and that breaking public-key cryptography would put the whole internet at risk.

Digest

1. Winning positions deserve capital, but access deserves scrutiny

  • Avi’s unconventional-opportunity example is Donut World in Iraq: outsiders identified an underserved market and, he says, now make roughly $10 million annually. His point is calculated risk in overlooked places, especially as AI automates conventional work. “If you’re willing to look in areas where nobody else is willing to look,” opportunities remain. Jonah jokingly translates that into abandoning trading to sell donuts abroad.
  • The trading analogue is Paul Tudor Jones’s “Losers average losers.” Avi argues against repeatedly adding to underperformers, especially after the original information changes. Proven winners deserve additional capital: growing revenue from $1 billion to $10 billion can be easier than moving from $100 million to $1 billion because product-market fit and relationships already exist.
  • Jonah describes wealth as self-reinforcing: good opportunities arrive more readily once you are in a strong position. He compares Bezos’s venture-investing advantage to a pipeline of strong deals seeking his name. Jonah’s own early angel-investing losses discouraged him just as his network began producing better deals. His prescription is to seek annuities from weakness and swing bigger from strength. He warns that a deal arriving through a Twitter DM or AngelList syndicate has likely already been shown to top people who passed; better opportunities may come through more private channels.

2. CoreWeave’s credit problem requires outside funding to keep arriving

  • Avi calls the recent sell-off an overreaction: Nasdaq fell 5%, and Intel, one of his largest positions, dropped from $120 to $90. He considers Intel attractive again but is not adding because he already owns his position. Jonah agrees the broader macro picture is fine, but says credit problems deserve more scrutiny than another tariff or geopolitical panic: liquidity and solvency problems can force damaging behavior.
  • Jonah cites CoreWeave’s 2032 bonds trading at 79 cents and CDS requiring 16 points upfront. His model forecasts free-cash-flow burn of $32 billion in 2026, $34 billion the following year, $36 billion the year after, then $29 billion and $31 billion. Those deficits require external debt or equity. The bond deterioration therefore matters directly to the company’s ability to finance its plans; he calls CoreWeave the most creditworthy neocloud.
  • Across hyperscalers and neoclouds, Jonah cites $641 billion and $231 billion of 2026 CapEx, respectively, describing total spending as roughly $1 trillion this year and $1.5 trillion next year. Aggregate free-cash-flow deficits reach $165 billion and $334 billion. CoreWeave represents roughly 10% of next year’s hole in his work; the Street estimates its gap at $20 billion, versus his roughly $35 billion.
  • Avi locates the financing engine in Google, Facebook, and other hyperscalers. Borrowing at 6%, 8%, or 9% would still leave them investing; 15% and genuine concern about Facebook’s creditworthiness would represent a different situation. He accepts possible neocloud trouble but questions its transmission. Jonah agrees Microsoft remains free-cash-flow positive and expects the largest hyperscalers to manage their funding needs.

3. Distressed neoclouds could subsidize the next phase of AI expansion

  • Jonah’s shale comparison carries the mechanism: producers overstated economics by excluding ancillary costs, expanded supply until oil prices collapsed, and then lost financing simultaneously. Larger operators acquired the wreckage. He expects a similar squeeze in compute, where spot prices currently exceed long-term contracted prices: convergence and falling prices undermine leveraged neoclouds, leaving hyperscalers positioned to buy them. He qualifies the company list—Lambda is “probably fine.”
  • Avi’s challenge is whether NVIDIA, Intel, Google, and the Nasdaq actually suffer lasting damage if hyperscalers simply acquire the capacity. Jonah’s researched conclusion is categorical: the “microcredit bubble” will not metastasize into a broader AI-chip or Nasdaq meltdown. Creditors will recover less than par and subsidize hyperscalers’ purchases at “cents on the dollar.” Contract defaults can still create substantial chip-stock volatility before orders transfer to stronger buyers, potentially with weaker supplier pricing.
  • The positioning follows that distinction. Jonah wants to avoid neocloud equity and debt, buy unrelated assets during spillover panics, and buy NVIDIA or Intel if they collapse on these fears. Copper remains attractive because it connects the infrastructure; he also likes regional electricity around new data centers, while admitting he does not know how to express that exposure. He would not buy a compute future here.
  • His longer-run demand case extends beyond hyperscalers, currently the “marginal barrel.” Jonah expects cheaper tokens to push computing toward the edge, creating another “$100 billion or $500 billion” market; he highlights the CPU intensity of that opportunity and Intel’s positioning. His Jevons-paradox argument is that cheaper compute creates additional demand for compute capacity, with prices staying relatively consistent over time.

4. Compute lacks the stable benchmark that makes commodity futures work

  • Jonah respects Don Wilson’s record, particularly establishing Cumberland early in crypto, but rejects treating Wilson’s compute activity as proof of a future multitrillion-dollar derivatives market. Exploration can be a relatively cheap option for DRW. His disagreement comes with an explicit concession: “I could be wildly wrong. Don could be right.” He expects compute futures to appear but doubts they will take off.
  • The first obstacle is an enduring benchmark. Jonah says oil’s chemistry has remained the same for tens of millions of years; an H100 contract loses relevance as buyers move to H200s, B200s, Rubins, Feynmans, and newer chips. Meanwhile, AMD, TPUs, Trainium, and custom hyperscaler ASICs could further fragment the market. Jonah distinguishes this from equity indices that successfully change constituents: an evolving stock index does not establish that rapidly changing compute can support a commodity future.
  • Physical delivery adds another layer: PCIe versus SXM, InfiniBand versus Ethernet, eight-GPU nodes versus 1,000- or 4,096-GPU clusters, location, uptime, and reserved versus spot capacity all affect what buyers receive. There is no tight, hub-delivered standard comparable to oil. Avi supplies the gemstone analogy: repeated attempts at diamond futures struggled because products were so individual, although lab-grown diamonds are beginning to permit greater standardization.
  • Jonah’s strongest objection is incentive alignment: incumbents profit from opaque prices and wide gaps between spot and long-term contracts. His LNG analogy highlights intermediaries such as Vitol, BP, and Shell benefiting from informational advantages. Why would compute incumbents surrender theirs? He expects financialization through ISDA-like bilateral agreements or brokered blocks, potentially settled through a clearing venue. A successful futures market, he says, would still have unusually extensive fragmentation and basis differences.

5. Bitcoin’s price resilience meets a separate cryptography anxiety

  • Avi’s closing market signal is straightforward: when bad news stops pushing an asset lower, an advance often follows. Bitcoin held up despite substantial Nasdaq selling and AI fears, which he considers constructive. He notes Hyperliquid nearly reached $100 before retreating and ZRO moved from $2.30 to $2. His bullishness on LayerZero draws on the earlier Brent and Helena interview about developments in computation.
  • Having dismissed AI-credit contagion as a reason to fear Bitcoin, Jonah introduces a different concern. He calls quantum risk a “hoax” but worries an open-source model—perhaps generation six or seven—could spawn “fifty million sub-agents” pursuing advances in breaking public-key cryptography. Watching AI solve mathematical problems has changed his confidence. He doubts Bitcoin developers are prepared for a six-to-twelve-month non-quantum threat, despite their engagement with a ten-year quantum horizon.
  • Avi says quantum is the more plausible risk, though further away, and that a mathematical break in public-key cryptography would compromise far more than Bitcoin. Jonah challenges Avi’s claim that this would put the whole internet at risk, pointing out that there is no public key for a JPMorgan account; Avi argues that public-key cryptography secures internet interactions. Jonah asks whether he should therefore hold his Bitcoin. Avi reiterates the broader threat and his ranking of the risks; the technical disagreement remains unresolved.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/market-update-what-breaks-first-bitcoin-ai-or-bo

item.title: Chamath: Bitcoin Goes to Zero, Robots vs. $40T Debt, Elon’s SpaceX Shares for 72M Kids | EP #304
item.description: Chamath says AGI has arrived, but power, permitting, cooling and skilled labor could constrain deployment and create a massive compute shortage over the next three or four years. His nearly 6 GW power position reflects the thesis, while Alexander Wissner-Gross flags distillation and weak willingness to pay as counterweights.
item.content:encoded:
Moonshots · Peter Diamandis、Salim Ismail、Dave Blundin、Alexander Wissner-Gross、Chamath Palihapitiya · 2026-10-21 · 122 min · 原语言 EN

Chamath says AGI has arrived, but power, permitting, cooling and skilled labor could constrain deployment and create a massive compute shortage over the next three or four years. His nearly 6 GW power position reflects the thesis, while Alexander Wissner-Gross flags distillation and weak willingness to pay as counterweights.

TL;DR

  • Chamath believes AGI has arrived, but physical deployment will determine who captures its value. He expects a “massive” compute shortage over the next three or four years, citing power, permitting, cooling, skilled labor, and utility politics. His nearly 6 GW of accumulated power assets express that thesis; Alexander Wissner-Gross counters that distillation and weak willingness to pay could complicate the scarcity trade.
  • Anthropic’s proposed $75–$100 billion equity commitment earns Chamath’s respect for sincerity, alongside skepticism about philanthropic outcomes. The initial 5% allocation depends on shareholder approval, while further grants remain discretionary. His question is the “fail safe to course correct”; Alex’s objection is that a privately controlled benefit fund does not deliver universal public ownership.
  • Musk’s promised SpaceX share for every American child is more consequential as an ownership model than as immediate income support. Peter estimates roughly $10.5 billion across 72 million children, about $146 each, against $2.6 trillion annually to distribute $10,000 per American. Chamath calls direct contributions “the better version of the giving pledge”; the panel sees potential in copycats, compounding, and teaching children to own capital.
  • Chamath prefers current cash flow and power to long-duration intellectual-property valuations, while admitting unusually low conviction about markets overall. He favors ranking companies by free-cash-flow yield and argues that new chip designs can be technically successful without generating equity returns because manufacturing capacity is already occupied. He is the “least invested” he has been in roughly 15 years: cash flow supplies “the oxygen to pivot.”
  • The fiscal escape route discussed is a larger, cheaper economy rather than repayment of the national debt. Against Peter’s roughly $40 trillion debt figure, Anthropic’s reported internal projection puts US GDP at $44 trillion by 2030 versus $30 trillion today. Chamath thinks next-generation GLP3s and cancer vaccines could substantially reduce healthcare spending, making debt “not that important” relative to economic output.
  • Free business ideas expose the disagreement over whether execution remains a human bottleneck. Chamath says ideas are “a dime a dozen” and founder resilience matters more; Salim sees an accessible starting point for people without entrepreneurial exposure. Alex, disclosing a financial interest in Idealab.ai’s venture, expects AI-operated businesses to make execution itself “too cheap to meter.”
  • AI security becomes a contest over infrastructure, research insights, and competing systems rather than a single alignment solution. The panel treats the alleged OpenAI recording-device case as one instance of a broader intelligence struggle, while Alexander Wissner-Gross warns against excluding foreign talent. Alex favors “defensive co-scaling” and human-machine integration; Chamath explicitly rejects any guarantee that greater intelligence produces benevolence.
  • Chamath’s Bitcoin conclusion is explicitly bearish despite his continuing indirect crypto exposure. He cites limits on the buyer pool, ownership-related security risks, and prospective AI-enabled cryptographic attacks, concluding that Bitcoin eventually “gets hacked and then it goes to zero.” He holds exposure through Digital Currency Group equity rather than owning crypto directly; the attack scenario is his prediction, not a demonstrated outcome in the conversation.

Digest

1. Anthropic’s pledge shifts scrutiny from generosity to governance

  • Peter values Anthropic’s proposed 5% share commitment at $75–$100 billion against a floated $1.5–$2 trillion IPO valuation. It remains “subject to stockholder approval.” An additional 2% could be allocated at the board’s discretion for every 50% increase above a valuation baseline, creating an escalating commitment without making those subsequent grants automatic.
  • The founders’ earlier commitments are larger: all seven pledged 80% of their equity, while roughly half the employees are pledging shares with matching support. Peter says approximately 20% of Anthropic is consequently dedicated to public benefit, implying $300–$400 billion at the discussed valuation, versus $130–$365 billion for OpenAI’s foundation.
  • Chamath rejects the opening choice between generosity and IPO marketing: “They genuinely believe that what they’re doing is the right thing.” His concern is execution. Large philanthropic bursts generally produce little quantifiable improvement, he argues, so the important question is their “fail safe to course correct” if this effort follows the same pattern.
  • Recalling a Giving Pledge pitch a decade earlier, Chamath calls it “reputation washing”: adding his name and wealth to a list without a meaningful outcome requirement. Peter proposes an “impact pledge” instead. Both argue that successful founders contribute intelligence, relationships, and operating ability alongside money, making passive delegation to unproven intermediaries difficult to justify.

2. Public equity ownership requires institutions that do not yet exist

  • Alex calls the emerging expectation that frontier labs surrender equity a “hyper tithe.” He interprets Anthropic’s private fund as a snub to public ownership and this administration, while acknowledging Congress has not created the sovereign wealth fund he wants. His proposed intermediate corporate category would exchange public equity participation for benefits such as lighter regulation.
  • The discretionary grants create a difficult boardroom conflict, Blundin argues: shareholders resist dilution while the public asks why an authorized allocation has not happened. Dave distinguishes philanthropy from structural reform. In an economy increasingly operated by AI, he wants new ownership and participation mechanisms rather than simply redistributing wealth after it accumulates.
  • Chamath asks whether labor should face no tax while capital pays substantially more: poorer households derive more wealth from work, richer households from capital. Alex distinguishes taxing gains from taxing wealth itself, calling wealth taxes widely unpopular. He nevertheless suspects concentrated wealth in a few frontier labs could make negotiated equity taxation more practical, without presenting that concentration as desirable.

3. SpaceX shares make children participants in capital appreciation

  • Musk’s promise is explicit: “Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many.” Peter estimates 72 million recipients, roughly $146 each and $10.5 billion overall, around 1.1% of Musk’s stake. He contrasts the Dell family’s $6.25 billion cash contribution: $250 for 25 million children.
  • Peter challenges the scale: an average US household earns about $87,000 annually, while distributing $10,000 per American would require roughly $2.6 trillion each year. Chamath nevertheless calls direct contributions “the better version of the giving pledge,” bypassing the donor’s difficulty distinguishing effective nonprofits and letting children participate in “capitalism and democracy.”
  • Blundin’s premise is that value increasingly accrues to assets rather than paychecks. Salim thinks the ownership conversation could matter “100x” more than the initial dollars as children compare selling with holding. Alex adds a political interpretation: a generation owning a possible SpaceX–Tesla combination could feel economically, and potentially regulatorily, aligned with Musk’s businesses.
  • Peter floats 50, 100, or 200 newly public-company copycats. The discussion also connects the gift to employee stock-purchase plans and a difficult transition from defined-benefit pensions to defined contributions, arguing that existing retirement promises are insufficiently funded. The gift matters partly because it provides a starting point for that conversation.

4. Energy may price the transition without becoming the final currency

  • In the Isaacson clip, Musk guesses conventional currency eventually stops mattering as economic capacity becomes orders of magnitude larger than today’s economy. Physical measures—power, energy, mass, and time—would remain relevant. Asked about human purpose, he concedes, “I do struggle with this question,” while expecting AI and robots to outperform humans at every task.
  • Chamath agrees directionally: fiat debasement could push exchange toward claims on embedded effort and productive resources. His speculative mechanism is a token representing access to data centers, power plants, turbines, or natural gas. Saving would also change: owning local compute and contributing it to productive pools could replace income from work that AI increasingly performs.
  • Alex is “not as convinced” energy becomes the ultimate currency. Thirty years out, he expects economics to look unrecognizable. His alternative is civilization becoming sufficiently intelligent to model and allocate scarce resources without today’s decentralized monetary signaling. He explicitly resists calling this centralized planning; the claim concerns collective capability rather than a government planner.

5. Chamath’s power thesis starts with an electricity deficit

  • Asked about nearly 6 GW accumulated in roughly two years, Chamath begins with ordinary electrification: vehicles, appliances, computers, and data centers all need electrons. Even assuming every planned project arrives on time and budget, he describes a 2050 shortfall as “1.4 terawatt hours,” or six Californias’ worth of electricity. That gap initiated his investment thesis.
  • Nuclear does not offer an easy timing escape. His objection to small modular reactors is “the S in the MR”: a small reactor faces much the same local approval effort as a large one. He favors an all-of-the-above supply response, but accumulated solar because it is among the cheapest options and can be deployed in about two years.
  • Blundin argues falling chip costs strengthen power’s relative importance. Today’s assumed data-center economics put roughly 10% into power and 90% into Nvidia; he expects that balance to invert as competing designs improve efficiency. For the terrestrial transition, his formulation is “wattage and tonnage”—electricity to run facilities and physical materials to build them.
  • Owning assets is only the beginning, Chamath cautions. Financing cycles, equipment supply, construction, and licensed labor remain difficult. Master electricians cannot be recruited as interchangeable workers, and shortages make them expensive. His conclusion is emphatic: the next three or four years bring a “massive massive massive compute shortage.”

6. AGI’s diffusion runs into cooling systems and utility politics

  • “I do think that we have achieved AGI,” Chamath says. “It cannot diffuse,” because building the infrastructure is harder than producing laboratory capability. He cites what he describes as a newly released Anthropic S-1 risk factor: hyperscalers will not provide enough compute. To him, that is extraordinary for such a fast-growing, well-funded company.
  • Peter cites Musk’s claim that 15 GW of chips are waiting for liquid-cooled data centers. Chamath adds that older-generation inventory also sits unused. As a mechanical-failure example, he recounts two coolant leaks involving Nscale and Microsoft, after which Microsoft allegedly invoked liquidated damages and exited. “Building things and mechanically building things is really hard.”
  • Utility coordination can be equally restrictive. Chamath recounts buying northern assets in a multistate power arrangement, then discovering that larger southern participants controlled development and offtake decisions. He singles out Oklahoma Gas and Electric and calls the structure “an organized mafia.” His example makes local relationships and institutional power concrete constraints on AI deployment.
  • Space does not eliminate terrestrial demand. Large technology companies might eventually move their compute off-world, but an insurer such as Humana cannot simply launch its own facility. Data sovereignty may require a private cloud or an air-gapped installation. Launch queues and managed-service availability therefore leave substantial domestic construction necessary, influencing winners over the next five years.

7. Getting long electrons faces an efficiency-and-demand counterargument

  • Panelists suggest residential or commercial-and-industrial solar paired with batteries: consume what is needed and sell surplus into the grid. Distributed compute pools such as Venice offer another route. Another example discussed is SPAN, which has a deal with NVIDIA for an in-home unit combining storage, a battery, and a GPU. The broader instruction is to find the cheapest, technically manageable way to “get long electrons.”
  • A panelist also sees opportunities beyond technical specialists. Local regulatory relationships can unlock projects, while corporate executives can secure future capacity through prepayments. The example is an insurer authorizing a billion-dollar commitment before compute sells out again. Understanding where capital sits and directing it toward construction can matter without knowing how to design models or power equipment.
  • Alex accepts supply constraints at the capability frontier but questions whether demand automatically absorbs everything built. OpenAI tried to sell consumers reasoning capabilities they did not want to fund, he argues. If models cannot be economically “metabolized” by customers, abundant energy alone does not create sufficient value.
  • Distillation is his second objection: even with no new power plants or data centers, mathematical progress could deliver much stronger models at a fraction of today’s energy footprint. Peter counters that uses will expand for decades. He cites 1,200-token-per-second Cerebras access: expensive enough to try briefly, but sufficiently compelling that “you will never go back.”

8. Alignment arguments diverge over stories, constitutions, and inspection

  • Musk suggests truth-seeking and curiosity, while worrying that dystopian fiction supplies AI with bad expectations about itself. Peter’s shorthand is “more Roddenberry, less Cameron.” His positive-future film competition drew over 5,000 submissions, with two winners being made. Blundin agrees training-data selection matters enormously, because choosing the dataset influences the model’s personality and decisions.
  • Chamath regards humans using AI against other humans as the greater concern. He also focuses on founding objectives: maximizing truth and alleviating all suffering could produce very different systems. He wants these canonical documents openly inspectable and sees that as an appropriate government interest, while acknowledging uncertainty about how such material is weighted in practice.
  • Blundin argues Chinese open-source models capable of self-improvement have changed the safety problem. In his view, relying on post-training alignment is no longer sufficient: “That cat is out of the bag.” He wants inspection and containment, potentially with international authority, rather than confidence that an initial training intervention permanently settles behavior.

9. Competition and human-machine integration offer a competing safety model

  • Alex calls both curated information diets and government oversight of “soul documents” brittle solutions. He recalls OpenAI’s founding as a counterweight to concern about a DeepMind singleton, followed by Anthropic’s emergence as another competitor. His preferred mechanism is “competition and defensive co-scaling”: diverse systems balancing one another and, in some cases, competing to be friendlier.
  • His second mechanism is humans merging with machines through brain-computer interfaces, uploading, or sideloading, carrying “human meat-body values” into superintelligence. Chamath rejects Peter’s suggestion that extreme intelligence might reliably produce wisdom or benevolence. Silicon, like humanity, could contain a distribution of outcomes, including dangerous systems that other systems must oppose: benevolence is not guaranteed.

10. AI’s fiscal promise is denominator growth and cheaper services

  • Musk says he concluded cutting the deficit from inside government was politically impossible: the presidency, Congress, and judiciary lack the appetite to reduce spending. Peter frames the scale as roughly $40 trillion of debt as of October 5, up $2.44 trillion in a year, with around $6.5 billion added daily and $3 billion paid daily in interest.
  • Peter cites Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark at the IMF in Bangkok: internal models project US GDP of $44 trillion by 2030 versus $30 trillion today, implying roughly 9–10% annual growth against the historical 2–3%. Chamath’s distinction is that technology need not eliminate debt; it can make the debt much less important relative to output.
  • Healthcare supplies his concrete mechanism. Next-generation “GLP3s,” RETA, and cancer vaccines could probably push healthcare below 10% of GDP and potentially halve its cost. He distinguishes dispersed waste—such as hospital upcoding—from dramatic fraud cases. Discontinuous health improvements could prevent use of expensive systems altogether, bypassing the incentives that make waste difficult to remove.
  • Peter imagines a Britannica-to-Wikipedia collapse in entitlement and defense costs, potentially requiring a crisis and several more years of technology: a currency “rebasing.” Blundin reads Musk’s DOGE-to-xAI pivot as adaptation to AGI arriving eight to ten years earlier than expected. Peter’s counter-risk is civil unrest forcing money printing and $2,000–$3,000 monthly checks.

11. Countries need resources that matter to the emerging AI powers

  • The discussion worries that Europe carries debt without the same AI growth lever; successful American AI drug discovery could pull foreign spending into the US. Chamath generalizes the concern: countries without valuable resources to trade could become “a vassal state” of the US or China. Existing regional alliances may consequently become less useful than access to strategically relevant assets.
  • A panelist cites Portofino reportedly using thermal-imaging drones to identify unauthorized air conditioners. With parts of Italy dependent on French electricity, Chamath sees limits to restricting demand rather than expanding supply: eventually, he argues, a country risks becoming “a living history museum.”
  • Peter sees a window for countries to develop power and data centers before space-based infrastructure changes the competition again. Citing attacks on Middle Eastern facilities, Alex extends colocation beyond electricity and compute to defense. His speculative endpoint is infrastructure that is “self-powering, self-defending, self-computing,” with physical protection becoming part of the investment opportunity.

12. Cheap ideas expose a disagreement about cheap execution

  • Peter introduces Idealab.ai as a free catalog of more than a million business ideas, drawing on 17 million sources and Bill Gross’s 31 opportunity-identification methods. Filters include geography, interests, startup capital, and market size.
