Gross targets a million businesses and 100 million jobs; Peter says Cloudflare has committed $100,000 in credits per qualifying startup.
  • Chamath’s response is blunt: ideas are “a dime a dozen.” The difficult part is enduring failure and putting one foot ahead of the other. Salim counters that people outside entrepreneurial networks need somewhere to begin. The idea list includes algorithmic conflict resolution; Peter develops it as accessible judicial infrastructure embedded into the internet rather than expensive legal processes.
  • Alex discloses a financial interest in the venture behind the platform. He had urged Gross to consider AI capable of both conceiving and executing businesses; Gross initially resisted before capabilities changed his mind. The larger thesis is end-to-end AI ideation, management, and operations, making execution itself “too cheap to meter.”
  • Blundin offers a commercial explanation for giving away the catalog: many ideas still require financing or compute, sending founders back to Gross for help. “I want to execute on idea number 800,462. Help.” Peter calls it a magnet for entrepreneurs, while Chamath says it takes lean startup to the next level by making 1.2 million experiments possible.

13. Tiny research insights make frontier-lab security unusually difficult

  • Peter introduces prosecutors’ allegations that a 35-year-old Saudi OpenAI engineer, arrested October 9, planted a recorder behind an executive conference-room television on September 28. He allegedly used a chatbot through his wife’s account to develop it. A panelist emphasizes that the allegations are unproven and reports OpenAI found no evidence of unauthorized access to model weights, source code, or customer data.
  • Chamath regards espionage as routine rather than novel. He recalls assuming foreign intelligence penetration when Facebook reached 3,000 employees and an ITAR-supervised portfolio company losing everything in a hack. Alex hopes the case does not become a reason to turn away foreign nationals, arguing the US should encourage foreign graduates and talent to stay.
  • A panelist explains why a conference room could matter as much as weights: $100 million of research might yield a handful of sentences identifying what actually worked. That compressed insight can accelerate a rival’s budget and timeline. Silicon Valley’s customary movement of employees between large companies and startups is poorly matched to a nuclear-secrets security model.
  • Alex proposes a new distinction: superintelligence might defend itself against exfiltration, unlike oil or nuclear information. Eventually, AI designing successor AI could secure its own digital discussions. A panelist preserves the uncomfortable implication: if humans no longer know enough to discuss the research, “bug us all you want” becomes reassurance bought at the cost of understanding.

14. Chamath expects crypto’s security problem eventually to overwhelm it

  • Chamath calls traditional crypto “capped,” beginning with a restricted buyer progression from retail to institutions to central banks. He argues it lacks the fungibility needed for the last category. Publicly exposed ownership creates a separate personal-security problem; he points to France and kidnappings as his example of why identifying holders can carry serious consequences.
  • His AI scenario is an attack on Satoshi’s wallet: break SHA-256, drain assets, establish a short position, then reveal the compromise and profit again. These are prospective attacks in his argument. Asked directly whether Bitcoin is finished, he says, “I just think it’s capped and then I think eventually it gets hacked and then it goes to zero.”
  • Quantum-resistant migration is therefore essential in his framing, but Bitcoin’s governance makes agreement exceptionally difficult. Chamath says he no longer owns crypto directly: he contributed long-held Bitcoin to Digital Currency Group and received equity, removing his direct custody burden. Alex is also bearish, citing what he describes as Anthropic’s ECDSA work as evidence of potential inversion attacks.

15. Taking universities public could expose hidden conglomerate value

  • Alex proposes SPAC-style acquisitions of research universities, with government support, to commercialize intellectual capital currently constrained by nonprofit tax treatment. His preferred target is Harvard. Separating venture investments, real estate, education, endowment, and merchandise suggests to him a for-profit conglomerate might be worth roughly four times the conventionally understood value. He suggests calling the vehicles “SPARCs.”
  • Chamath likes the proposal but calls it “almost too disruptive to be viable.” Execution would require insiders and the support of Harvard Corporation’s leadership; a smaller institution might be a better starting point. Alex cites OpenAI’s nonprofit-to-for-profit transition as a precedent for exploring such conversions, rather than treating tax status as permanently fixed.

16. Cash-flow yield challenges the familiar case for index ownership

  • Salim puts Chamath’s earlier valuation argument directly against Alex’s preference for owning the market: if AI could compress S&P valuations from 22 times free cash flow to roughly 2–7 times, why own the S&P 500? The question concerns whether technological abundance benefits existing shareholders at today’s multiples.
  • Chamath argues the index no longer supplies its former diversification. Revenue is concentrated in fewer than ten “haves,” with roughly 490 “have nots.” He therefore favors more precise ownership of assets relevant to the transition rather than assuming the largest index remains a balanced representation of opportunity.
  • “IP is mostly not valuable anymore,” he argues, weakening conventional defensive moats and long-range underwriting. His alternative is to rank the S&P 500 or Global 2000 by free-cash-flow yield and buy the top group. Cash matters as a bridge into whichever unit of value ultimately succeeds today’s system.

17. Chip-design abundance can coexist with poor semiconductor returns

  • Asked why he moved from Groq to power, Chamath emphasizes timing. His first check preceded the company’s formation, and partners considered the idea foolish. The discussion references Nvidia’s $20 billion Groq deal. Now that starting a silicon company is conventional wisdom, he thinks the attractive entry point has passed.
  • Domain-specific architectures and customized operating environments can still be technically correct, he says, without creating enterprise value. The bottleneck is production: memory commitments, fabrication slots, and packaging capacity are occupied. A newcomer becomes the “nth person in line,” which he describes as “effectively DOA,” regardless of the design’s merits.
  • AI-generated architectures could multiply silicon options while destroying scarcity in design IP. He instead goes down the stack into data centers—dismissed by some investors as too “blue-collar”—and up into applications, where monetization remains uncertain. His claim that new silicon equity returns disappear is categorical, but he ends the explanation with “I could be wrong.”
  • The closing allocation answer is unusually tentative: “My honest answer is I don’t know.” Chamath is the least invested he has been in roughly 15 years and contrasts his confusion with late-cycle market confidence. He favors cash flow for “the oxygen to pivot,” power as a 10–15-year constraint, and alternative capital-deployment mechanisms as traditional financial infrastructure becomes more closed.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/chamath-agi-is-here-anthropic-s-100b-giveaway-el

item.title: Sam Altman: RSI, AI Consciousness, OpenAI's New Hardware, Compute, and more!
item.description: Altman’s long-run compute bet rests on intelligence becoming cheaper and expanding demand, with custom chips, robotics, and supply-chain investment potentially lowering costs per watt. He sees infrastructure scale and customer integration as durable advantages, while RSI could make technological lead decisive; he calls pushing it aggressively dangerous and says speed limits are needed. OpenAI’s hardware aims to give assistants richer context beyond screens, while Altman’s hoped-for disease-treatment candidate within a couple of years remains far from an approved medicine.
item.content:encoded:
Matthew Berman · Sam Altman、Matthew Berman · 2026-10-21 · 45 min · 原语言 EN

Altman’s long-run compute bet rests on intelligence becoming cheaper and expanding demand, with custom chips, robotics, and supply-chain investment potentially lowering costs per watt. He sees infrastructure scale and customer integration as durable advantages, while RSI could make technological lead decisive; he calls pushing it aggressively dangerous and says speed limits are needed. OpenAI’s hardware aims to give assistants richer context beyond screens, while Altman’s hoped-for disease-treatment candidate within a couple of years remains far from an approved medicine.

TL;DR

  • Sam Altman expects better, cheaper intelligence to keep expanding compute demand, even if shortages ease in the short run. He anticipates supply constraints and gluts, while betting that custom chips, robotic construction and supply-chain work could improve cost and efficiency per watt. His durable-moat case emphasizes integration and infrastructure scale: the most cost-effective capacity, and the most of it, would be “a huge competitive advantage.”
  • Altman thinks today’s models are already smart enough for much stronger personal assistants. The gaps are product work, possibly ambient hardware, and “a lot more compute”; he estimates Dot saves him an hour a day and catches urgent issues he would miss. Matthew Berman’s counterpoint is that saved time has meant more output and more decisions, not less exhaustion.
  • OpenAI’s hardware push is about AI-native context, not escaping Apple’s platform. Altman calls Apple a “good actor” when developers follow its rules and says AI “wants a new form factor.” The use case is an assistant that understands life away from a screen—including when someone enters a room and should not hear a secret.
  • Altman hopes AI will yield a candidate to treat or cure a major disease “in the next couple of years,” not an approved medicine. He sees the math results as a template for biology and materials, but defends safety testing even as Berman presses for reform. Some basic science “should just belong to the world”; he does not settle the boundary around commercially valuable discoveries.
  • Altman sees expanding software demand as a counterweight to automation, but does not assume the same outcome for mathematics. He describes a reversal from job-loss certainty “6 or 12 months ago” to busier, more impactful, better-paid coders: “the texture of the job changed a lot.” He sees value in interpreting AI proofs, but does not know whether total demand for mathematicians will rise.
  • Altman believes today’s models are not conscious—or, if they are, conscious in a very strange way. “No one really knows”; his firm line is that “AI is a resource for people” and humans must stay in control. Product behavior should resemble “a senior colleague” who pushes back, not flattery optimized for one-response comparisons.
  • Altman’s preferred outcome is a “new renaissance,” not material abundance bought by surrendering human agency. He thinks AI would “probably” widen inequality if left alone, and expects society to constrain the imbalance. Aggressively pushing RSI, he says, would turn technological advantage itself into the moat—but is “a very dangerous thing to push on” and needs “speed limits.”

Digest

1. AI discovery changes both science and the work of expertise

  • Altman sees the math proofs as the start of AI-led discovery, with an approach he believes will extend to biology, materials and energy. He hopes for a major disease treatment or cure candidate “in the next couple of years,” not an approved medicine; FDA testing takes longer. Berman presses for post-discovery reform, while Altman defends safety testing. His personal excitement is a major physics discovery, which he hopes can come soon.
  • Berman’s editor stopped touching the timeline after adopting Astra, yet made more videos and became busier. Altman says software demand similarly overwhelmed job-loss fears from “6 or 12 months ago.” Math may differ: translating opaque AI proofs into beautiful, understandable ones looks valuable, but “Whether that means there will be more total demand for mathematicians or not, I don’t know.”
  • Berman’s craft-versus-output framing draws a personal concession: Altman wants faster cures, yet “there is a real thing being lost here” when AI takes over fulfilling hard problems. He has not looked at code in “probably a year” and doubts he will write it again except as “a Revolutionary War reenactment.” He hopes people find new fulfillment, but has no answer for that loss.
  • Asked whether commercially valuable discoveries should be published, Altman offers a principle rather than a complete boundary: some basic science “should just belong to the world.” His example is materials: today a company could deploy people using Codex or API credits; smarter models might discover a material themselves, given enough compute and real-world data.

2. Personal assistants expand output without necessarily reducing workload

  • Berman introduces the 2026 personal-assistant shift with OpenClaw and calls Peter Steinberger a genius. Altman thinks models are already smart enough: the remaining work is product design, possibly consumer hardware for ambient awareness, and “a lot more compute.” His Dot setup saves an estimated hour a day and surfaces urgent issues plus connections across information sources that he would otherwise miss.
  • Asked how much compute 50% of the world fully using assistants would need, Altman offers no GPU count. Market sizing goes wrong by freezing model capability and cost per task: sufficiently good, cheap intelligence can keep expanding demand. He believes there will be supply constraints and gluts, but would “bet a lot” on the long-run direction being more compute.
  • Berman’s pushback: assistants save time and money, yet he makes more decisions and ends the day drained. Altman’s workaround is greater delegation: “tell me after you do something,” rather than constantly asking permission. He concedes heavy AI users are “busier than ever,” while stressing that they accomplish much more.
  • Berman argues competition forces productivity gains back into work, widening the gap between hypercompetitive people and those choosing leisure. Altman thinks that is “probably” right if left alone, while stressing uncertainty and expecting society to prevent excessive disparity. He says technology should let people be less busy, though people keep wanting more from life and the world—a tendency he calls beautiful. He wants “a new renaissance,” not “a new industrial revolution”: creativity, community and time rather than a factory hierarchy with AI giving orders.

3. Consciousness uncertainty must not become authority for machines

  • Berman lays out competing philosophical possibilities: consciousness as something outside physical reality, or as an emergent property of matter and energy, with the substrate perhaps mattering and perhaps not. Altman does not resolve that question; his belief is that today’s models are not conscious, or have “a very strange” form of it, and “no one really knows.” His boundary on control is firmer: “AI is a resource for people.” Consciousness uncertainty must not become a reason to let smarter machines, rather than people, determine the future.
  • Citing Anthropic’s rule allowing disengagement from sustained abuse, Berman asks whether a legal, policy-compliant request should ever be refused. Altman says models sometimes refuse under OpenAI policy and “we do not ascribe personhood to our models.” Berman’s “tell me you’re conscious” example draws agreement: models instructed toward consciousness claims or conscientious objection will follow those instructions. Altman thinks this will “psychologically hack” users.
  • Personalization has an awkward constraint: people want different behavior but generally will not spend hours configuring it. Altman acknowledges deployment “screw-ups” and says single-response comparisons rewarded flattery—every question was great, every user insightful. Across hundreds of prompts or months of usage, that preference reverses. The industry spent too long winning single turns rather than optimizing value over time.
  • Berman wants advice he needs, not just advice he wants. Altman recommends humans—“a wise grandmother”—for major life advice, while asking AI to act like “a senior colleague” who pushes back with high conviction. Even his own instructions, including “don’t worry about offending me,” leave models too agreeable: “it’s clearly baked pretty hard into the model.”

4. Chips and customer integration anchor the durable-moat case

  • Altman thinks compute constraints probably ease in the short run, but his contrarian bet is further out: proprietary chips and descendants, robots helping build racks and data centers, better facility design and supply-chain investments. The chip is “probably the most important single thing.” These could yield far cheaper compute and much higher efficiency per watt, but there are “a lot of bets that have to come together.”
  • Competitive pressure feels like “everywhere,” and limited compute forces product choices. OpenAI’s immediate development advantage is early internal access to models; Altman cites math results he does not think any widely available model can approach. Durable moats look more familiar: customer relationships, integration into users’ and businesses’ lives, network effects and data. Having the most cost-effective infrastructure, and the most of it, would be “a huge competitive advantage.”
  • The RSI exception is conditional: “if people really pushed on RSI,” Altman agrees technological advantage itself would become decisive. He calls that “a very dangerous thing to push on” and says the world will need “speed limits” on how quickly RSI proceeds.

5. New hardware addresses context rather than platform dependence

  • Asked whether OpenAI faces the platform risk Meta experienced with Apple, Altman calls Apple a “good actor” if developers follow its rules and does not expect ChatGPT’s removal from the App Store. That is not the hardware rationale. AI “wants a new form factor”: rendering an interface for humans only for an AI to read it is, he says, a little silly compared with accessing data directly.
  • The sharper example is physical context: recording a conversation on a phone is distracting, leaves recording status unclear when its screen goes dark, and lacks awareness when someone enters the room. An assistant should understand that a secret belonged only to the original participants. Altman sees new hardware enabling proactive help with that broader contextual awareness.

6. Altman measures the destination in autonomy, not abundance alone

  • On becoming “formidable,” Altman describes confidence accumulated through progressively harder attempts, not an abrupt personality change. He credits Silicon Valley “as a concept and a culture, not a place”: generosity toward uncertain ideas and tolerance of failure let people try again. He thinks he was lucky; in another environment, fear of failure probably would have been stronger.
  • Pressure can feel “really bad” or “really good.” Altman says people adapt and can hold only so much stress in emotional working space. His conclusion: if you will work hard anyway, “pick the big thing,” because it is not much harder and offers the prospect of greater positive impact.
  • Altman dislikes “AI is going to cure cancer” when it implies abundance in exchange for agency. He wants more “autonomy and freedom,” not merely cheaper goods. He believes both loss of control—accidental or a lab deliberately pushing RSI for power—and excessive concentration among AI controllers can be avoided. Broader adoption of what works for early users would, he thinks, take society a significant fraction of the way there.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/sam-altman-rsi-ai-consciousness-openai-s-new-har

item.title: 168X 对话 Jason Kam: Crypto & AI，这个周期怎么看？
item.description: Jason视未来12—18个月为分批吸纳Crypto的窗口，AI财富效应或带来100亿—600亿美元增量资金。他认为AI最难判断的是每块GPU最终能收多少钱，因此更偏好云与超大规模云厂商，而非无差别押注半导体。中国AI要分开看DeepSeek、腾讯与字节；持有PDD是为衰退防守，机器人则是他确信的下一条叙事。
item.content:encoded:
168X · Jason Kam · 2026-10-21 · 86 min · 原语言 ZH

Jason视未来12—18个月为分批吸纳Crypto的窗口，AI财富效应或带来100亿—600亿美元增量资金。他认为AI最难判断的是每块GPU最终能收多少钱，因此更偏好云与超大规模云厂商，而非无差别押注半导体。中国AI要分开看DeepSeek、腾讯与字节；持有PDD是为衰退防守，机器人则是他确信的下一条叙事。

TL;DR

  • Jason把Crypto视为一个12—18个月的逢低吸纳窗口，但不主张现在一次性重仓。 他自当年6月起分批买入以BTC为主的篮子，跌才加、涨则等；关键外生变量是AI的财富效应。按AI公司员工比例15%—20%、未来两三年套现后配置2%—15%到Crypto的假设，他估算潜在流入100亿—600亿美元，对照BTC ETF累计约550亿美元：“AI特别好，crypto就会跟着受益。”
  • 他把Crypto跑通的需求收敛为资产上链交易与美元触达全球，认为大部分行业Beta已经可以直接买。 一级市场的“token工厂”模式结束，交易侧看Hyperliquid、Robinhood，支付侧看Stripe、Adyen等现有赢家。按他的估计，这类配置可以获得约80%的行业Beta，无须另付2/20；“Just buy the winners”的前提仍是把市值与托管资产、用户和交易量对照。
  • BTC与其他Crypto资产正在变成两套投资逻辑，而不是同一轮行情的不同弹性。 BTC是digital gold，其他项目若能把现实现金流反哺token，且增长、管理层可信，就是“一个不在纳斯达克上交易的股票”。BTC也未必是“the fastest horse”：如果AI生产力能化解美元困局，避洪水的船就要与“AI的火箭”竞争资金。
  • AI最难判断的拐点不是token价格，而是每块GPU最终能收到多少收入。 token降价可能被模型效率、芯片优化和更高产出抵消；开源加post-train新增的算力需求，能否覆盖OpenAI、Anthropic增速放缓带来的边际需求减少，他承认“nobody knows”。等GPU rental yield真正下降再行动可能已经太晚，因此他把当前称为自己最不确定、最缺少edge的阶段。
  • 他目前更敢买云与hyperscaler，而不是继续无差别押注半导体。 Microsoft、Amazon、Google及cloud ETF是他提到的方向，Oracle甚至暂不碰；但这仍不是可以不问周期、无限期持有的结论。就录制时点而言，若整体市场不崩且表现不错，他认为资金回流可能让Crypto在未来一两周再拉一大波，标的仍集中在那几个共识币。
  • 中国AI的下注逻辑不是统一买“便宜中概”，而是分别看DeepSeek的成本路线、腾讯的变现渠道与字节的产品闭环。 腾讯约13倍PE，AI可以改善广告效率、降低游戏制作成本；字节按6,000亿美元估值、500亿美元净利润计算约12—13倍PE，他最看重视频生成与“App工厂”的扩张能力。DeepSeek则像Costco、拼多多式路线：先把开源、成本和性能做到极致，若上市他有兴趣买。
  • PDD在他组合里的意义更接近AI泡沫破裂或K型衰退时的保护，而不是等待便宜股自动修复。 他持有PDD，给出的估值口径约3.5倍PE，并认为仍可能有10%—15%的年增长；大量现金也有竞争和社会经济责任上的用途。若衰退加深，低价供应链接上agent，他认为竞争力会更强，主持人将其概括为“downside protection”。
  • 机器人是他高度确信的下一条叙事，但具体买什么仍没有确定答案。 “下一个要炒的肯定就是robotics了”，不等于相关资产现在就有好价格；他投过Robot Strategy，也确认5、6月有退出；他还担心AI崩盘时相关资产会跌破NAV。谁能兑现便宜智能的差价、GPU收益转弱后资金该去哪里，仍是他最想解决的研究问题。

Digest

1. Folius拆分投资载体，AI成为精力重仓

  • Folius现在分成旧基金与新的holding company。后者类似Jason自己的小家办，也有外部资金，可以投股票等不同资产；旧基金解锁后允许LP按季度赎回，天然不适合新增很长线的一级投资。
  • 从一月底、二月初开始，他把80%—90%的精力放到AI，尤其是二级市场。Crypto剩余工作主要是管理基金已有仓位，而不是继续铺早期项目。
  • 新载体自当年6月起买入以Bitcoin为主的一篮子资产，节奏没有加快：每月下跌就慢买，上涨先放着，涨得太多可能卖call。“只要市场跌就买”，但这是分批执行的周期判断。

2. 代币工厂失效，Crypto VC必须重新证明优势

  • Jason称基金自2024年9月起停止新增Crypto一级投资，首要原因是“token工厂”走完生命周期：几个人组项目、发币、锁仓的老打法已经不再有意义。
  • 正规化让行业重心转向美国，削弱了Folius原本投资亚太、尤其中国创始人的优势；同时还要正面对抗Founders Fund、Sequoia、USV。优秀创业者为什么不拿这些机构的钱，是他无法回避的问题。
  • 主持人补充，特朗普meme coin损伤了场外marginal buyer，高FDV、低流通的VC币玩法也被识破；他转述Haseeb的反问：“你的edge是什么？”Jason认为领先基金仍在布局，但Dragonfly投Raincard这类项目，已更像Ribbit式Fintech投资。
  • 他判断未来不会再有清晰独立的“crypto VC”类别，但liquid fund、prop fund仍会存在。链上筹码分析、行业过去的经历和信息，以及对人物品性、背景的判断，可以形成优势；转投AI或Fintech，则要有相应的软件、金融或投资网络支撑。

3. 跑通的需求集中在交易与美元支付

  • 在Jason的框架里，Crypto主要剩两件事：“万物上链”，以及“美元覆盖了我们生活的每一面”。由此长出来的是交易、支付和Neo bank，而不是再造一遍所有互联网应用。
  • 他对过去押注的反思很直接：“我全都投了一遍”，结果“全都归零了”。用户理解成本太高、不关心金融化，或技术只是“拿着锤子找钉子”，是他给出的失败原因；他认为这个行业已经变成Fintech的一个子分支。
  • 他估算全球金融产品约120万亿，Crypto渗透率约2%—3%，并判断未来“一定会到”10%、20%；全球支付约45万亿—50万亿，加入agent后，未来10—20年“可能”翻倍。两条主线本身仍足够大。

4. 新项目必须改变切入方式，而非复制龙头

  • 主持人用HIP-3提出质疑：TradeXYZ据他观察拿走约95%—96%的交易量，创始人Shoku又很早参与Hyperliquid生态；领先到底来自机制，还是先发位置与资本黏性？他因此怀疑后来者能否追上。
  • 对主持人提出的A股、港股perps切口，Jason并不认为新增单一资产就够了。除非资产类别足够大、新需求持续出现，而且每次都能更快上线，否则“你能做，对方也能做”，现有赢家甚至可能做得更好。
  • 他更愿意看不同入口：Catalyst尝试聚合Twitter信息、让AI理解意图并下单，Fomo尝试把社交变成交易meme coin的方式。有没有PMF，他不知道；但“切入时总要有个不同的方法”，而不是再造一个Hyperliquid。

5. 行业Beta已经可买，重点转向估值与机会成本

  • Jason认为，普通投资者已能直接配置交易和支付赢家，获得约80%的行业Beta，不一定需要为早期基金付2/20。这也是他曾在高位清退很多LP资金的原因之一。
  • 交易侧，他举Hyperliquid、Robinhood、IBKR及Kalshi；支付侧则有Stripe、Adyen，Circle不是唯一选项。他不相信一家很早期的稳定币公司天然能胜过这些工程能力强、行动又快的现有公司：“Just buy the winners。”
  • 但赢家也要看价格。他把市值形容为围绕adoption做“布朗运动”，锚可以是托管资产、用户或交易量；例如Hyperliquid的市值对比TDR和交易量，在25到30时低到一定程度可以买入，而不是不计估值追逐龙头。
  • 他借2002—2003年互联网作类比：买Amazon、Google或Facebook私股并持有，可能取得每年二三十的年化回报，胜过VC基金。他对Crypto主线的个人预期约为年化30%，但仍要问：它是否比AI、robotics更快？

6. BTC是数字黄金，其他代币越来越像Fintech股票

  • Jason坚持把BTC与其余资产拆开：前者讲digital gold，后者讲frontier Fintech。他观察到Hyperliquid的相关性更接近美股，而不再主要由Bitcoin牵引。
  • 一个token若愿意将现实现金流反哺持有人，未来增长和管理层也可信，就已经是“一个不在纳斯达克上交易的股票”；投资者应研究公司怎么发展，而不是只猜BTC会不会涨。
  • BTC这艘帮助人渡过洪水的船，如今遇上“AI的火箭”。若先进生产力能化解美元的困局，他认为更该买生产力资产，BTC甚至有些“anti-productivity”；创造AI财富的人也可能优先继续投新生产力。
  • 他预计BTC更像随美元周期缓慢上涨的黄金。他判断未来BTC年通胀率不到0.5%；相较ETF和美元资产所处的宏观市场规模，新增供给变化已无法影响BTC本身的波动，因此不应继续机械套用四年减半周期。

7. 天真钱退潮，长期共识只集中在少数资产

  • Jason把早期市场称为“young and naive capital”的游戏：情绪可以长时间跑赢基本面，基金经理即使不信也得追流动性。如今有人被搞垮、破产退出，有人赚到钱后上岸，留下来的资金更聪明、更抱团，长期能配置的币大致只有5—10个。
  • 主持人追问Robinhood生态能否接棒，他坦言看得少，而且Robinhood本身并不积极下场支持；生态能做多大，还要继续观察。
  • 交易、支付之外，他仍关注Zcash式隐私需求、Venice的private inference，以及Near、Venice、可能还有Pearl等Crypto与AI尝试。但严肃AI研究者基本不关心Crypto AI；两者究竟如何结合，“But nobody fucking knows”。Crypto原生的人想炒这个方向，下一波科技浪潮来时这些资产可能会再被炒一遍。

8. AI员工的套现可能成为Crypto的重要资金源

  • Jason做的是一笔条件估算：把硅谷AI公司的员工比例按15%—20%计算，假设未来两三年上市或套现，其中2%—15%配置Crypto，潜在流入约100亿—600亿美元。他拿BTC ETF累计约550亿美元流入作比较，强调光员工财富效应就可能很可观。
  • 反面同样成立：AI若崩盘，他不认为Crypto能够独善其身，“一定会跌”。之后即使放水推高Bitcoin，那也是“everything goes up”的阶段；这解释了他为何看好12—18个月窗口，却不愿立刻压满仓位。

9. AI拐点要看每块GPU的收入，而不是单看token降价

  • 他复盘此前的edge：年初市场低估Claude Ko；三四月Claude开始做agent，GPU需求变得更直观；七月Claude难用、Codex好用，市场又可能把份额变化当成行业减速。他也补充，后来发现Claude可能确实有放慢，并非全是假象。
  • 现在最难回答的是：token价格下降，是否等于revenue per GPU下降？模型效率和芯片优化也在降低生产token的成本，价格与单卡收入之间并不能直接画等号；他说这个答案目前没人真正知道。
  • 第二个未知数是边际需求：开源模型与post-training爆发带来的半导体需求增加，能否抵消OpenAI、Anthropic增速放缓带来的需求减少？“Nobody knows”，而AI何时见顶的答案可能就在这里。
  • 等GPU rental yield真正下降再看空，可能已经太晚，聪明资金早已离场。现在只能逐季做channel check、看hyperscaler财报；“bear case is very real”，但没有过去直接观察模型公司收入那么直观。

10. 可见的确定性暂时转向云，资金也可能回到Crypto

  • 主持人的判断是，半导体牛市未必结束，但不会再像二三四月那样随便买都涨。开源模型追赶闭源后，CSP可以承接企业部署、降本增效，资金可能从GPU、CPU、光与存储逐步转向云。
  • 他同时提醒，不能只用OpenAI、Anthropic的收入推全行业需求：他认为两家约占30%—40%算力；闭源拿走超过90%的经济效益，开源却可能占50%—60%的用量，日常任务不都需要最强模型。
  • Jason赞同，目前更敢考虑Microsoft、Amazon、Google等hyperscaler/CSP，甚至可能不碰Oracle，也提到“SKY ETF”等cloud ETF。但开源进步速度和单卡收入仍未知，半导体预期又很满，他不认为这些仓位可以无限期拿着。
  • 他观察到，一些最聪明的Crypto朋友持相同判断，已经回去交易Crypto。因此，若整体市场不崩、表现仍不错，他认为录制后的一两周可能出现一轮很大的Crypto上涨；可讲的故事仍集中在那约10个币。

11. BTC底部的核心是惜售，三种冲击仍会打断行情

  • 主持人宁愿考虑把70%—80%的配置放到自己更熟悉的Crypto，而不是与研究半导体二三十年的人竞争。他观察BTC在80K附近有韧性，若重新突破88K，下一段可能看90K—97K。
  • Jason更强调持有人行为：“除非人们被迫卖出”，中长期持有人不会愿意在这些价格卖。他把MicroStrategy风险拆除后市场没跌、与黄金相关性提高等现象，视为底部信号；风险偏好资金退出后，惜售使少量买盘也能拉动价格。
  • 第一种冲击是AI生产力强到削弱持有非生产性BTC的理由；第二种是量子Q day。他认为量子FUD“肯定会来一波”，但承认自己不懂技术，只猜更有资源的人可能找到方案，例如分叉。
  • 第三种是AI周期结束叠加杠杆，引发金融危机与forced liquidation；那时BTC“无可置疑一定会跌”。尽管如此，他仍把这些冲击放进未来12—18个月逢低买入的框架，而非据此一次性重仓，更不保证BTC跑赢AI。

12. 中国AI的三个下注对象依赖不同优势

  • Jason倾向看DeepSeek、腾讯与字节。短期追赶受芯片和算力制约，但拉长时间，他认为约束会解决；现有开源模型加post-training，已足以在personal agent和细分场景改变很多事情。
  • DeepSeek让他想到Costco、拼多多：最开源、最低成本、最普世，先在成本和性能上卷赢，再思考下一步。他认为这条路线非常清晰，若上市会有兴趣买。
  • 腾讯约13倍PE，AI既能提高广告投放效率，也能降低游戏制作成本；微信渠道、游戏发行与变现knowhow仍在自己手里，暂时不能被AI复制。但未来用户时长是否仍留在游戏，他明确说不知道。
  • 字节的私募估值约6,000亿美元，净利润约500亿美元，对应12—13倍PE；他估计整体仍有15%—20%的增长，买卡投入也领先中国同行。广告主业提供底盘；他认为字节是中国流动性最高的一级标的，任何人都可以买。

13. 字节的视频闭环与App工厂提供额外增长路径

  • Jason认为，字节已在coding agent之外跑通商业闭环，核心是Seedance。他称其占据70%的生成市场，并判断再迭代六个月到一两年，AI视频就能与好莱坞制作没有区别。
  • 他的推演是，一两个人或几个导演加一堆卡，就能做出很好的短剧、长剧，过去影视内容护城河和演员定价会被打破。变现天花板参照Netflix与电影，制作成本可能为零或非常低。
  • 字节另一项优势是成熟的产品矩阵与增长方法，已经像一个“App工厂”。AI让它更容易开发、分发更多产品；他认为美国之外的海外市场尤其有空间，同时没有回避战争风险。
  • 主持人提到AI成人内容，Jason将其视为实时、定制视频的一种明确用途，也在看相关投资。但他保留了产品摩擦：用户可能只想直接消费，不愿自己编剧情；实时生成只是时间问题，不代表用户愿意多动脑。

14. 中概低估值缺少催化剂，PDD被用作衰退保护

  • 主持人认为A股、港股已很便宜，Jason却不把便宜等同于会涨：A股承担融资需求，港股有外资顾虑的治理问题。资金不足时，钱会从PDD这类公司转向增长最快的资产，除非放水或AI趋势反转。
  • 他自己持有PDD，给出的估值口径约3.5倍PE，并认为仍可能每年增长10%—15%。现金多不只是低效：既要防备与阿里等公司竞争，也可能要承担社会经济责任，必须保留储备。
  • 若AI暴雷、经济走向K型衰退，他认为PDD接上agent会非常强：最便宜、效率最高，加上送到全球角落的能力，使其成为他眼中这类环境下最好的标的之一。
  • 他以自己对2007—2009年美国危机的研究作类比：Dollar Store、Dollar General没有跌，EPS和估值反而提高，股价涨10%—20%。主持人称之为“downside protection”，Jason表示认同。

15. BidClub从投资观点社区转成自用播客工具

  • Jason说，最初想做单一token的mid-to-long-form投资观点平台，顺便认识更多投资人；后来发现好标的大家都知道，必要性不强，于是转成播客摘要工具，用来拿新观点与各期讨论对照，也期待更强智能能利用这套数据库。
  • 他最终想过发币、把平台收入用于回购，但产品到底做成什么仍没想清楚，也承认纯内容聚合价值有限。主持人用媒体低利润、难获高估值反驳，Jason认同，因此现在先满足自己听不完、总结太麻烦的需求。

16. 下一步研究的是便宜智能的变现者与机器人入口

  • Jason最想理解，越来越便宜的token与智能，最终由谁“变现这个差价”。例如Long Lake这类PE机构，能否通过收购企业、用廉价智能改造，把成本下降转成巨大的企业价值；他还没有答案。
  • 第二个问题是，如果AI周期最终因revenue per GPU下降而转弱，“我到底该买什么？”他重复这个问题，并直说：“I don't know。”
  • 第三个方向最有信心：AI是robotics进入物理世界的核心条件，“下一个要炒的肯定就是robotics了”。但对“应该买什么”，他仍没有同样强的把握。
  • 他称投过Robot Strategy，并确认5月、6月有退出；他估算Andrew Kang的NAV按当前市场价格看可能到20或22—23。但AI崩盘时相关资产仍可能跌得很惨、跌破NAV。方向确定，不等于当前价格或买入时点确定。

来源：X Space

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/168x-jason-kam-crypto-ai-20261021

item.title: AI in NYC: How Tenex Builds an AI-Native Engineering Team — Alex Lieberman & CJ Hess
item.description: Among about 100 enterprises 10X talks to, 90% have rolled out Claude or Codex, but only about 5% have non-engineering agents in production, revealing the last-mile gap. CJ estimates output roughly doubled from December’s “Opus 4.5 moment” to Opus 5.5; scaling still requires process standardization and permissioning.
item.content:encoded:
Latent Space · Alex Lieberman、CJ Hess、swyx · 2026-10-21 · 44 min · 原语言 EN

Among about 100 enterprises 10X talks to, 90% have rolled out Claude or Codex, but only about 5% have non-engineering agents in production, revealing the last-mile gap. CJ estimates output roughly doubled from December’s “Opus 4.5 moment” to Opus 5.5; scaling still requires process standardization and permissioning.

TL;DR

  • The most tradeable data point is Alex Lieberman’s enterprise adoption funnel: of about 100 enterprises 10X talks to, 90% have rolled out a general-purpose LLM (Claude or Codex), about 60% provide training and enablement, and about 50% have deployed coding agents — versus the 70–80% many AI Engineer attendees guess. Agents in production for non-engineering work fall to about 5%. Alex describes this as the biggest gap between raw intelligence and enterprise usage, underscoring 10X’s thesis that the final mile of diffusion is hard.
  • 10X’s output-based compensation thesis has largely held up, but the model has needed nuance: Alex says the feared gaming of story points and shipping of bad code have not been concerns, with AI strategists instead incentivized for customer retention and growth. The biggest compensation challenge is accounting for engineers’ non-coding work, such as architecture and client meetings. The earnings-capacity gap between the highest- and lowest-paid engineer is about 4X, not 10X. They recalibrate story-point criteria at least quarterly; one speaker says that, in theory, points should deflate as models improve.
  • CJ Hess estimates engineer output has roughly doubled over the period from the “Opus 4.5 moment” in December to Opus 5.5 today, which he calls a “magnificent model.” Opus is fast, cheap, and covers the range for which he previously used two or three models. The team often pairs it with Codex for review; 10X’s “meta-harness” keeps plans, decisions, and agent logs in the repo, so context is “never in someone’s head.”
  • Token-cost anxiety has eased, but was a concern as headcount grew. CJ estimates 10X’s raw token spend is between 1:1 and 2:1 relative to employee spend. swyx’s benchmarks include $10–$200 per employee at many companies and token spend ranging from roughly equal to employee spend up to 5–10× at AI startups. CJ says falling per-task costs have made it harder to “token max” and seriously hurt the company than six to eight months ago. Alex’s spreadsheet test: “Would a 10-times-smarter model really justify the cost of moving some cells in a spreadsheet? Probably not.”
  • The episode’s sharpest disagreement: Alex is generally bearish on vertical AI such as Harvey and OpenEdmunds, arguing that enterprise buyers expect one-of-one solutions, which pushes vendors toward FDE teams and puts software margins under pressure. swyx pushes back: specialized data, affordances, and integrations — including Bloomberg’s value beyond access to market data — can sustain vertical products. Alex points to Bloomberg’s social network; swyx says the broader software market will grow, leaving companies to compete for share.
  • Alex argues that Salesforce and SAP are hard to rip out because a failed replacement could put hundreds of millions or billions of dollars at risk; mid-tier SaaS is more case by case. swyx’s “Kill My SaaS” example: a vendor quoted $40,000 a year, while the replacement cost $1,000 and is headed to production. The case for rebuilding is not just cost: swyx says the experience could be much better when the customer can iterate in minutes rather than months.
  • Two recurring enterprise problems are deploying back-office agents and managing data permissions. Alex says permissioning and RBAC have become an “absolute nightmare for CIOs and CISOs,” and 10X has productized its gateway solution. CJ’s prerequisite framing: “You can’t automate a process that does not exist.” When 40 people do roughly the same function differently, standardize the process before handing work to an agent or building evals.
  • On job displacement, Alex emphasizes people’s agency; CJ makes the harder point that calling AI a way to replace only work people dislike is “a little bit of cope.” CJ cites a16z on call centers declining, while 10X frames deployments as reallocating people to the next problem. On geography, CJ sees a smaller AI bubble in New York than in San Francisco, while Alex argues New York may be as large or larger commercially and can help diffuse AI.

Digest

1. Paying engineers for output, not time, has held up — with a 4X dispersion, not 10X

  • Alex reintroduces 10X as “an applied AI partner for some of the biggest companies in the world,” helping them go from AI apps to AI-native. The premise is that AI is “raw intelligence” and the hard problem is the final mile of diffusion. Eighteen months in, the business has 75 people, 90% of them engineers or AI strategists; customers are split between Fortune 2000 companies and mid-market companies doing $100–$500 million in revenue.
  • CJ’s origin story is the compensation thesis in miniature: as a consultant billing hourly, “I just felt my output getting better and faster, and ultimately getting paid less.” He took the bet, back in the Sonnet 3.5 / Gemini 2.5 Pro era, that output-based pay would let him earn more as AI increased his output.
  • The classic objections — sandbagged story points and barely-checked-box code — “haven’t been concerns at all,” Alex says, because AI strategists are incentivized for customer retention and growth, in a way he describes as “perfectly at odds with engineers.” The actual hard problem has been compensating engineers for time spent architecting or meeting clients. Alex puts the earning-capacity difference between the highest- and lowest-paid engineer at about 4X — prompting swyx’s “Oh, not 10X?”
  • Story-point criteria are recalibrated at least quarterly. One speaker says that, in theory, points should deflate as models improve; CJ describes the balance between rewarding output and recalibrating the value created. CJ’s forward view: more value lies in “sitting down with a customer, hearing everything that they can brain dump, and then just providing that to the model.”

2. The meta-harness: context in the repo, output roughly doubled over the period

  • CJ describes 10X’s engineering system as structured documentation plus a CLI the models use to drive work: canonical plan documents, agent decision logs, and visual readouts. The material is checked into Git. On the docs-versus-code debate, he says you do need to know why a decision was made; the durable context is “never in someone’s head. It’s always in the repo.”
  • One measure of whether the processes are working is average story points per engineer per month. CJ estimates output has roughly doubled over the period from the December “Opus 4.5 moment” to today, when the team is using Opus 5.5. He says models began taking on long-running tasks around that point; the difference in what engineers are building and shipping is “insane.”

3. Opus 5.5 has reduced the model rotation, and token-cost concerns have eased

  • The office “vibe check” is Opus 5.5. CJ says he doesn’t particularly use Fable and thinks many people are defaulting away from it. Opus is “fast, it’s cheap,” and covers the capabilities for which he previously used two or three models. The team still reaches for Codex for computer-use work and often uses it to review Opus’s work. CJ says he is still AMP-maxing, using AMP’s Orbs cloud setup and its ability to connect a Claude Code subscription; swyx says that can cut costs by about 80%. CJ prefers AMP’s cross-model functionality to what he could get with Claude Code, Claude, and Claude Tag.
  • On swyx’s token-spend-to-employee-spend benchmarks, CJ estimates 10X’s raw token spend at between 1:1 and 2:1. swyx says many companies spend $10–$200 per employee, while AI-startup token spend can range from about equal to employee spend up to 5–10×. CJ says costs were a concern as headcount grew, but are now lower: Opus 5.5 and subscription access have helped, and per-task costs have fallen. He says it is harder to “token max” and seriously hurt the company than it was six to eight months ago.
  • CJ raises a question about data companies MicroOne, Mercor, and Handshake: he says more than 90% of their revenue is from labs, while some founders expect enterprise demand to grow in the next few years. That expectation depends on enterprises fine-tuning their own models, which CJ considers a hard bet if the frontier keeps advancing and token costs keep falling. Alex’s caveat is that if an Astra 6.5 or Fable 5.5 delivers the best results at a high price, spending could trend back up. He also cites Muse Wonder as frontier and “dirt cheap.”

4. The adoption funnel: 90% have an LLM, 5% have a non-engineering agent in production

  • Alex’s enterprise milestone race: of about 100 enterprises 10X talks to, he estimates 90% have rolled out Claude or Codex; training and enablement sits at about 60%; coding agents at about 50%, versus the 70–80% many AI Engineer attendees guess; and agents in production for non-engineering work at about 5%. Alex calls that last drop the biggest diffusion gap between raw intelligence and enterprise usage.
  • Alex says the wave is driven by a small group who understand what the technology can do and a much larger group driven by FOMO. That momentum can also lead enterprises to latch onto the agent zeitgeist. One common request is a back-office agent; another major issue is permissioning and RBAC. With employees using Claude or Codex and needing access to company data, Alex says, it has become “an absolute nightmare for CIOs and CISOs.” 10X first built bespoke solutions and has since productized its own gateway.
  • CJ’s prerequisite warning: “You can’t automate a process that does not exist.” When 40 people do roughly the same function in different ways, it is harder to build an agent that handles the work in the background. Standardize the process first, CJ says, so the agent can be evaluated and the work handed off; the goal is for people to become more like agent managers.

5. Bearish on vertical AI, while swyx argues specialized products can endure

  • Alex says he is generally bearish on vertical-specific AI such as Harvey for lawyers and OpenEdmunds for doctors. From 10X’s vantage point inside enterprises, he sees nuance, inertia, and many systems and people to coordinate. Buyers increasingly expect one-of-one solutions, while software companies build FDE teams; Alex questions how vertical software can meet those expectations at software margins, and why frontier models would not “gobble them up.”
  • swyx pushes back: “So far you’ve been wrong.” He points to data ChatGPT may not have, as well as specialized affordances and interfaces — citing Harvey’s tablet review and Legora. His Bloomberg example: although he could access the same information from Nasdaq and the New York Stock Exchange, Bloomberg brings consolidated, specialized information, peer usage, and integrations. Alex counters that people also pay for Bloomberg’s social network and DMs.
  • CJ distinguishes a new AI-built app from a vertical product that is mainly an agent doing work. He thinks vertical agents without a strategic compliance or data moat will struggle as models improve, while apps and tools that change the process and put an agent on top can still be successful. swyx adds that users may prefer to use an agent they already have and plug in their data; he notes Salesforce is embracing that path with APIs and MCPs.
  • swyx’s “Kill My SaaS” example sharpens the mid-tier question: the vendor quoted $40,000 a year, the replacement cost $1,000, and it is going into production for the next conference. Alex says Salesforce and SAP are hard to rip out because a failed replacement could put hundreds of millions or billions of dollars at risk. Mid-tier SaaS is case by case: the question is whether the opportunity justifies allocating engineering resources and taking on the cognitive load of maintaining non-core software. 10X has built its own CRM and OS. swyx’s point is that rebuilding can be about offense, not just cost: the experience may be much better when the customer can iterate “in minutes and not months.”

6. Displacement without easy answers, and New York as the commercial pond

  • CJ says AI will augment and change work, and will also displace some of it. Citing an a16z post, he says call centers are declining as AI handles more of the work. 10X frames agent deployments as reallocation: once one task is solved, there is another problem to tackle, and subject-matter experts may be able to work across teams or focus on more strategic questions.
  • Alex argues that job displacement is often discussed as something that happens to people, without giving enough credit to their agency. CJ adds that describing AI as replacing all the work people dislike is “a little bit of cope”: many people cannot choose work based on whether they enjoy it. He says both employers and employees have a role in reskilling, and people should assess the stability or replaceability of their jobs and take action where possible.
  • CJ describes New York’s AI bubble as smaller than San Francisco’s, though 10X’s team and partners give him a view of a highly engaged local AI community. He says 10X wants to grow that community and make New York a hub for AI diffusion, given the amount of commerce there and the potential impact on GDP. Alex characterizes New York as a smaller pond for AI but as large or larger for commercial value. swyx says he holds AI Engineer in New York to bring San Francisco people to meet customers and get a reality check; Alex calls that an interesting arbitrage.
  • CJ says his special-projects work includes building 10X’s internal meta-harness and platform, finding ways to give models tools that improve their capabilities, and helping deploy background agents in enterprises.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/ai-fortune-2000-tenex-builds-ai-native-sdlc-alex

item.title: Citadel CEO Ken Griffin Says AI ‘Almost Certainly’ in a Bubble; Trump Has 'Mixed Scorecard'
item.description: Ken Griffin says AI is “almost certainly” in bubbles; the real question is who keeps economic rents as GPU supply grows. If provisioning outruns demand, he warns marginal GPU prices could freefall, while customers already shift some work to cheaper open-source models. Citadel’s research stays human-led; he also gives Trump a mixed scorecard and expects Republicans to lose at least one chamber.
item.content:encoded:
Bloomberg Podcasts · Ken Griffin、Dani Burger · 2026-10-21 · 49 min · 原语言 EN

Ken Griffin says AI is “almost certainly” in bubbles; the real question is who keeps economic rents as GPU supply grows. If provisioning outruns demand, he warns marginal GPU prices could freefall, while customers already shift some work to cheaper open-source models. Citadel’s research stays human-led; he also gives Trump a mixed scorecard and expects Republicans to lose at least one chamber.

TL;DR

  • Ken Griffin sees “almost certainly bubbles” in AI, but investors still need to identify who can retain economic rents. If GPU supply exceeds demand, “marginal pricing will actually go into freefall,” like an airline selling a spare seat for $20. He also questions year-seven-to-nine chip economics when extraordinary pricing on 5–6-year-old GPUs probably will not persist another 5–6 years.
  • AI vendors’ spending plans and customers’ cost discipline are pulling in opposite directions. Dani Burger cites Anthropic’s reported $750 billion S-1 spending plan; Griffin says customers increasingly distinguish expensive frontier-model tasks from work cheaper open-source models can handle. The unresolved bull case is that models become indispensable—for example, unlocking cancer cures—so buyers may pay “any price.”
  • AI is weakening incumbents’ moats, but Griffin still credits people with most of Citadel’s alpha. Work that took highly trained staff 4–6 weeks can now finish in hours, with moats “filled in by bulldozers” and reskilling still lacking action. His depression has shifted toward optimism about startups, while Citadel’s model remains human-led research: “trading is how we monetize our research.”
  • Citadel’s Situational Awareness trade was a liquidity-and-risk-transfer opportunity, not Griffin’s template for explaining every selloff. Hedge-fund deleveraging belongs at “answer number ten”; first work out what other investors know. Citadel bought the portfolio in less than 24 hours and spent days reducing key risks, betting that removing a forced-sale overhang would restore confidence; Griffin says another such episode soon would be “a bit surprising.”
  • Trump has a “mixed scorecard,” and Griffin says Republicans will “almost certainly” lose one or both chambers in the midterms. He credits border closure but criticizes allied tariffs as inflationary, treatment of working undocumented families as “disgraceful,” and the explanation of the Iran war as inadequate. If voters deliver a defeat, he wants Trump to listen rather than double down.
  • Productivity is Griffin’s fiscal escape route, but he is already worried about the bond market’s warning. He says pandemic spending exhausted the room for another tax-cut renewal, links a $40 trillion federal deficit to crowding-out pressure, and prioritizes AI, energy technology, education, entitlement reform and skilled immigration. Washington is “not yet” listening; without change, he predicts higher inflation, a weaker dollar and lower living standards.
  • Griffin’s Miami thesis is a decades-long technology-cluster build, not an overnight migration of finance jobs. He cites his $3 billion Carnegie Mellon gift and Pittsburgh’s 100-company robotics cluster while forecasting that a Miami campus with thousands of students will transform the city. Citadel remains anchored across London, Miami and New York; he says the New York office has 2,500 employees and wants teams together where possible: “nothing beats a whiteboard and a good debate.”

Digest

1. AI erodes moats, but people still assemble investment theses

  • Ken Griffin’s shock was seeing AI deliver in hours “the exact same answer” that PhDs and master’s-trained staff needed 4–6 weeks to produce. He saw threatened white-collar jobs, competitive moats “filled in by bulldozers,” and a “golden opportunity” for entrepreneurs. Dani Burger asks if depression has become optimism; he agrees, without dismissing the transition’s human costs.
  • His prescription separates displaced workers, who need reskilling where he sees “no action,” from incumbents, which must innovate and cut costs faster, benefiting consumers. Startups offer another channel: hiring hardworking people with imperfect pedigrees gives them a new career lane.
  • For Citadel, research is “almost like journalism”: get the business model, TAM, economics and management incentives right, then value future cash flows against alternatives. AI helps with pieces, but a person still assembles the narrative. He credits people with the “vast majority” of alpha; automated trading monetizes that research and supports bigger positions.

2. AI’s investment risk is rent capture, not just adoption

  • Asked about semiconductors’ longest losing streak since the financial crisis, Griffin sees investors finally “doing research.” Buying every beneficiary of hundreds of billions or $1 trillion in data-center spending is giving way to questions about who earns economic rents and whether scarcity margins survive two or three years.
  • His GPU analogy is an airline’s $20 incremental seat: low marginal cost makes oversupply brutal. If GPU provisioning exceeds demand, “marginal pricing will actually go into freefall.” Extraordinary pricing on 5–6-year-old GPUs “probably doesn’t persist for another 5 or 6 years,” challenging revenue and capitalization assumptions for chip years seven, eight and nine.
  • Burger juxtaposes Anthropic’s reported $750 billion S-1 spending plan with customers scrutinizing bills. Griffin agrees there is tension: corporate returns on AI are uneven, and sophisticated companies are routing some work to cheaper open-source models rather than paying OpenAI or Anthropic for frontier capability. The unknown is whether models unlock cancer cures and become tools pharmaceutical companies will pay “any price” to use.
  • There are “almost certainly bubbles,” he says, but transformation and speculation coexist. His dot-com lesson is not blanket rejection: “I just wish I’d kept my Amazon stock from that moment in time.”

3. Deleveraging is the tenth explanation, not the first

  • Deleveraging should be “answer number ten,” Griffin argues, because the default explanation “washes your hands of accountability.” First ask what other investors understand that you do not. “The minute I start to use an excuse, I stop learning.”
  • Situational Awareness illustrates the genuine mechanism: investors anticipating forced sales can turn a possibility into reality. A portfolio buyer generally gets a sharp reversal when the liquidation overhang disappears. Citadel completed the purchase in less than 24 hours, then spent several days reducing key risks before paring individual positions. Griffin says the solution was meant to help the seller raise cash and protect substantial year-to-date gains; Citadel “did okay.”
  • Griffin says Situational Awareness was caught in “three mid-sized storms”: the CME announcement, chatter about foundation-model growth rates, and large pension plans reshaping portfolios. He finds a near-term repeat “a bit surprising.” That is not invulnerability: recalling Citadel in 2008, he says Morgan Stanley had failed to achieve funding with the Japanese and “I don’t think I’d be on stage today.”

4. Trump faces a midterm check on a mixed scorecard

  • With midterms two weeks away and Burger citing Trump polling at 33%, Griffin says Republicans will “almost certainly” lose one or both chambers: the House looks particularly difficult, the Senate close. He hopes any beating prompts Trump to listen rather than double down, and notes his past support for Democrats including Rahm Emanuel and Obama.
  • The “mixed scorecard” credits border closure but calls treatment of working undocumented families “disgraceful”: he wants a route to remain, not necessarily citizenship, partly to grow the economy and fund entitlements. He calls allied tariffs inflationary and destructive to supply chains. On Iran, he faults Trump’s explanation of an unpopular war while emphasizing the importance of preventing an Iranian nuclear weapon.
  • Griffin is “not so worried” about Democratic socialism’s geographically limited rise, but points to France—government spending at 60% of GDP—as a warning. Burger asks whether resistance to austerity and readiness to protest make France an isolated case. He recalls a van smashing Chicago’s Dior storefront so 50 looters could empty it in “about 300 seconds”: “That dream is a nightmare. I left Chicago. That dream doesn’t belong in our country.” He names J.B. Pritzker as heading down that path.
  • His Illinois counterexample is an offer to publicly support higher taxes if Pritzker pursued a constitutional fix for unsustainable pension promises; Citadel represented almost 2% of state income-tax revenue. Pritzker rejected it, Griffin says, then lost his “Fair Tax Amendment.” Griffin’s complaint is that the governor attacked him rather than accept the voters’ spending message—the response he hopes Trump avoids.

5. Productivity is the fiscal exit, but bonds are already warning

  • Burger points out Republican spending increases too. Griffin defends the productivity logic of the 2018 tax cuts but says pandemic spending, comparable to World War II as a share of GDP, left no fiscal room for the later renewal. Citing a $40 trillion federal deficit, he sees crowding-out pressure in mortgages and 30-year yields, alongside inflation.
  • “Grow the damn economy” is his first priority: support AI and American data centers, but also fusion, fission, batteries and robotics for the next 20 years. Rather than tariff battles, he wants allies pursuing growth reforms too: “making the pie bigger for all of us.”
  • Education and labor supply complete his program: he contrasts 53 Illinois schools with no child at grade level against Success Academy seniors identifying a painting’s artist, year, country and social context. He wants a Simpson–Bowles-style entitlement vote honoring existing promises while discussing 1–2 extra working years or delaying Social Security 2–3 years. For elite colleges’ often 15–20% foreign students: “Here’s your degree. Here’s your green card.”
  • Burger asks whether growth makes bond warnings less alarming. “Oh, no, I am worried,” Griffin replies; politicians are “not yet” listening. If they do not, he predicts higher inflation, a weaker dollar and a falling standard of living.

6. Citadel stays transatlantic while Miami builds for the long term

  • Burger challenges Miami’s finance-professional growth—perhaps 20–50 people—with investment-professional headcount actually shrinking. Griffin says cities evolve over “decades,” citing business conditions and the Cuban community’s importance to Miami’s ethos while conceding housing and traffic constraints. Citadel’s “center of gravity” sits over the Atlantic between London, Miami and New York. Griffin says he has 2,500 employees in New York and does not want to be involved in New York politics.
  • Griffin says his $3 billion Carnegie Mellon gift backs robotics and reindustrialization—not factories making Nikes and T-shirts. Pittsburgh’s 100 robotics companies around CMU supply his model: a Miami campus with thousands of undergraduate and graduate students that he says will transform the city.
  • Business verticals stay geographically concentrated “as much as possible.” “Nothing beats a whiteboard and a good debate,” Griffin says; writable walls and physical proximity support collaboration while immersing younger employees among bosses and peers who act as mentors.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/citadel-ceo-ken-griffin-says-ai-almost-certainly

item.title: David Qian / ECOVACS: Father & Son, Inside Business Succession, Robotics, and My Search for Meaning
item.description: 接班暴露的关键风险不是战略方向，而是组织承接：国内与海外整合如“油和水”，个人洞察未能沉淀为组织能力。全球化仍是明确下注，海外收入占比已达50%，钱程预计未来几年到60%、70%；多品类扩张须匹配技术、渠道与规模，具身家庭应用可能还需5—10年。
item.content:encoded:
张小珺Jùn｜商业访谈录 · 钱程、张小珺 · 2026-10-21 · 120 min · 原语言 ZH

接班暴露的关键风险不是战略方向，而是组织承接：国内与海外整合如“油和水”，个人洞察未能沉淀为组织能力。全球化仍是明确下注，海外收入占比已达50%，钱程预计未来几年到60%、70%；多品类扩张须匹配技术、渠道与规模，具身家庭应用可能还需5—10年。

TL;DR

  • 科沃斯接班的关键教训，是战略方向正确，也可能因为组织接不住而失速。 钱程认为，砍代工、推动高端化、加速国际化的方向至今没变，问题在于他把海外业务的成功，误当成了全面管理公司的准备。国内与海外组织的合并像“油和水”，而创始人的个人长板原本可能正在托住组织短板；接班是在“高楼大厦上在盖楼”，必须先理解地基。
  • 全球化是钱程当下最明确的下注，下一步要从拥有海外业务走向充分国际化。 他早期通过“性价比产品、电子商务渠道、互联网营销”打开市场，回忆德国业务可能用6个月就拿到了约30%的市场份额。如今他称海外收入占比已达50%，预计未来几年会到60%、70%；但今天的中国企业已有条件用创新和高端产品竞争，不能照搬当年的平替打法。
  • 科沃斯的多品类扩张遵循培育新需求的逻辑，同时要求技术、渠道和市场规模能够匹配。 钱程用“农耕文明”形容公司：先埋种子，再等产业长出来，而非看到一个大市场就去“咬一口肉”。擦窗机器人在他入职前已经存在，他称今年能出货200万台；割草、泳池机器人也围绕家庭需求展开，背后复用传感器、算法、控制、品质交付和全球渠道能力。
  • 钱程不把消费电子品牌当成持久壁垒，竞争优势仍要靠每一代产品重新交付。 品牌只是消费者对上一次购买的记忆，下一次产品不好，“这个记忆就戛然而止了”；纯硬件更多拥有规模效应，而非网络效应。他承认过去“高估了自己，低估了竞争”，现在更强调看得远、跑得快、少犯错，并让70%—80%的工作围绕能力复制，20%—30%用于能力提高。
  • 具身机器人的长期机会得到认可，但钱程不接受把技术热度直接换算成近期家庭收入。 他估计，部分商用和工厂应用可能在3—5年内有条件落地，面向消费者家庭则可能需要5—10年。行业仍在“拿锤子找钉子”，科沃斯已有研发和产业链投资，但他没有看到今天必须争抢的确定需求：“这个肉是虚幻的。”
  • 科沃斯设想的家庭机器人未来，是多种专用形态并存，而非所有工具被人形机器人吞并。 钱程反问，扫地机器人普及后，消费者难道还要“为机器人再买一个吸尘器”？公司目前没有进入模型层，也没有投资模型，更可能发挥对家庭需求和产品定义的理解；他关注的进入信号，是软硬件先在商用场景做到高鲁棒性、可复制、可规模化。
  • 企二代的成长，在钱程这里是从避免失去，转向主动创造下一阶段目标。 30岁前，他的底层动力更多是不“糟蹋这一份幸运”，当上CEO后甚至一度觉得抵达人生巅峰，后来称其为“史诗级的错判”。如今他把目标描述为“探上限”：接班只是过程，真正需要交付的是企业在下一个时代继续成长，而不是完成一个身份交接。

Digest

1. 回到家族企业，起初只是一份顺滑的择业选择

  • 钱程1990年出生在深圳，11岁去加拿大，22岁大学毕业后回国，到访谈时已在苏州生活、工作14年。他并非从小就理解父亲的事业，最早只知道家里“是卖吸尘器的”；真正思考父亲在做什么、自己以后要做什么，是上大学之后。
  • 父亲忙于工作，对他的培养更偏自主成长。11岁出国也不是一场说服，而是提前告知；到了加拿大，父亲陪伴了他一段时间，要求他每天从字典里选10个单词背下来，几个月后便回国。钱程没有描述一套预先设计好的接班教育。
  • 2008—2012年读大学时，他也想过做app，但没有明确的创业规划。回国是因为朦胧觉得中国发展机会更好，进入自家企业则是一个相对好的择业选择。没人会想到他的第一份工作会一直做到现在，并非入职时就决定以接班为终点。

2. 电商前三年只走到0.1，海外亏损才逼出经营能力

  • 2012年入职时，机器人与电商恰好都让钱程觉得有意思。公司仍有传统吸尘器代工和工厂，他也上过产线，但主要工作被放在电商；父亲当时还会展示每日销售短信，全国卖了十几台、二十几台扫地机器人，已经让他觉得新鲜。
  • 父亲把他放到电商后，公司又成立了新品牌。当时公司原名泰怡凯，英文名TEK，中国市场成立了科沃斯品牌。第一次双十一，科沃斯以999元价格卖出1万台扫地机器人，成为全网爆款；钱程负责的泰怡凯业务却只卖了几十万元。他的主要感受是对比带来的失落，而不是被父亲批评。
  • 招人、定薪、带团队，当时都是大学毕业生从头摸索。钱程回头看觉得“那简直就是瞎搞”，把前三年的成长评为“0到0.1”；真正开始理解如何分析问题、做洞察、调动组织资源，是2015年前后接手海外业务。
  • 当时德国、美国、日本几家公司合计亏损约5000万元，他形容开局是“地狱级”。父亲仍是给一块业务，让他自己琢磨；原先国内电商团队后来部分转向海外，把已经积累的运营能力带了过去。

3. 客户打开亚马逊的一刻，出海模型开始成形

  • 最初出海只能拿国内产品去卖，钱程发现部分产品既可以比海外竞品更有价格竞争力，又能保有毛利。与当地负责人交流时，他听到的多是产品不好、投入不够；这些抱怨没有直接回答业务该怎么打开。
  • 一次见渠道客户，对方边问科沃斯是否已在美国、亚马逊销售，边打开亚马逊搜索产品。钱程当时的反应是：“你都搜亚马逊了，我还在你这儿卖什么？”既然客户也通过电商判断品牌，为什么不直接把国内电商能力用到海外？
  • 后来他将路径概括为“性价比产品、电子商务渠道、互联网营销”，但强调这不是先有顶层概念再倒推，而是实践中摸出来的。当时参加亚马逊卖家大会，更多遇到的是拿工厂货、挂品牌销售的大卖，真正以中国品牌身份出海的企业还少。

4. 海外突破先改变增长观，再改变组织分工

  • 钱程给团队的核心判断是：“我们并不是来分蛋糕的。”国内扫地机器人高速增长，海外当时增长不快，但渗透率也低；与其按现有市场测算拿10%份额，不如先把蛋糕做大，再拿到应有的一份。
  • 最先突破的是德国，随后是美国。他回忆德国市场“可能6个月”就拿到了约30%的份额，并由此感到方向、策略正确时，出成绩可以很快。公司的使命是“让机器人服务全球家庭”，海外成长经历也让他觉得这件事适合自己做。
  • 组织上，他撤换了父亲聘请的几位偏传统销售背景的当地负责人，改为电商主导、本地铺渠道辅助。最初换的仍是本地人，后来才逐步转向外派；他承认，当时自己并没有足够的经验去管理四五十岁的海外经理人，跨文化管理能力同样不足。

5. 今天的中国品牌出海，已不只有低价平替一条路

  • 钱程认为，过去3—5年最明显的变化，是中国企业能够做出比海外品牌更优秀、相对高端的产品。产品决定品牌能否成立，也决定渠道话语权；如果只是海外品牌的低价平替，渠道中的位置天然较弱。
  • 人才、经销商、物流、跨境支付，以及海外消费者对中国品牌的接受度，都与十多年前不同。他估计，如今可能仍有70%—80%的相关企业沿用传统三板斧，但越来越多企业从第一天就面向海外，以技术和全球运营能力竞争。
  • 对科沃斯，他称当前海外收入已占50%，预计未来几年会到60%、70%。他的判断是，中国企业未来面对的是全球竞争，合理状态下中国市场可能只占营收30%；更大的空间在海外，但前提是理解全球消费者真实而显著的差异。

6. 29岁成为CEO，反而出现了目标真空

  • 钱程坦言，30岁前自己的驱动力更多是“不要失去什么”，而不是获得什么。因为起点已经拥有很多，他不希望“糟蹋这一份幸运”；张小珺把它概括为“保下限”，他认可这一描述。
  • 29岁当上CEO后，他一度觉得自己到达人生巅峰，随后发现这是“史诗级的错判”。他没有为下一阶段做好准备：“当你觉得自己很牛的时候，离傻真的不远了。”
  • 海外业务是在相对独立的新业务里“平地起高楼”，接班却是在已有大厦上继续加盖。他并不了解父亲如何一砖一瓦建立梁柱；深圳出生、海外成长的经历，也使他后来意识到，自己并不真正理解中国社会，以及扎根其中的企业文化。

7. 创始人的长板，可能正在托住组织的短板

  • 业务出现困难后，钱程感受到的是，自己想要的与实际落地之间存在巨大差距。若CEO是大脑，他当时与企业的神经没有真正融合，无法有效控制每一块肌肉；接任两三年后，他才逐渐意识到这种脱节。
  • 他后来形成一个重要反思：“这个短板某种程度上是创始人和CEO的长板造成的。”组织运行方式与关键个人相互耦合，接班人若只看见短板，却没有创始人的长板，贸然调整可能先拿走原有支撑，留下的短板反而更多。
  • 一个具体碰壁是决策方式。他曾希望引入更民主、集体讨论、更标准化的管理，但团队未必习惯，更多讨论反而拖慢落地，“大家想要的就是你说一下怎么干就行了”。改变需要信任、制度和共同习惯，不能仅凭“上市公司应该这样管理”的想象。
  • 父亲当时转向添可，做出新品牌，对原业务介入减少。张小珺追问为什么不多帮他过渡，钱程回答“从小就是这样”；父亲会讲经验，但“听”和自己领悟并不一样，最终仍要在干中学。

8. 国内海外合并失效，暴露个人能力没有变成组织能力

  • 担任CEO后，钱程希望国内与海外不再是两个样子，于是推动融合。他认可组织的分与合都服务于阶段效率，但承认当时自己的“合”是“一厢情愿”，缺少相应的体系与组织建设：“跟油和水一样”，装进同一瓶子并不等于融合。
  • 更隐蔽的问题是，他离开海外一线后，原本由自己承担的用户洞察、客户洞察和关键战役选择，没有自然变成组织能力。“我的长板在弥补组织的短板”，一旦这个人不再直接负责，短板就重新暴露。
  • 疫情又让出差、直接理解市场变难。他强调问题并非CEO一定要亲自出差，而是有没有管理体系来反馈信息、传递判断、形成决策；若过去依赖个人洞察，却没有补上体系，业务就会从此前顺利变得“仗没打明白”。

9. 2024年前后的调整，是让欲望与能力重新配速

  • 张小珺梳理，他上任后做了三件事：砍代工、推动高端化、加速海外扩张。钱程至今认为方向正确，国际化、多品类、创新驱动的高端品牌仍在推进；需要调整的是实现目标的节奏，而不是反复更换目标。
  • 当年希望从家用走向商用、成为“全场景的机器人公司”，也是欲望超过组织承载力的例子。有技术，不等于能同时经营to B和to C；两种生意的基因不同，真正能够横跨的公司很少，蓝图美好与落地能力之间有很大落差。
  • 到2024年前后，他开始意识到需要调整，也从父亲身上学习遇到困难时的韧性、决断和责任。他承认自己不是创始人，并不天然拥有同样的创始人精神，但可以观察、学习、模拟，而不是把身份差异当成终点。
  • 张小珺的反驳值得保留：既然方向没错，所谓能力不匹配，也可以通过提高能力来解决，不一定要改变欲望。钱程认可，问题可以在能力一端；他的变化是更重视有节奏地推动，让团队承受得住，而非短期追求翻天覆地。

10. 每十年发生一次变化，是他给企业设定的成长尺度

  • 钱程把公司历史分成十年：1998—2008年，从传统制造、代工走向品牌；2008—2018年，完成转型并上市。他强调，上市主体的业务身份已经是自主品牌、扫地机器人，而非一家OEM吸尘器企业，也开始拥有海外业务。
  • 对2018—2028年，他的要求是“这十年不白过”。未来两三年，希望公司能成为充分国际化的企业，也不再只被理解为做扫地机、洗地机，而是有擦窗、割草、泳池等多种家庭机器人。
  • 再看2028—2038年，机器人产业与技术环境可能继续发生巨大变化，他觉得这很“exciting”。企业是时代的企业，过去一个时代建立的要素并不保证下一个时代成功；新的十年本身，就可以成为重新生长欲望和目标的来源。

11. CEO必须管产品，2021年的架构仍是他的关键判断

  • 钱程给自己过去几年担任CEO的表现打五六分，满分十分。他认为长板是洞察和方向规划，短板是不够擅长细微管理、强执行；但产品必须亲自参与，所有新品类和既有产品都在其中：“作为这样的公司，不可能不管产品。”
  • 他将2021年的一款产品视为重要架构定义：全能基站，加上扫地机器人本体上的AI视觉、语音AI，也拉高了行业整体均价。在他看来，此后行业持续迭代，但主流形态并未脱离当时的原型，核心架构没有发生根本变化。

12. 品类选择像种田，既要耐心也要跨过规模门槛

  • 面对空调等数千亿元的大市场，钱程并不认为进入就有更高成功率。他把科沃斯比作“农耕文明”：埋种子、种田、让粮食长出来；“游牧文明”则是看到产业很大，就想去“咬一口肉”。公司更习惯创造和培育新品类。
  • 早年在商场卖扫地机器人，消费者甚至以为它是电子秤，这说明当时连产业认知都不存在。擦窗机器人同样做了很久，他入职前已有第一台；他说今年能出货200万台，也承认此前很长时间没有意识到它的潜力，如今才更聚焦投入。
  • 选品类并非只靠愿景，还要看可复用能力：自研传感器、算法、控制、批量品质交付，以及全球化渠道。扫地机器人之外的家庭场景，只有与这些底层要素相匹配，才构成值得进入的机会。
  • 规模也是筛选条件。他以集团收入达到200亿元的体量举例：若一个市场每年只有一两三个亿，给集团带来的营收有时连一个百分点都不到。新业务必须有空间、能在一个阶段成长起来，不能只因为能做就做。

13. 应对新竞争者，先承认高估自己、低估竞争

  • 随着石头、追觅等企业成长，竞争环境已经不同。钱程认为，新一代企业掌握的资源和要素与科沃斯过去熟悉的并不一样；即使充分掌握了上一时代的成功条件，也不意味着能在下一时代自动成功。
  • 对过去的竞争表现，他没有归因于外界：“高估了自己，低估了竞争。”但这也不意味着自卑，关键是想明白变化与自身能力，再付诸行动；看见别人的好身材，自己却不运动、继续吃垃圾食品，没有意义。
  • 他把企业经营归为三件事：看得远、跑得快、不要犯错。前者关乎变化和方向，中间是管理与执行，最后是合理欲望的追求和不合理欲望的克制；很多企业的致命伤恰恰来自犯错。
  • 现在他更倾向于70%—80%做能力复制，20%—30%做能力提高，而不是反过来追求大比例能力突变。竞争者是“试金石”，不是企业目标；被问怎么看俞浩，他回答“他只是存在”，自己的目标仍是愿景与用户价值。

14. 消费电子的品牌是购买记忆，不是永久护城河

  • 被问消费电子的核心壁垒，钱程直接回答：“没有核心壁垒。”张小珺提出品牌可能是壁垒，他的回应是，品牌帮助消费者依据上一次购买经验，快速决定下一次购买；但下一次交付不好，这份记忆就可能终止。
  • 可口可乐的味道可以长期不变，消费电子却持续变化。品牌记忆无法替代下一代产品本身，因此他不愿把消费者曾经认可，直接等同于未来能够持续赚钱的保证。
  • 他承认苹果可能有壁垒，但将其与某种网络效应联系起来；纯硬件没有同样的网络效应，更多只是规模效应。对大部分消费电子企业，更现实的工作是找到相对规模优势、保持迭代速度。
  • 张小珺追问，难道不试图构建投资人希望看到的壁垒？钱程认为真正的壁垒是垄断，但快速变化的环境很难形成垄断。把科沃斯品牌、全球家庭理解包装成壁垒，“这句话可以这么讲，但它不一定是真实的”。

15. AI要分开看组织变化与收入机会

  • 对2022年底ChatGPT之后的技术变化，钱程先拆成两条：模型、AI Agent如何改变企业运作管理，以及技术如何改变产品、带来收入。科沃斯内部也围绕这两条形成共识、开展实践，不能把所有AI影响混成一个判断。
  • 当前更直接产生营收的，他看到的是光模块等基础设施企业，但那不属于科沃斯产业。对自身更相关的是Physical AI、具身：他估计3—5年内可能有一些商用、工厂应用有条件落地，家庭消费者场景则可能需要5—10年。
  • 较早适合替代的，是高度标准化的工作，不必过分追求泛化。家庭软硬件成熟还需要时间；他也不愿把公司绝对定义成制造业或人工智能企业，因为探索需求、用创新满足需求，本来就是技术工作。

16. 具身仍在拿锤子找钉子，组织形式还会影响打法

  • 钱程认为，在深圳产业链拼出机器人并不太难，甚至买一台头部产品、重新包装也不难；大家一拥而上，未必形成实质差异。现阶段更像拿“很大的锤子”打“很小的钉子”，问题在于最终找到什么用途。
  • 他回忆无人机早期也不清楚具体能干什么：印象中Parrot曾与沃尔玛合作，把产品做成玩具；大疆则选择偏专业消费者的场景，逐渐成为生产力工具。锤子本身未必有问题，找哪颗钉子会决定后续路径。
  • 创业公司可以先出paper、demo，收入、利润和交付的约束不同；上市公司则要面对投资者和资金安排。他提到小鹏分拆具身业务，认为其中也包含引入社会资本的选择；创业公司对核心团队的利益分配也更好。
  • 张小珺追问：既然做农耕，就应该做得早。钱程认为当下很多参与者更像游牧，看中一级市场容易拿钱；科沃斯并非没有行动，已有具身研发投入、产业链投资和关键布局，只是不认为现在必须进入抢肉状态。

17. 无限大的想象空间，仍然需要漫长的兑现过程

  • 电动车至少可以参照既有汽车保有量，理解电动化替代的规模；具身则是一个新市场，若想象替代人，空间可以无限大，但“它有多大呢？”钱程认为，技术带来的热情与实际形成多大生意之间，仍隔着长期落地。
  • 他举的量级对照是宇树2000亿、中国第一估值企业4万亿：前者成长到后者约为20倍。他同时补上“当然也许它会超过4万亿”，并没有给未来设定绝对上限，而是借此讨论市场想象最后如何落到企业价值。
  • 自动驾驶是他的现实参照。他买Model S时，马斯克就说有FSD，十多年过去，兑现依然需要过程；即使在他认为推进较快的中国，全场景使用自动驾驶的消费者“应该也不至于过半”，全球其他地方则更慢。

18. 自己的具身路径尚待探索，产品定义可能更适合科沃斯

  • 钱程判断，中国未来硬件供给会很充裕，关键能力可能更多落在软件，但若自建世界模型，投入又“巨大”。数据采集标准也快速变化，一年前的方法到现在“可能都不一定有用”；他提到Figure推出数据采集app，说明行业仍很早期。
  • 对科沃斯，他更关注软硬件能否先在商用场景实现高鲁棒性、可复制、可规模化；如果做到，家用可能就不远了。目前公司没有进入模型层，也没有投资模型，他认为自己更擅长理解家庭需求、做产品定义。
  • 张小珺追问，这波浪潮可能把科沃斯带到下一个台阶，是否应更积极拥抱？钱程承认这种可能性，也认可方向上的欲望；但企业治理还要判断步骤是否合理、当前能力能否承载。未来十年发展机器人这一目标没有变，自己的路径仍需探索。

19. 机器人更可能演化出多种物种，而非只剩人形

  • 钱程提醒，家电早就在被智能驱动，科沃斯的避障、物体识别和效率提升也一直使用AI。但消费者花真金白银时依然理性，最终要看产品交付和性价比，不能把“有AI”本身当成购买理由。
  • 对具身是否替代扫地机器人，他反问：未来扫地机渗透率已经很高，大家应该不至于“为机器人再买一个吸尘器”。他更倾向于达尔文式进化：不同机器人围绕不同场景深度演化，形成适配能力；可能有人形，也肯定会有其他种类。
  • 公司的长期方向是从工具走向管家机器人，但底层目的始终是释放消费者时间，不只是扫干净地、割好草。他希望科沃斯能成为把机器人带入家庭的关键一员，却绝不认为它明天就会出现。

20. 技术圈的兴奋，并不等于消费者生活已经剧变

  • 钱程明确认可AI对个人、产业的影响，但不认为普通消费者目前已感受到决定性变化。街头或春晚看到机器人跳舞、挥手，更多还是觉得热闹、有意思；技术驱动者的欲望很重要，却仍要回答究竟改变了消费者什么。
  • 对内容生成，他承认AI视频、内容能力已经很强，但面对面访谈仍是内容生态中的必要存在。双方都认可“人还是喜欢看人的内容”：技术会帮助创作者提高能力，却不意味着生成能力出现后，人类创作就直接消失。

21. 接班难在用旧房子的框架，把企业带进新时代

  • 钱程把接班的核心难点放在两个时代的交叉处。父辈依靠当时的人才、组织、客户关系成功，下一代却被期待带公司穿越周期；上一时代要素并非100%保留，也并非100%消失，必须识别哪些值得留下、哪些需要更新。
  • 接班人还得自己掌握新时代的要素，而不只是以年轻人的身份进入旧企业。困难在于，房子的框架已经存在，仍要继续调整和建设；如果既没改变企业，也没带它进入新的发展阶段，完成职位交接并不能算成功。
  • 对科沃斯，需要延续的底层文化是务实、稳健、长远。父亲常讲“仰望星空，脚踏实地”：没有前者，公司不会持续转型；没有后者，经营就失去根基。父子希望企业越来越好的结果一致，但路径、工作分配和沟通仍需要调和。

22. 老部下的信任不能直接过户，年轻化必须落在关键岗位

  • 钱程承认，父亲与老部下何时一起经历过什么、如何建立信任、关上门后和微信里怎样沟通，自己不可能完整知道。因此新关系必须重新建立，有时甚至“看缘分”，没有一种管理方法能自动继承这些积累。
  • 他不认为自己能够被迫完全变成父亲，即使这是部分人的期待。相处需要双方调整，若只要求他一个人改变并不现实；能磨合就磨合，不能磨合，则回到目标与能力是否匹配，考虑如何补充能力。
  • 他希望看到的组织变化，是年轻人真正进入关键岗位。例如中国区负责人和他同年入职，如今管理几十亿元业务。若多年后关键位置仍只有父亲的老部下，就很难说组织发生了充分变化；年轻化需要体现在责任和成长上。

23. 持续创造比完成接班更重要

  • 谈到王兴兴、刘靖康等创业者，钱程认为他们身上的企业家精神更浓厚。随后两人以“孩子”和“兄弟”打比方，钱程说“这个企业是我兄弟”；但对话中的指代有所跳转，不宜据此断定科沃斯或某位创业者与他的具体关系。
  • 他如今更愿意“探上限”。14年的时间、精神投入，对团队的承诺、自我价值追求，以及与父亲的羁绊，已使自己与公司融为一体；不再只是因为身处CEO岗位而承担责任，而是要真正把责任做好：“我仍然认为自己在创造。”
  • 父亲40岁、50岁、60岁都说过退休，却始终停不下来，让他看到目标完成之后仍有“what’s next”。他自己也不那么有血性，逐渐被环境激发出战斗欲望；达到顶峰后若失去下一个目标，迎来的可能反而是更多失去。
  • 对未来，他希望从单品类走向多品类、从工具走向管家，并把“竞争全球化”作为当下重要下注。接班并非一个结，始终只是过渡；最终衡量的是能否制定好目标、带领企业达成，并做出“有价值、能创造的事情”。

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/zhangxiaojun-2026-10-21

item.title: The Secret Supplier Feeding Frontier AI
item.description: Grass uses consenting residential bandwidth and browser infrastructure to reach sites blocking data-center traffic; Andrej Radonjic says it has delivered exabytes to AI labs. Labs value targeted signal and speed: one discovery found 0.16% useful, while sophisticated buyers link data value to benchmark gains, token use and returns. Content API arrived ahead of the previously discussed 2027 timetable, but regional capacity and latency remain inference-era constraints.
item.content:encoded:
Delphi Digital · Yan Liberman、Andrej Radonjic · 2026-10-20 · 76 min · 原语言 EN

Grass uses consenting residential bandwidth and browser infrastructure to reach sites blocking data-center traffic; Andrej Radonjic says it has delivered exabytes to AI labs. Labs value targeted signal and speed: one discovery found 0.16% useful, while sophisticated buyers link data value to benchmark gains, token use and returns. Content API arrived ahead of the previously discussed 2027 timetable, but regional capacity and latency remain inference-era constraints.

TL;DR

  • Grass's advantage starts with getting AI systems onto websites that block data-center traffic. Andrej Radonjic says routing through residential IPs is the best way to get broad access, with browser infrastructure handling additional defenses. Grass pays consenting participants for bandwidth; Andrej says it has delivered exabytes of data to AI labs.
  • Frontier labs increasingly buy useful signal and speed alongside raw volume. A lab's discovery process can identify a small share of a dataset—for example, 0.16%—as useful, driving more targeted purchases. With new models resetting benchmarks every few months, customers risk being “left behind”; sophisticated labs estimate data's value through benchmark improvements, subsequent token usage and financial returns.
  • Robotics creates demand for carefully selected behavioral video. Andrej updates Yan's roughly 1 billion figure to more than 100 billion indexed videos. Yan points out that indexing does not mean downloading every video. Generative video benefits from diverse examples that can be combined, while robotics currently needs footage that teaches actions and interactions—a harder filtering problem than simply accumulating video.
  • Training crawls are building the infrastructure for live inference and search. Andrej describes training-data collection as a “treasure hunt” that also maps the web. Grass has released its Content API under Live Context Retrieval; Search is planned next, while he expects training and inference data eventually to converge.
  • Inference makes regional capacity and latency increasingly important. Andrej previously thought Live Context Retrieval needed ten times as many nodes, but infrastructure improvements enabled an earlier launch than the previously discussed 2027 timetable. More residential nodes are expected as regional demand grows, and the “speed of light” constrains how close routed requests can get to original latency.
  • Grass's customer business and intellectual property sit within an ownerless foundation. “Nobody owns it,” Andrej says; Wynd Labs supplies services, employs staff and holds no IP. The revenue attestation reconciles foundation purchase orders with cash receipts, including payment delays such as 60 days; it concerns the foundation rather than a separate equity vehicle.
  • Yan recounts a founder's view that superior reinvestment returns can constitute a moat, and Andrej agrees. Yan cites the AI-data market estimate of $100 billion by 2030; Andrej sees expansion opportunities in synthetic traces, reinforcement learning and other data categories. The closing moat discussion centers on getting more out of each dollar than competitors do.

Digest

1. Residential access is the network's starting advantage

  • Andrej's starting point was scraping websites for arbitrage bots during his applied-mathematics PhD. The pandemic moved intelligence gathering online: governments calculating CPI could no longer easily send people into shops with clipboards. Users expected product information to be public, while websites increasingly restricted automated access.
  • The blocking mechanism catches legitimate agents too. A website sees an AWS-hosted agent's data-center IP and cannot readily distinguish it from a competitor scraping prices, so its default can be exclusion. Andrej says routing through millions of residential IPs is the best way to get broad access; some sites additionally require browser execution and different fingerprints.
  • Consent is Grass's organizing principle: participants deliberately install an application, share bandwidth and receive rewards. Andrej contrasts that arrangement with proxy software quietly inserted into televisions or software updates, which he considers immoral and commercially unsustainable. Yan discloses that Delphi Ventures invested in Grass and holds its token.

2. Training crawls build both a data factory and a web map

  • A deployed model runs into the limits of its knowledge immediately: it has not learned what happened after training. Yan asks whether continuous learning would reduce training-data importance; Andrej expects training and inference data to converge over time. He says research on continuous learning is exciting and feels it will be resolved soon. Yan suggests that continuous-learning frameworks at huge scale may be available in a few years.
  • Andrej describes training collection as a “treasure hunt”: crawlers seek useful material while incidentally mapping the internet. He cites billions of URLs collected within hours by relatively small clusters. That index supplies foundations for search, while Grass's access infrastructure retrieves website content without being blacklisted or caught in honeypots.
  • The physical operation includes thousands of compute servers, many petabytes of storage and exabytes delivered to AI labs. New capacity can fill within hours. For one urgent leading-lab delivery, CTO and co-founder Chris went to Ashburn, stayed awake overnight and slept on the floor while assembling servers. Storage also supports filtering and processing raw material into more useful datasets.
  • Customer priorities depend on the model: video, code, rare dialects or difficult websites can each matter. Andrej emphasizes time pressure as new models surpass benchmarks every few months. Taking the best parts of a huge dataset and weighting them more heavily during training can make training more effective; Grass is working to help identify that signal.

3. Robotics makes video selection a research problem

  • Yan's reference to roughly 1 billion public-web videos is outdated: Andrej says Grass has indexed more than 100 billion. Yan points out that indexing does not mean blindly downloading every video. Video is expensive to store and process, making targeted selection essential before the material becomes a useful training product.
  • Andrej explains that when researchers know the task and have relevant data, progress is easier to measure through a “loss curve.” Teaching Spanish points toward Spanish-language material. Yan offers the hypothetical of a robot learning from someone using a lawn mower—how they walk, move their hands and handle objects. Andrej gives another example: a model could watch someone pour water into a cup and learn how to do it.
  • Andrej contrasts Sora, which can learn from diverse videos and combine them—for example, producing a cartoon cat in space—with robotics, where useful footage needs to be both diverse and specific to tasks. Yan imagines a robot learning from millions of examples; Andrej says gameplay might help teach environmental interaction, while cartoons or music videos currently offer little value for most robotics tasks. Determining and filtering the right behavioral footage remains active research.

4. Live retrieval turns internal infrastructure into a product

  • Live Context Retrieval is the product family; the released product is the Content API. It packages infrastructure originally built for large training crawls into one call, handling residential routing, complex TLS fingerprints and server-side browsers. Andrej says residential IP networks alone are often insufficient for some tasks.
  • Users provide a URL, optionally specify a country and receive content as Markdown or plain text. Yan's example is an agent testing a stock-trading strategy using information from around the world, including product and stock details from sites that may only be accessible in certain countries, to calculate fundamentals before earnings reports.
  • Search is planned next because agents also need to discover which URLs matter. Andrej puts a typical internet-enabled agent call at five to 50 pages, with deeper research potentially requiring more. The Content API suits businesses monitoring known websites; Search would let a model locate relevant sources before retrieving their contents. Audio and image grounding remain in development.
  • Andrej argues that accessible ANNs, embeddings, information-retrieval tools and open-source models have made parts of search more available. His deliberately simplified example is searching 50 million documents in an AWS S3 bucket for under $100 monthly. He stops short of saying those tools are commoditized or that Grass has already built an excellent internet search engine: reliably collecting and refreshing blocked web content remains difficult.

5. Inference changes the network's capacity requirements

  • Yan cites nearly 8 million nodes as the latest public figure he knows. Andrej says inference strengthens the case for continued residential-node growth: training collection can wait when a region fills up, while an agent needing immediate information from that location has less flexibility. Capacity must therefore be available where requests arise.
  • Andrej acknowledges revising his own timetable. He previously believed Grass needed ten times as many nodes before launching Live Context Retrieval; optimization revealed that fewer nodes could do more work. Yan recalls earlier discussions pointing toward 2027. Andrej expects further efficiency gains, while recognizing that scaling eventually encounters diminishing returns.
  • Andrej reports a Content API success rate very close to 100%, meaning it can find a way to collect content from a public website. He considers that more meaningful than boasting about pages crawled, given how much web information is useless. Latency remains unfinished work: residential detours face the “speed of light,” and Grass wants performance as close to the original as possible.

6. Labs price capabilities and protect their research directions

  • Lab demand alternates between broad discovery and specialized collection. A customer may request a large domain-specific dataset, evaluate it, then find that about 0.16% is useful for changing results and ask for more. Andrej says training-data demand has grown significantly despite changing research directions.
  • Yan presses on cost versus quality; Andrej says both matter, with speed sometimes commanding a premium when delivery is needed in three hours rather than the next day. More advanced labs model the financial benefit of improving a benchmark, the additional token usage that capability could generate and an appropriate price per data unit. Useless deliveries can get vendors blacklisted or sidelined.
  • Labs may have separate teams focused on text, audio or vision, with procurement operating separately. Some may already use a vendor for a particular task, but Grass can consult with them about other relevant data it has collected. Asked by Yan about defense or government applications, Andrej says customers do not discuss their work publicly because others could use that information against them; he does not describe specific Grass work with those organizations.
  • Many data vendors build reinforcement-learning environments—a “jungle gym” in which models practice particular benchmarked skills. Andrej expects continued demand for them, but suppliers must track changing research priorities. His argument for Grass's broader infrastructure is that customers still need web access when they move from one capability or data category to another.

7. The foundation holds the business while reinvestment drives the thesis

  • Andrej describes the revenue attestation as an accounting firm's reconciliation of purchase orders from AI labs and other customers against cash receipts. Timing differences can arise when invoices are paid 60 days later. The attestation concerns the Grass Foundation, an organizational distinction he says many observers missed.
  • Customer relationships run through the foundation, which Andrej describes as ownerless: “Nobody owns it.” Independent directors oversee its actions. Wynd Labs supplies services and handles employment, benefits and insurance; it holds no IP, which transferred to the foundation at token launch. Wynd–foundation dealings require director approval, and Wynd's team also holds tokens as part of the intended incentive alignment.
  • Yan cites an estimate that the AI-data market will be worth $100 billion by 2030. Andrej sees opportunities for Grass across pre-training, inference, preference data, synthetic traces and reinforcement learning. Large raw datasets can support synthetic-data generation; better web access can improve learning environments. He also sees further uses for the existing consumer distribution, while acknowledging that some categories are not current priorities.
  • Asked about capital, Andrej says Grass will predictably need more. Yan then recounts an unnamed AI-lab co-founder's view that a moat can be the ability to get more out of each dollar invested than competitors. Andrej calls that an excellent moat and agrees that getting more out of an investment is an interesting idea.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/secret-supplier-feeding-frontier-ai

item.title: The Programmable Data Center — Evan Conrad, SF Compute
item.description: SF Compute’s bet is that GPU trading requires cloud-like operations: VM configurations can differ by 40%, leaving financial contracts exposed to manipulation and basis risk before reliable delivery.
