item.title: How Toto Wolff built the most valuable team in F1
item.description: Mercedes combines F1’s scarce team ownership with roughly $1 billion in revenue and a 30% margin, though Collison’s roughly 15x EBIT framing uses current earnings that Wolff says were considerably higher than at the transaction. Owner control supports a ten-year horizon, but the “$200 million and a bit” cap forces lap-time trade-offs, and DAS’s ban after one year leaves regulatory durability an unresolved risk.
item.content:encoded:
Cheeky Pint · Toto Wolff、John Collison · 2026-10-20 · 71 min · 原语言 EN

Mercedes combines F1’s scarce team ownership with roughly $1 billion in revenue and a 30% margin, though Collison’s roughly 15x EBIT framing uses current earnings that Wolff says were considerably higher than at the transaction. Owner control supports a ten-year horizon, but the “$200 million and a bit” cap forces lap-time trade-offs, and DAS’s ban after one year leaves regulatory durability an unresolved risk.

TL;DR

  • Mercedes now has operating profits to support its valuation alongside the scarcity of owning an F1 team. Wolff reports around $1 billion in revenue and a 30% margin, with dividends and limited stadium-related capital expenditure. Collison’s roughly 15x EBIT framing switches the transaction valuation from £4.6 billion to $4.6 billion and uses current earnings; Wolff says earnings at the transaction were “considerably less.”
  • Owner control lets Wolff make decisions against a ten-year horizon rather than a manager’s contract. Mercedes helped finance his stake and gave him authority to act outside the corporate hierarchy. Wolff invokes Dietrich Mateschitz’s advice to entrepreneurs: “You need to be like a downhill ski racer, but you need to be able to stop and walk back up the hill.”
  • F1’s spending limits exchange some scientific freedom for closer competition. A cost cap of “$200 million and a bit” forces choices between near-term lap time and longer-term research, although Wolff rejects the claim that speculative R&D has disappeared. Regulatory durability is another investment hurdle: Mercedes’ push-pull steering innovation worked, but was banned after a year.
  • Mercedes evaluates engineering against the car’s performance and people against their contribution to the team. Simulations establish expected lap-time gains, but those gains still require a driver who can extract them. Wolff’s answer to engineers becoming attached to projects is “You fall in love with the result”; exceptional ability does not earn an exemption from “No dickheads.”
  • Wolff’s formative investment success depended on selling as well as finding opportunities. After a lucrative SMS-business sale, his CFO challenged valuations disconnected from monetization and compared them with an industrial business producing 30 million in EBIT. They exited all but one of nine investments, beginning in late 1999 and continuing through 2000; Wolff credits luck and the incentive to protect his own life-changing wealth.
  • F1’s audience growth combines entertainment with a sporting outcome viewers believe is real. Wolff initially doubted Netflix and declined the first season, but now describes a year-round reality show whose foundation remains “Entertainment follows sport.” He cites 42% female fans and sees live sport as resilient in an AI-heavy world because “Humans watch humans.”
  • Wolff wants durable private ownership with management that can eventually operate without him. He doubts public markets suit a sport that moves “from mania to depression within a week,” despite Collison’s argument that today’s audience is different. His succession plan would probably divide his responsibilities among two or three people, with any future chairmanship requiring clear limits on intervention.

Digest

1. Driver speed is sensory, while team performance requires character

  • When Collison asks for racing’s equivalent of cycling’s power-to-weight metric, Wolff says there is no single equivalent. An eight-year-old beating ten-year-olds can signal potential, but resilience, technical communication and sponsor relationships also matter. “The stopwatch never lies” when drivers share machinery; it does not explain everything underneath the result.
  • Wolff describes exceptional speed as an unusually fine connection between body, car and road. Hamilton once said, “The car understeers from the front axle to where I sit,” describing a sensation engineers could not readily identify. Collison’s formulation is that great drivers strap the car onto themselves; Wolff calls that underlying sensitivity genetic.
  • Wolff’s own path into racing was late: at 18, an accidental visit to an F3 paddock gave him a sense of identity, but he lacked the karting background that teaches the fundamentals of positioning a car. He nevertheless raced through junior formula and GT, touring-car and sports-car stages with some success.
  • The visible racing operation conceals 2,500 people across engine and chassis hubs; around 150 travel, including marketing, with 90 in technical and operational roles. Wolff insists there are 2,500 potential stars and applies the All Blacks’ “No dickheads” rule. Humility, integrity, honesty and enthusiasm matter: there is “no place for the genius asshole.”

2. A fixed budget makes lap time the investment hurdle

  • With a cost cap of “$200 million and a bit” annually, engineering resources force explicit choices: compute for a front wing arriving in three months competes with longer-term laboratory work. Collison suggests speculative R&D had to disappear; Wolff corrects him. Some remains, but its prospective lap-time contribution must justify diverting resources from current cars.
  • Wolff originally opposed the cap because Mercedes’ resources protected it against smaller competitors. Former F1 chief Chase Carey told him, “We need to protect you from yourselves.” Wolff now acknowledges closer competition, while retaining the tension: unrestricted engineering, even within a budget, could produce a leading car five seconds faster than the next.
  • Technical allocation starts with an expected lap-time contribution, then follows simulation, CFD, wind-tunnel measurements and mathematical models against that expectation. Wolff considers this more measurable than Stripe’s task of predicting customer demand. A theoretical tenth of a second can nevertheless disappear if the driver feels unsafe or cannot extract the modeled benefit.
  • Collison presses on engineers demanding another simulation for a beloved idea. Wolff says forceful advocates who pushed experiments beyond reason are no longer in the organization. Technical management must stop work that fails the overall lap-time objective, regardless of a department’s interests. “You fall in love with the result,” rather than the component.

3. Regulatory defensibility is part of the engineering return

  • Mercedes tests contentious innovations through an internal mock trial: inventors prosecute their own proposal, other engineers defend it, and Wolff and general counsel judge. Dialogue with the FIA should begin early when legality is uncertain. If something is “100% defensible,” however, Mercedes may deploy it first and make its argument afterward.
  • The sharpest example is DAS: pushing and pulling the steering wheel changed front-wheel toe, allowing tire surfaces to heat through dragging. Wolff found the extra steering-wheel movement deeply uncomfortable; the F1 drivers wanted to try it, and it worked. He believes a mechanical driver-operated control helped make the system defensible.
  • DAS was banned after a year. Asked why it did not simply become an accepted capability, Wolff answers, “I don’t know,” suggesting Mercedes might have lost the political argument as rivals objected to replication costs. His experience is that regulators may respect an innovation for a season before banning it, although intervention can arrive earlier.
  • On the compression-ratio dispute, Wolff argues that cold-engine measurement was clearly specified and rivals had misread the rules. He declines to confirm claims that Mercedes deliberately engineered advantageous thermal expansion. A compromise eventually changed measurement, but he says it made no difference for Mercedes: the months-long fight was about “the sheer principle of innovation.”
  • Protecting an edge is imperfect: Wolff says Mercedes firewalls some work, but eventually 20 or 25 people need to know, and personnel can move between teams. Contractual limits vary; he cites up to 12 months in the UK and three months in Switzerland. He says innovations will eventually leak.

4. The dot-com windfall became valuable because Wolff sold

  • Wolff’s early investment activity was a hybrid of sweat equity, small investments and success-linked ownership. Inspired by Netscape, Yahoo! and AOL, he searched German-speaking markets for analogous businesses, then offered financing or listing help for equity. Some prospects were not yet incorporated; his eventual investment vehicle remained a company rather than a conventional fund.
  • His standout example is sms.at, a free SMS portal used by two million people against an Austrian population he puts at roughly nine million. Its teenage operator said he accessed telecom SMS servers, switching countries when shut down. Wolff incorporated the business and approached operators who hated it but wanted an accommodation; he says it sold to T-Mobile for “250 million” within two years.
  • After the deal, his CFO compared its tiny revenue and uncertain monetization with a specialized aluminum business generating 30 million in EBIT. Wolff initially defended the internet’s customer potential; the CFO insisted valuations were unsustainable. Collison’s observation is that investor mythology celebrates early entry and permanent ownership much more readily than the commercial judgment to sell.
  • That challenge prompted a review of nine investments. Beginning in late 1999 and continuing through 2000, they exited everything except an Israeli startup they could not sell. Wolff emphasizes luck and his own incentives: after financial hardship, securing generational wealth mattered. Managing others’ money, with fees and potential carry, might have made him more aggressive.

5. Entrepreneurial ownership changes the decisions a team can make

  • Mercedes had bought Brawn, the 2009 champion, but had only one race win before Wolff’s 2013 arrival. Asked why Williams could match that, he challenged the budget comparison: Mercedes’ additional 100 million went toward Schumacher and Rosberg, while Williams had pay driver Pastor Maldonado. At comparable operating resources, Wolff was targeting the top six, not championships.
  • Mercedes concluded the team needed entrepreneurial authority rather than corporate administration. Wolff initially declined because he was a Williams shareholder and wanted to remain an entrepreneur. Mercedes offered equity and helped finance what he could not conservatively afford. He says the resulting framework lets him make quick decisions and run the team “like a 20-person organization.”
  • Collison compares this freedom with founder-led technology companies. Wolff contrasts his ten-year perspective with managers incentivized over three- or five-year contracts and exposed to dismissal for unapproved decisions. Dietrich Mateschitz’s analogy captures the ability to reverse course: “You need to be like a downhill ski racer, but you need to be able to stop and walk back up the hill.”
  • INEOS entered through sponsorship discussions before COVID, when teams were loss-making and valuations were low. Jim Ratcliffe offered “X hundred million” in sponsorship if he could obtain equity; the arrangement left Mercedes, INEOS and Wolff with one-third each. Wolff values Ratcliffe as an experienced, contrarian resource who does not interfere with operations.

6. Scarcity supports the valuation, but cash generation supports the business

  • Wolff separates ownership motives: scarcity, a lifelong sporting ambition, greater visibility and financial fundamentals. F1 has only 11 teams, with another potentially possible under the rules but little enthusiasm for adding one. Trophy buyers may want prominence or participation; a fundamental investor must examine demographics, league income potential, team earnings and continued growth.
  • Collison first cites a £4.6 billion transaction valuation, up 7x in a few years, then frames it as “$4.6 billion” and approximately 15x EBIT. Wolff reports around $1 billion of revenue and a 30% margin, while stressing that revenue and earnings when he sold were “considerably less.” The exchange does not reconcile the currencies.
  • Unlike the earlier marketing-expense model, some teams now earn more than 30% EBIT margins and distribute dividends. Mercedes has limited capital expenditure because it does not own a stadium, while also missing some associated revenues. Wolff says he could probably generate 30% more than the prior sale valuation, but regards finding the right partner as more important.
  • Wolff favors “fundamental cash flow, and profits” over revenue-based valuations; applying some US sports comparables, he says, would imply 10–12 billion. His long-term optimism also rests on live sport’s resilience to technological change: “Humans watch humans.” The attraction is the individual’s drama and glory, rather than simply discovering how quickly a machine can travel.

7. Entertainment expands the audience because the sport remains credible

  • Wolff admits he did not believe Drive to Survive would work. Mercedes and Ferrari skipped season one while fighting for the championship; he thinks their absence might have helped by giving smaller teams an underdog narrative. COVID then brought multigenerational viewing, while F1’s ability to contain its traveling operation allowed racing to resume.
  • Today’s attraction includes personalities, social media, controversy and politics: a “12-month live reality show.” Wolff insists the foundation is credible competition governed by rules. “Entertainment follows sport, not the other way around.” He cites 42% female fans and identifies young women, roughly 15–25 in his recollection, as the fastest-growing demographic.
  • Collison finds Netflix too focused on soap opera and suggests more technical or racecraft programming; Wolff calls that an idea they had not considered. Audience expansion also remains geographically uneven: F1 is visible in affluent US cities, but much less developed in the middle of the country, where Wolff identifies NASCAR as the established presence.
  • Asked how Mercedes serves these audiences, Wolff broadens the question to stakeholders. His “customer” is someone who makes life better: family, employees, sponsors, shareholders and fans create different priorities. Keeping employees in a good place contributes to a faster car; sponsors need to see a worthwhile investment or platform.

8. Commercial alignment does not eliminate structural tensions

  • Teams receive a substantial share of F1’s profits without owning the league. Liberty and public shareholders own Formula One; the FIA governs and polices the sport, receives payment for services, and granted commercial rights through a 100-year agreement. Wolff describes relations as more aligned today, although profit distribution remains a recurring issue in five-year contract renewals.
  • Wolff doubts a stock-market listing is the right long-term structure. Williams’ listing was unsuccessful, and race results effectively create reporting events around 20 times a year: sentiment goes “from mania to depression within a week.” Collison challenges whether today’s larger sport changes the answer; Wolff remains uncertain about that possibility but prioritizes control.
  • Circuit design exposes another trade-off. Collison argues destinations and good racing can conflict, citing Monaco; Wolff initially resists that framing. On Madrid, he praises the execution but says the layout insufficiently accommodated overtaking with the new cars. Because it is not permanent, he thinks next year’s layout will change to provide more straights.

9. Succession requires distributing authority and limiting interference

  • Wolff rejects legacy-building as the objective: the team must be able to live without him. He believes his role will be divided among two or three people he is currently vetting, already demonstrating different strengths. The structure will lack his particular owner-entrepreneur credibility, but he expects a solid management team can succeed.
  • Continued family ownership probably rules out a clean break; an executive or non-executive chairmanship may follow. Its boundaries must be precise: maintaining relationships is different from interfering in daily operations or criticizing successors from the sidelines. Family members must earn operational responsibility, and his children currently have no interest. For now, he still enjoys running the team too much.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/toto-wolff-built-most-valuable-team-f1

item.title: A World Model of Life: Biohub's Alex Rives on Virtual Cells, Measurement, & the $1.8B Data Push
item.description: Biohub’s $1.8B initiative joins the Department of Energy, NIH, Google DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs, and Meta to map molecular readouts and imaging. Rives calls observability a fundamental bottleneck; a laser phase plate adds phase contrast in cryo-electron tomography, but virtual cells still cannot meaningfully simulate cells. Atlas drafts target one or two years, with a comprehensive map within five.
item.content:encoded:
The Cognitive Revolution · Alex Rives、Nathan Labenz · 2026-10-20 · 65 min · 原语言 EN

Biohub’s $1.8B initiative joins the Department of Energy, NIH, Google DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs, and Meta to map molecular readouts and imaging. Rives calls observability a fundamental bottleneck; a laser phase plate adds phase contrast in cryo-electron tomography, but virtual cells still cannot meaningfully simulate cells. Atlas drafts target one or two years, with a comprehensive map within five.

TL;DR

  • Biohub just announced a $1.8B expansion of its Virtual Biology Initiative, coordinating the Department of Energy, NIH, Google DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs, and Meta on data generation for a general model of cellular biology. The effort aims to build contextual maps — spatial biology linking molecular readouts to imaging “at the scale of hundreds of billions or more cells” — with an open call for other funders and the worldwide scientific community to join.
  • Rives sees observability as a particularly fundamental bottleneck for virtual cell models, but not the only one. “There’s so much about the cell that we just can’t measure”; progress requires models, data generation at scale, and observation tools. He says today’s models “just don’t meet the definition of a model that could actually simulate the cell in a meaningful way and serve as an oracle for experimental biology.”
  • The attainable five-year target is an “information-theoretic model of the cell” — a probabilistic transition function from cell state plus inputs to a distribution of next states — building toward “a world model of life.” In “the limit of infinite data and compute,” architectures probably end up the same; cellular biology is far from that limit, so inductive bias still matters.
  • Measurement hardware is where Biohub’s thesis gets expressed: the laser phase plate — “the most powerful standing-wave laser in the world” — brings phase contrast to cryo-electron tomography, helping scientists make out individual molecules and how they interact in the living cell. Biohub also uses whole-organism zebrafish imaging to track every cell from embryo to fully developed organism.
  • The LLM playbook transfers to biology: pretraining on statistical patterns, elicitation, then “RLVR for biology” with lab verification — “empirical AI” that asks a question, performs the experiment, learns, and proposes a better one in a recursive loop. Unlike math and coding, verification must happen in the laboratory, not through fast computation.
  • Timeline and payoff: first drafts of health-and-disease cell atlases within one or two years, a “pretty comprehensive map” within five — then the question becomes “How do I intervene to reverse a state that’s pathologic?” Rives says he has thought less about EHR data; he worries that without a causal basis, models could learn “a bunch of correlations,” while acknowledging that health records could help get existing drugs and care to the right patients.
  • The man building toward curing all disease tracks little about his own health: “I have a watch that tracks my sleep. That’s about as far as it gets.” On fusing language and biology latent spaces, he is unsure; the biological facts we most want to know may not be represented in text and can require experiments to discover.

Digest

1. “Curing all disease” means a world without disease — not a promise of immortality — and medicines you can program

  • Pressed by Nathan on whether the mission implies living forever, Rives calls himself “a practical person” and sets his sights on a world without cancer, infectious disease, or chronic and degenerative conditions, rather than promising immortality.
  • The therapeutic ambition goes beyond the “current medical paradigm, the therapeutic paradigm of pills and molecules” toward “far more programmable medicines” grounded in “reading and writing the programs of biology.” Disease is part of the program and “often unfolds in very regular ways,” which could provide new tools for understanding and intervening.
  • Nathan’s two-part taxonomy — learn the causal structure, then design the intervention — Rives accepts as “the classic framework of drug development,” but argues the information-theoretic view of cells as systems of rules and code “opens up a wider aperture” than target-then-molecule.

2. Why virtual cells fall short: you can’t model what you can’t measure

  • Rives says the cell is “maybe the right mesoscale” for thinking about biology, spanning molecular events and the larger context of tissue, physiology, and the organism — and notes that the transformer does not have the multiscale structure to represent all those levels.
  • More fundamental than architecture is observability: “There’s so much about the cell that we just can’t measure. Sometimes we can’t see it at all.” He points to new measurement and observation technologies as a source of many advances in biology.
  • Three legs must advance together — modeling, data generation at scale that reveals “the information architecture and programs of the cell in their statistical structure,” and observation tools. Rives says today’s so-called virtual cells do not meet the definition of a model that could meaningfully simulate the cell and serve as an oracle for experimental biology.

3. The five-year object: an information-theoretic cell model, en route to “a world model of life”

  • Architecture agnosticism, properly hedged: in the limit of infinite data and compute, models are “just function approximators” and probably end up the same. Cellular biology is far from that limit; protein biology, with sequencing at scale, is an area where researchers can get closer. Away from the limit, inductive bias matters.
  • Of biology’s two ways of thinking — bottom-up from chemical and physical principles versus the emergent informational view of “the cell as an information-processing machine with a genome that encodes the programs that run life” — Rives says the latter could be attainable via AI in the next five years.
  • The first concrete target, aligned with Nathan’s input/output framing, is a transition function from state and inputs to the next state — probabilistic, since the cell transitions “to a distribution of possible downstream states.” The eventual model would represent molecular complexity and cell programs, allowing development and interactions to unfold: “a world model of life.”

4. The $1.8B push: DOE, NIH, DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs, and Meta coordinate on data

  • The Virtual Biology Initiative was announced in April; the flagship partnership — Department of Energy, NIH, Google DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs, and Meta — was announced “the day before yesterday,” with an open call for other funders and the worldwide scientific community to join.
  • The effort aims to dramatically expand contextual maps of cellular biology: spatial biology showing cells in tissue, linking molecular-level measurements to imaging “at the scale of hundreds of billions or more cells,” and producing the first datasets for training contextual information-theoretic models.

5. Measurement is the moat: a laser phase plate and transparent fish

  • The laser phase plate, imagined by Holger Müller at Berkeley decades ago and supported by Biohub’s investment for years, uses “the most powerful standing-wave laser in the world” to shift the electron beam’s phase and provide phase contrast in cryo-electron tomography. That contrast helps scientists make out individual molecules in their living context and understand what they are and how they interact.
  • Biohub’s program includes increasing the parameters measured per cell, expanding the field of view and number of cells observed simultaneously, and opening up the temporal and molecular dimensions.
  • On Nathan’s scale-bridging concern — “a single point mutation in a gene can cause disease” — Rives says identifying an entire system down to the molecular level is not possible in the near future. The answer is to learn at the mesoscale and build models that integrate across biological hierarchies. Cells in culture and transformed cells are imperfect proxies for in-situ tissue, but retain core machinery and can still teach us about cellular biology. Biohub’s imaging institute is developing tools across levels of complexity: zebrafish are transparent, so its microscopes can track every cell from a one-cell embryo to a fully developed organism, or follow labeled immune cells moving through living tissue.

6. “In mice” isn’t the bug — evolution-wide transfer is the feature

  • Nathan asks why treatments that work in mice seem not to work in humans more often, given how much biological machinery is conserved. Rives says over-relying on model organisms can fail both ways: you may think a cancer cure works when “it only works in mice,” or miss a human-relevant mechanism because mice do not provide a good proxy.
  • The precedent from Rives’ ESM background: ESM and AlphaFold were not trained just on human proteins. Information across evolution is essential; a model trained only on human proteins would not be accurate.
  • Across life, and especially vertebrates, much core molecular machinery is conserved, while “the programs are completely rewired, but they’re built with the same building blocks.” Organoids are a newer experimental proxy for human biology, but Rives argues that rather than seeking a perfect proxy, models can learn from information across different systems.

7. Pretraining, elicitation, then RLVR with lab verification — “empirical AI”

  • Rives expects biology to follow shared AI principles: pretraining learns the underlying system from statistical patterns, then elicitation brings out “the part of that model which is relevant to the problem.” He connects this to the Hinton, LeCun, and Bengio vision of learning variables and parameters rather than encoding them by hand, with scaling laws as a clear expression of that progress.
  • The hoped-for next step is “RLVR for biology” and “empirical AI”: systems that ask a question, perform an experiment, learn from it, propose a better experiment, and repeat the cycle. Unlike math and coding, biology requires systems that can verify predictions in the laboratory.
  • Timelines, as hedged: atlases of cellular biology across health and disease are “a scaling challenge” addressable with today’s technology — first drafts within one or two years, and a “pretty comprehensive map” within five with a focused, coordinated effort. Such maps could support classical analysis as well as models that identify disease-relevant cell states and help answer: “How do I intervene to reverse a state that’s pathologic and bring it into a healthy state?”

8. Open questions: EHRs, latent fusion — and Rives’ own biomarkers

  • Rives says he has not thought as much about health records. His concern is that patient-history models could produce “a bunch of correlations” without linking them to deeper causal factors in biology. He also sees potential for records to improve care by getting existing drugs and mechanisms to the right people, while arguing that this alone would not reach the biological fundamentals required for a step change.
  • On co-training language and biology into one latent space, he is genuinely uncertain. Language can draw on centuries of empirical knowledge, but the biological facts we most want to know are not represented in text, cannot be derived from first principles or existing knowledge, and may only be discovered through experiments. Fusion may be hard at first because bridging data is scarce, though he says it could be interesting eventually. Protein language models already develop features for unknown biology — “novel concepts that we don’t have words or names for yet” — amid billions of sequenced proteins whose functions are mostly unknown.
  • Nathan’s million-Bryan-Johnsons proposal — longitudinal human phenotyping with micro-biopsies and sensors — gets a qualified yes: Rives says the data would be “immensely valuable” and likely to happen over time. Biohub focuses on its technology layer, including continuous monitoring that measures more parameters, including molecular ones, to link bottom-up and top-down views.
  • Asked for personal health advice, Rives says, “I’m not the right person to ask for that kind of advice” and barely thinks about it: “I have a watch that tracks my sleep. That’s about as far as it gets.”

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/world-model-life-biohub-s-alex-rives-virtual-cel

item.title: 168X 对话 Frank Trading：AI Trade 结束之后，下一笔大交易在哪里？
item.description: Frank 认为四年 AI 牛市可能接近尾声，OpenAI、Anthropic 的 ARR 不及预期，云厂商 free cash flow 转负。供给追上需求后，外溢订单可能回流龙头；他的英伟达／AMD 配对交易押注相对强弱，开源也可能分流 token 计费收入。SOXX 收回并站稳 515 才是他尝试翻多的门槛，11月3日中期选举与衰退或滞胀风险仍可能改变方向。
item.content:encoded:
168X · Frank Trading · 2026-10-20 · 49 min · 原语言 ZH

Frank 认为四年 AI 牛市可能接近尾声，OpenAI、Anthropic 的 ARR 不及预期，云厂商 free cash flow 转负。供给追上需求后，外溢订单可能回流龙头；他的英伟达／AMD 配对交易押注相对强弱，开源也可能分流 token 计费收入。SOXX 收回并站稳 515 才是他尝试翻多的门槛，11月3日中期选举与衰退或滞胀风险仍可能改变方向。

TL;DR

  • Frank 认为四年 AI 牛市可能已到尾声，但长期看空不妨碍短线翻多。 他把 OpenAI、Anthropic 的 ARR 不及预期视为增长与融资信心的拐点。云厂商 free cash flow 已转负，若投资意愿和融资放缓，维持同等规模的基建会更困难。“不要跟股票谈恋爱”，相信 AI 是产业革命，不等于相信 AI 股票还能继续涨。
  • 指数空头最顺的一段可能已经过去，后续更依赖小仓位与关键价位。 他披露在纳指 31,250 附近重仓做空、SOXX 跌破 555 左右后加仓，如今认为最流畅的一段下跌可能已经过去。SOXX 的 500、515、530 是逐级反弹观察位；要收回 515 并站稳、包括在韩国交易时段站稳，他才认为有尝试做多的理由。
  • 他的 reverse bottleneck 瞄准订单外溢退潮后的弱者，而非无差别空掉 AI。 大小厂同时扩产后，供给迟早追上需求，客户会回到龙头；英伟达／AMD 等 pair trade 交易的是相对强弱。“半导体和猪有什么区别呢？没有区别，都是一样的。”
  • 11月3日中期选举是政策分叉，不能预设选后 AI 会获救。 Frank 认为民主党“一定会打 anti-AI 的牌”，若横扫两院，会卡数据中心建设，提高债务上限的谈判和放宽金融公司、大银行监管的政策也可能回撤；长债可能是最优标的。若两党分控两院，他反而认为对股票更友好。
  • 他的明年基准是衰退熊市，比特币能否接棒则没有确定答案。 他认为 AI CapEx 一降，美国经济可能“立刻就衰退”；油价、服务业通胀若不退，则可能走向滞胀。降息且金融条件不紧时，黄金、比特币可能承接资金，但若演变为信用危机，比特币也难独善其身。
  • 非 AI 多头里，他已经买入印度，DIA 则已结束短线任务。 他认为印度基本面“并没有变差”，油价与卢比冲击下仍有强劲内资承接；亚洲 long-short 交易平仓也可能带来买盘。Jio IPO 与 Oil Dollar Window 是额外催化；DIA 只是长债利率回落后的估值修复仓，现已离场。
  • 消费端的新配对是多 ROST、空 XLY，押注财富效应退潮后的消费降级。 他近期新开 XLY 空头，并点名希尔顿、RCL、Starbucks：这些公司仍在前高附近，但股市下跌可能削弱消费能力。对低价零售商 ROST 的多头保留居民仍有购买力的前提；对空腿则说：“下周只要加息，这些公司全都会死。”
  • 开源削弱模型能力的稀缺性，长线机会仍可能留在龙头与端侧。 他所谓“token 计费必然走向终结”，指收入大头从目前可能 80%—90% 的 token 收费分流，而非彻底消失。模型缩小、成本下降，让他看好 Qcom、ARM 等端侧方向；对真正长期投资者，他仍认可英伟达、台积电的龙头地位与估值。

Digest

1. 看空四年牛市，不等于放弃任何一段反弹

  • Frank 开场先划清长期观点与中短期操作：他认为持续四年的 AI 牛市可能已经结束，但若美联储、沃什、特朗普、伊朗或 AI 内部出现大利好，仍可以平空翻多。做交易不能因为自己的 ego，错过与长期判断方向不同的行情。
  • 他举 9 月中旬的交易为例：当时已经非常看空，但看到纳指 100 跌不破，又认为 9 月 FOMC 倾向于 double cut，仍抄底 SMH、SOXX 等半导体股票，做了一轮反弹后在高点附近退出。在他看来，这与长期看空“并不冲突”。
  • 对刚出现的反弹，他的解释却是集中空头回补，而非趋势翻多。“不要接 falling knife”：他判断这轮内生性暴跌不会立刻出现 V 型反转，盘前或盘中看到涨得好就买，更接近上当，而不是抄底。

2. ARR 不及预期，先击穿的是继续融资的信心

  • Frank 把 OpenAI、Anthropic 的 ARR 双双不及预期视作 AI growth 的拐点。低于 3,000 亿美元估值进场的早期投资者或许不慌；但今年 6 月按约 1.5 万亿美元估值买入 Anthropic、现在回到成本线甚至被套的人，再被问要不要新份额，未必愿意继续加码。融资意愿减弱，可能进一步影响后续融资和扩建。
  • 他提到 AI 公司的 CapEx：9 月大约只有 8 月的 40% 多、6 月的 10%—20%。他的逻辑是，云厂 free cash flow 早已转负，不借钱就很难维持相同甚至更大规模的基建；ARR 不及预期会削弱投资者继续投入的“信心和决心”。
  • 主持人追问：下个月的 Anthropic、以及包含 2027 年 OpenAI IPO 在内的事情，谁来兜底？他的回答是“没有人兜底”，并称 OpenAI 去年 10 月试探特朗普时，对方明确说不会兜底。市场里还有其他 AI 公司，并不存在必须拯救某一家模型厂的最终买家。
  • 尚待验证的分叉是：ARR 不及预期究竟因为有订单却产能跟不上，还是因为客户改用千问、DeepSeek、Gemini？他列出的跟踪项包括付费需求、收入增速、新增收入、企业客户换模型、多模型分流与私有部署，以及云厂是否愿意提前向美光等公司锁定产能、交付周期是否缩短。

3. Beta 空头转向小仓位，515 是尝试翻多的门槛

  • 他披露在纳指 31,250 附近开始重仓做空，SOXX 跌破约 555 后再次加仓。如今最流畅的一段下跌可能已经过去，而 AI 泡沫结束尚未成为市场共识；后续消息可能把多空来回打，因此倾向保持小仓位空头，再按技术位置调整。
  • 他给多头的门槛是 SOXX 收回 500、515，尤其 515 须站稳，在韩国交易时段也能站稳；500、515、530 是逐级反弹参考。套牢者不必等三个位置全部走完：反弹失败就减一点，失守关键位再退一步，而不是等到无法回头才处理。
  • 这次下跌的速度、幅度和六七月份那波相近甚至更快，但 VXN 距 7 月高点仍差将近 10 点。Frank 的解读是，这一波很多人根本没有买 put；暴跌是因为真的有人在出货。他把六七月份的回调看作杠杆破灭、基本面未坏，而现在认为基本面坏了，市场上很多人也在出货。
  • 当主持人问什么信号才算真正的转折，他说已经看到了：ARR 不及预期，SOXX 两周跌了快 20%，韩国市场已经跌崩。多头应该反过来问，出现什么转折点之后才值得做多，而不是继续追问何时才算进入熊市。

4. 现金是可选项，保住利润比证明信仰重要

  • 对看不懂的行情，他的反问是：“这个钱我一定要赚吗？”他提到在 Robinhood 存美元、年化 7% 的做法，称自己也存了不少；“一年 7% 也不少”，没有必要每一局都参与。
  • 他自报年内收益 440% 多，账户基本没有特别大的回撤；一些朋友年中曾赚 10 倍、20 倍，后来 YTD 收益却归零、转负，甚至有人爆仓。他惋惜的不是他们不够相信 AI，而是没有保住已经赚到的钱。
  • 主持人据此推断，未来 6—9 个月他是否都会留现金，Frank 随即回应：“明年看不了那么远。”他确认的只是明年走衰退路径的基本预期，并没有把当前仓位外推成未来半年不变的配置。

5. Reverse bottleneck 交易的是短缺红利消退

  • Frank 用生猪解释半导体周期：短缺时所有人一起养猪，等供给同时出来，猪价反而暴跌。“半导体和猪有什么区别？没有区别，都是一样的。”他认定供需不会恰好相等后静止，扩产最终一定会把紧缺推向过剩。
  • 在他的观察中，2025 年后涨得较少的反而是英伟达、台积电；Intel、AAOI、GSS、TTMI 等公司因龙头产能不足，拿到外溢订单、收取高价，才出现基本面反转。等供给够了，客户既然买英伟达就能满足需求，为什么还要把多余预算分给 AMD？
  • “当供给追上需求，过去的赢家就会变成输家。”他用英伟达／AMD，以及 Lumentum／AAOI 的股价比值说明相对强弱：Lumentum 自身一直暴跌，但比值近期在上升。他认为这种 pair trade 合理。
  • 模型会越做越小、越便宜，可能不再需要那么多半导体；美国即便需要很多半导体，也没有电。Frank 预期需求减弱与供给放量会产生错配，而“市场交易的是预期”，所以现在就开始做这件事；至少可以把这个想法放在心上，不一定要做。

6. 民主党若横扫两院，长债可能比股票更有利

  • 以 11 月 3 日中期选举为分界，Frank 当时的估计是：民主党拿下众院近乎确定，拿下参院的概率六成多。因此他列出三种可能：民主党横扫两院、两党五五开、共和党横扫两院；他认为共和党横扫的概率非常小，暂不考虑。
  • 他的政策逻辑来自地方反对：居民觉得数据中心抢电，且在当地没有很强的正外部性，甚至有很强的负外部性；就业者也担心 AI 抢工作。民主党在野时“一定会打 anti-AI 的牌”，若横扫两院，他认为会在地方政府层面卡数据中心建设，理由包括就业、居民电费、土地和水资源。
  • 风险不限于 AI。提高债务上限的谈判，以及放宽金融公司和大银行监管的政策限制，也可能面临回撤。在民主党横扫的情景下，他认为最优标的是长债，其他板块可能都会跌；若两党五五开，他反而觉得对股票来说可能是比较好的环境。

7. 和平协议也不能立即修复炼油瓶颈

  • 主持人提出另一种剧本：未来两周会不会突然出现俄乌战争平息、伊朗达成和平协议，让局势平息？Frank 不认同：“他要是想达成协议，早就达成了。”只剩不到两周，他判断特朗普搞不定了。
  • 他区分原油与成品油：原油有一定出口量、供应够，不代表汽柴油问题解决；炼油厂被炸后，crack（裂解价差）持续扩大，汽油、柴油价格仍在攀升。炼厂恢复需要相当长时间，即使伊朗投降、美国投降或原油供给恢复，也不可能立即改善居民与工业的用油情况。

8. 基准是衰退或滞胀，比特币要看资金如何定义它

  • Frank 把美国描述为 K 型经济，提到 2024 年第三季度曾触发 Sahm Rule；在他的判断里，这几年的美国经济增长完全靠 AI CapEx 支撑，因此 CapEx 一降就可能“立刻衰退”。他的明年基本预期是衰退路径，甚至可能出现“史无前例的衰退型大熊市”。
  • 若衰退促使联储停止加息或降息，黄金与比特币可能承接热钱；但比特币盘子小，能接多少他也“不好说”。若油价与服务业通胀不退、联储仍很强硬，则可能走向更坏的滞胀；他认为软着陆或“金发女郎”剧本的概率非常低。
  • 主持人凭记忆提到比特币与纳指的相关系数约 0.3—0.4，对它能否独强保留看法。Frank 承认“看得不是特别清楚”：股票受连续财报 miss、下调预期的盈利压力约束，币则更像筹码游戏；若大资金按“数字黄金”交易，经济变差、利率下降后持有成本变低，比特币反而可能走牛。
  • 极端情况则是另一回事：若 CoreWeave 暴雷或破产、Oracle 也破产，出现类似金融危机的场景，“所有东西都要跌，包括比特币”。他也澄清，以前说比特币“看归零”只是情绪上的反应，“不代表我的真实想法”，不能当作他目前的确定判断。

9. DIA 多单只是利率回落后的估值修复

  • 谈到主持人看到的 DIA 多单，Frank 先更正：已经走了。他把 DIA 当作成熟公司占主导的仓位：此前 AI 高增长预期推高实际与名义利率，压缩这些公司的估值；OpenAI、Anthropic 的 ARR 不及预期后，AI 增长预期破裂、美国长债利率下降，才给了估值修复机会。
  • 他并不把 DIA 当作衰退或滞胀中的避风港：大银行持有企业债，CAT 的相当一部分增长来自 AI 相关采购，GS 的并购、做市收入也可能受影响。若 AI 投资和股市活动继续冷却，这些公司的盈利同样有问题；“DIA 只是短线的一个打野仓位”。

10. 印度多头押的是基本面与资金流背离

  • Frank 认为印度基本面没变差：上半年增速很快，银行坏账率接近历史低位。下跌来自缺油、采购中东原油消耗美元，继而压低卢比、吓跑外资。按他的估计，外资每月大概卖出 500 亿美元；股市却只跌十几个百分点，而非他设想的 30%，说明内资承接很强。
  • 印度还是许多亚洲 long-short 交易中的韩国空头配对腿。若韩国开始暴跌，pair trade unwind 可能带来印度反弹。
  • 另一催化是他所说“下周”上市的 Jio：他称这是印度史上最大的 IPO，规模大概 1,000 亿美元以上，认购倍数很高。他把 Jio 描述为印度首富的公司，业务包括类似淘宝、微信、珠宝、视频和运营商的服务。他判断做 global macro 的基金会参与，换卢比的过程会带来卢比回流，并配置其他印度公司。
  • 他还看中 Oil Dollar Window：印度央行通过指定银行，向几家大型国有油企提供采购原油所需的美元。基本面没有转差、内资承接强，再叠加这些催化，是他上周已经买入印度的理由；他形容印度当周“一枝独秀”，自己也赚了一些钱。

11. 多 ROST、空 XLY，押注财富效应退潮后的消费降级

  • 他最近两天新开 XLY 空头，也一直做多 ROST；空头仓位包括 Hilton、RCL 和 Starbucks。这是他对 K 型经济崩溃的另一种表达：一旦股市财富效应消退，居民消费能力会大幅下降，非必需消费面临压力。
  • ROST 是他描述的低价服装零售商，逻辑不是居民会更富，而是仍有消费能力的人可能选择更便宜的商品。
  • 他强调 Hilton、RCL、Starbucks 尚未怎么跌，仍在前高附近或离前高不远；他的判断是：“下周只要加息，这些公司全都会死。”更广的空头候选还包括 Ralph Lauren、Airbnb、Booking、Marriott，都是其衰退判断向消费端的延伸。

12. 开源冲击的是能力稀缺性与 token 收费模式

  • Frank 用技术扩散解释闭源优势为何会收窄：英国最先发明蒸汽机和纺纱机，也采取严格保密措施，工业革命成果仍扩散到法国、德国和全世界。开源与闭源的差距可能在不同阶段扩大或缩小，但他认为闭源模型的相对优势会持续缩减。
  • 不做证明数学定理、推导没人研究过的公式这类前沿任务时，他反问，用 DeepSeek、千问、Gemini，对比 Opus 5.5、Extra 6，“真的能感觉出什么区别吗？其实很难”。开源不必在所有领域击败闭源，只需越来越多日常任务能以更低成本完成，客户就有理由分流。
  • 他认为开源真正改变的是“能力的稀缺性”，让大客户重新掌握模型选择、部署方式和价格谈判的主动权；模型能力下沉的速度，会超过很多客户提高付费预算的速度。OpenAI 和 Anthropic 开发 Haiku 这类更便宜的模型应对竞争，也会影响自身盈利。
  • “token 计费必然走向终结”是他的强判断，但他随即限定：不是完全没有 token 计费，而是财报收入大头会从目前可能 80%—90% 的 token 计费，大幅分流到私有部署、使用开源模型等模式。他认为单靠 token 计费，支撑不了两家市值 1 万亿美元以上的公司。

13. 长线仍看好龙头，下一段利润可能转向端侧

  • 他的收尾并非否定 AI：虽然不认为 LLM 会带来 AGI，仍视其为人类历史上非常重要的工业革命。若持有者是真正长期投资者，英伟达、台积电被套不必惊慌；他认为两者估值便宜，尤其英伟达，并认可其 GPU 设计与 foundry 龙头地位。
  • 对 Intel、AMD、MU、海力士、AAOI、GFS，他则劝套牢者重新评估能否承担后果。“赚钱可以赚 10,000%，但亏钱只要亏 100%，就归零了。”他没有把对 AI 未来的乐观，平均分配给所有半导体股票。
  • 端侧是他保留的另一长期方向：未来模型成本会越来越低、模型会越做越小，隐私与低延迟场景将支持端侧产品。他点到 Qualcomm、ARM、NXP 等公司，认为 AI 产业链利润分配可能从半导体切换到端侧；如果端侧真的出现，Lattice 这样的公司可能就不会那么好。

来源：X Space

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/168x-frank-trading-ai-trade-20261020

item.title: Vol.238 宏观漫谈112｜全球资本市场，集体“缺钱”？
item.description: 李丰称，全球流动性见顶后，市场进入资金相互抽取、谁的钱都不够用的阶段。数据中心新债减少，部分债券收益率约14%；Anthropic估值据传可能下调，IPO暂停或延期，融资压力显现。这并非即刻崩盘判断；月底议息、三季报和美国中期选举将检验资金承接力。
item.content:encoded:
高能量 · 李翔、李丰 · 2026-10-20 · 87 min · 原语言 ZH

李丰称，全球流动性见顶后，市场进入资金相互抽取、谁的钱都不够用的阶段。数据中心新债减少，部分债券收益率约14%；Anthropic估值据传可能下调，IPO暂停或延期，融资压力显现。这并非即刻崩盘判断；月底议息、三季报和美国中期选举将检验资金承接力。

TL;DR

  • 李丰的总判断：全球资本市场已进入“谁的钱都不够用”的阶段。 2020—2021年印出“人类历史上从来没有见过这么多的钱”，经过2022—2024年的充分流动与集聚，各蓄水池水位被推到高位；没有新放水后，“大家就只能互相抽水”。方法论是：“金融的基本面就只有一个问题，就是钱有多少和去了哪里”，AI公司泡沫的大小“永远只取决于钱的多少”。
  • 流动性见顶的证据链在密集出现。 美股科技股只能“涨了A就得B跌”地轮动；八月以来数据中心新债较第二季度明显减少，部分发行人的债从假设票面利率8%被折价卖到约14%；Anthropic路演后传出估值要下调，“两千亿看来是难了，现在可能讨论的是一千五百亿”。英伟达、黑石等参与投资的澳洲数据中心公司，以及Oura Ring的IPO接连暂停或延迟。李丰在高点把裸空英伟达加到两倍（仓位很小、单倍无杠杆），作为流动性观察。
  • 美国在自我互搏：数据中心债和国债在抢同一池水。 强美元抽来的钱竞标美债倍数不低但收益率没下去，一级交易商兜底占比显著走低；AI CapEx支撑经济增长，国债顺利发行又是财政维系根本，总量不够时“两件事是个互搏的过程”。抽水的边际效应递减：三、四、五月那轮（避险加鹰派预期）最猛，九月已远弱于彼时，十月若再加息，扰动可能更小。
  • 顶部不等于马上崩盘。 周期到顶后要经过“两三次、四次不同级别的反弹”才会“咔嚓”，且咔嚓通常由黑天鹅触发；当下相信AI持续上涨的人仍明显多于看空者，“没有向下的共识之前，不会咔嚓一下”。催化剂集中在未来两周半：月底议息、三季报（台积电九月环比下降、美国拟建数据中心接近一半延宕或搁浅，资本市场已从“谁投得多谁涨”转为“谁花穿了谁就被惩罚”）、以及中期选举。Polymarket显示众议院易手概率接近九成，参议院易手概率超过一半。
  • 2026年中国经济大致定型：像2021年，靠外贸扛增长。 九月进出口“超级超预期”，中美关税缓和延至明年初；消费弱恢复，投资可能是负拉动项，全年GDP李丰直观估计“4%到4.5%”。财政侧，发债不少但前八个月支出同比只增1%多，政府没有像往年那样靠前投资。李丰坦言不知原因，可能是把进度往后推，作为进出口出问题时的缓冲，也不排除确实缺钱。
  • 信贷端的大手术：影子银行、助贷和互联网借贷环节受到强约束。 去年十月对民间借贷和助贷的限制，媒体解释为不允许利率超过年化24%；之后上限调到四倍LPR，8月1日助贷新规执行。李丰的体感是，催收短信从一天十几条到八月中旬后“一条都没收到”。居民短贷下半年增量急剧减少；他猜测一部分人凑钱还旧债，填不上的可能转成坏账，但也提到提前还贷、不再续贷等因素。场景型消费贷仍有逻辑，但银行与平台之间不能再形成不透明的资金池。
  • 中国在为可能的快速下跌提前做配置再平衡。 公募风格漂移管理办法拟从12月1日起实行，并设一年缓冲期，管控“宽基窄投”；保险买红利股（分红率不少已超4%，甚至5%）的股价波动不计当期损益，买科技股则持有期间的波动也计入损益，引导长钱配置蓝筹。平准资金方面，国家队此前打出的约1.2万亿元子弹，李丰称大约九成已收回。港股新股近期多数破发；茶百道相关股票交易涉及冻结四十多亿元；A股未解禁明星股（长鑫、宇树等）则有炒作后回落的压力。
  • 人民币策略：对美元尽量不持续贬值，对其他货币在波动中小幅升值，底层涉及去美元化。 粗略估算全球贸易结算中美元约占50%；李丰猜测，中国贸易中今年约一半用本币结算，约占全球贸易8个百分点，其他区域贸易也在增加本币结算。央行买黄金、发展香港离岸人民币产品是相关背景；社保赴港支持相关事项则是李丰提到的一个小信号。一级市场也在降温：热点投资不再那么集中、机构进入募资周期；李丰明确说，美国新公司（包括早期公司）融资和新基金募资都比去年困难。

Digest

1. 九月金融数据：直接融资占比49%，M2放缓是融资结构切换的镜像

  • 李丰开篇拆解：九月债券与股票相关的直接融资占比约49%，又一次超过贷款；“贷款增速同比少增”与此“其实是同一件事”——从“存了贷、贷了存”的货币派生，转向直接发债、发股，货币乘数减少，M2同比增量也会减少。
  • 本期政府债券发行量不低，但政府存款并没有完全反映出债券发行带来的高增长；李丰也提示可能有滞后效应。

2. 财政之谜：发债不少、花钱很慢，今年政府没有像往年那样“靠前投资”

  • 前八个月财政收入同比约增5%，支出只增1%多；往年惯例是尽量靠前投资，把钱在一、二季度用出去，形成当年的“实体工作量”。2021年是特殊例外：出口超预期，政府投资进度到三季度才较快兑现。
  • 李丰坦承“不知道这里边有什么原因”，列了几种可能：专项债不易挪作他用；有一部分债可能用于还债、化解隐性债务；或者有意把投资进度往后推，作为进出口等方面出问题时的缓冲。他也不排除政府确实缺钱，但强调专项债有特定用途，不容易随意挪用。

3. 2026年中国经济大致定型：像2021年，靠外贸扛增长

  • 九月进出口“超级超预期”，部分得益于中美元首会谈后关税竞争缓和，并至少延续到明年初；叠加美国购物季，全年外贸可能保持高增长，即使AI相关投资减弱、相关出口减少，购物季也可能补上一块。
  • 李丰的判断是：消费从通缩意义上看已企稳，CPI同比为0.9%，属于轻微通胀或弱恢复；消费对今年增长的贡献可能较小。若政府投资也弱于进度预期，投资可能成为负拉动项。两相抵消后，全年GDP“4%到4.5%”是他的直观估计。
  • 十一旅游数据因假期安排和统计口径不同而难直接同比；悲观和乐观解读都有口径问题。李丰认为总量可能略高于去年、同口径大致差不多，出境旅游则比去年增加很多。

4. 非银存款单月减少1.9万亿元：多重因素合流

  • 证券、保险、基金等非银金融机构存款九月减少1.9万亿元。李丰认为可能与风险偏好降低、季末银行考核拉存款（存款利率上行或出现利率较好的存款产品）、理财到期或赎回、权益市场波动等因素有关。
  • 他猜测回到居民存款中的资金主要来自债券类、银行理财类，不主要是股票资金，但数据没有细分，也不排除有一部分股票资金。

5. 影子银行的切除手术：催收短信从一天十几条到一条没有

  • 政策线索：去年十月对民间借贷和助贷有过一轮约束，媒体解释为不允许利率超过年化24%；之后利率上限调到四倍LPR。8月1日助贷和互联网贷款平台相关新规执行后，李丰的体感是执行“非常严”。
  • 李丰作为常被企查查列为公司高管的投资人，从去年年底开始每天收到十几条催收短信，持续到今年五月；从八月中旬以来则“一条都没收到”。李翔感叹：“一下子世界安静了。”
  • 对应到数据，居民贷款里短贷出现负增长，银行层面的居民短贷增量下半年急剧减少。李丰猜测有人想尽办法凑钱还旧债，填不上的可能转成坏账；但他也提到，过去贷款利率较高、如今存款利率较低，提前还贷和还贷后不续贷也可能是因素。
  • 李丰估计，若按T+3计算，这种情况可能延续到月底；逾期三个月或六个月仍未偿还的，可能会被处理为坏账，但他不知道具体如何处理、能否一次性冲掉。

6. 平台消费贷不会因此消失：贷款要跟着消费场景走，资金池不能再造

  • 李翔观察到独立互联网金融平台空间变小，而携程、网易、抖音、京东等带消费场景的平台仍较活跃。李丰谈到的政策意图包括：解决高息、多头借贷问题；避免银行与借款人之间隔着过多中介、造成信息缺失；降低层层加价后的社会平均借贷成本。
  • 监管关注的另一条线是资金池：2018年资管新规针对银行形成的资金池，现在也不能让平台在自己与银行之间形成不透明的资金池。李丰认为消费贷款要跟着消费场景走，并提到美国也有类似情况。
  • 李翔提到平台以广告和金融变现；李丰补充，中国消费者还没有那么明显的个人服务订阅付费习惯，因此平台会寻找其他收入来源。

7. 本期核心命题：全球到了“谁的钱都不够用”的阶段

  • 李丰的结论是：“今天到了几乎谁的钱都不够用的时候。”2020—2021年全世界出现了“人类历史上从来没有见过这么多的钱”，2022—2024年间资金流动、转移和集聚，把各个蓄水池的水位推高；没有新的大规模放水，大家就只能互相抽水。
  • 他概括金融的基本面是“钱有多少，钱去了哪里”，并认为AI技术创新是长线过程，但AI公司的泡沫大小取决于钱有多少。
  • 李翔追问，会不会不是钱不够，而是资产价格太贵。李丰回答，两者有关：资产越贵，越往上推就越有止盈盘，需要更多钱；从过去大规模放水推高估值所达到的高点再往上，需要更大规模的流动性，而“看起来没有”。

8. 抽水的实证：新兴市场承压、法国国债受挑战、美债“钱来了但不便宜”

  • 李丰认为，美国九月升息使美元走强，资金因此流向美国；新兴市场汇率承受贬值压力、各国维稳汇市，印度等市场受影响。他也提到日本、韩国等市场的动荡，以及欧洲汇率和法国国债收益率面临的挑战。
  • 美债发行则出现另一种现象：规模较大的国债发行约两三百亿美元，竞标倍数较高，但收益率没有下去；一级交易商兜底认购的占比显著降低。钱参与了认购，却没有让美国以更低成本融资，李丰称这是个“神奇的现象”。

9. 涨A就得B跌：美股轮动是流动性不足的表现

  • 李丰观察到，美股科技股上涨时产业链内部轮动明显：七姐妹上涨，存储、光模块等就可能下跌；光模块上涨时，存储、七姐妹或数据中心相关股票又可能下跌。钱不够让各环节一起涨，只能在产业链之间轮动。
  • 他此前买了英伟达裸空，即只做空、不对冲；九月底科技股上涨时在高点又加了一倍。仓位仍很小、没有杠杆，作为观察流动性的尝试，因为英伟达是这一轮AI的象征。他说目前还赚了一点。

10. 缺钱的迹象：数据中心债折价、明星IPO接连暂停或延迟

  • 八月以来新发的数据中心债数量明显少于第二季度；九月尤其十月以来，一些盈利和自由现金流较差的AI数据中心企业发行的债在二级市场出现较大折价。李丰举例说，票面利率假设为8%的债，可能已被卖到收益率14%，反映投资者担忧风险，也可能是企业募集资金不够。
  • 李丰转述，Anthropic开完说明会后，第二天传出IPO估值要调低：“两千亿的估值看来难了，现在可能讨论的是一千五百亿。”他还提到，Anthropic披露的信息显示其第三季度收入增长不错，但拆看七、八、九月后，九月增速可能较低。
  • 一家澳洲数据中心建设公司，投资人包括英伟达、黑石等，原计划以数百亿美元估值IPO、融资数十亿美元，最后没有发出而暂停或延迟。Oura Ring原计划以150亿美元以上估值在美国发行，pre-IPO路演后也决定暂缓。李丰认为，这些例子可能显示即使是受追捧的公司也未必能募到足够多的钱。

11. 美国的自我互搏：数据中心债和国债在抢同一池水

  • 李丰认为，美国维持强势美元、把全球流动性抽到美元相关资产的同时，数据中心投资和国债发行都需要大量资金：数据中心及其债券支撑经济增长，国债顺利发行又是财政和政府维持运作的根本。钱的总量不够时，两者互相争夺资金。
  • 他观察到，美股剧烈波动、下跌之后，美债收益率明显回落，像是有一部分钱从股票回到债券。即使美元资产最能吸水，李丰认为也到了“顶”的阶段；这不是说马上崩溃，而是大家都抽不到足够多的水。

12. 抽水的边际效应在递减：三、四、五月是最猛的一轮

  • 李丰复盘，上一轮剧烈抽水发生在三、四、五月：美伊战争带来避险需求，同时市场面对美联储主席更换和鹰派预期、从降息转向升息的预期变化。那轮抽水带来新兴市场更大的动荡，并伴随存储、CPU、光模块等一轮上涨。
  • 九月这轮没有美伊战争那样的地缘政治避险需求，扰动远小于三、四、五月；若十月再升息，李丰认为影响可能仍有，但会比九月更小。李翔总结：“它其实也是边际效应在不断递减。”

13. 顶部不等于崩盘：“没有向下的共识之前，不会咔嚓一下”

  • 李丰原本考虑加英伟达裸空，但决定等未来两周半的波动过去。他认为周期到顶后不会马上直线下跌，通常会经历两三次、四次不同级别的反弹；快速下跌往往由公司之外的黑天鹅触发。
  • 他判断，相信AI公司持续上涨、业绩持续变好的人，仍明显多于认为有泡沫、快到顶的人。过去三年相信AI的人在金融市场得到奖励，正循环不容易打破；但建立信心很慢，跌下来则会快得多。

14. 接下来两周半的三件大事：议息、三季报、中期选举

  • 月底美联储议息，几乎所有重要公司在接下来两周或两周半内公布三季报，下月初还有美国中期选举。李丰提到，Polymarket上众议院易手概率接近90%，参议院易手概率超过一半；若失去一个院，会影响政策执行，也会加剧两党博弈。
  • 他把民主党控制和管理AI安全视为一个重要叙事，并提到约八个州在抗议数据中心建设，主要是民主党州；纽约也对Anthropic上市提出了涉及安全管理的不同意见。特朗普则要求把AI称为“超级智能”，甚至要求AI改称SI。

15. 三季报预判：从“谁投得多谁涨”到“谁花穿了谁就被惩罚”

  • 李丰认为，一季度末到二季度中是科技行业最FOMO的阶段：大家害怕自己不够AI，披露激进的AI CapEx计划，也出现“token maxing”等做法。之后遇到内存等产业链涨价、电力配套不足、居民抗议等问题；截至九月下旬，美国披露的拟建数据中心项目接近一半会延宕或搁浅。
  • 英伟达给客户提供的以租代买方案大约从二季度末开始。资本市场的态度也变了：年初谁投得多谁涨，到了七月份之后发布半年报，变成谁花穿了谁就被惩罚。
  • 李丰举例，台积电九月环比低于八月；Anthropic第三季度收入虽增长，但按其公布信息拆看，九月增速可能很低。他猜大公司三季报整体仍会增长，但八、九月可能不如预期；这仍需等财报揭晓。

16. 中国的提前再平衡：公募新规、保险红利股会计与平准资金

  • 七月股市波动后，监管开始要求基金按募集时的说法合理配置，并对少数极端集中配置案例作出处理。公募基金风格漂移管理办法拟从12月1日起实行，设一年缓冲期，方向包括控制“宽基窄投”和风格漂移。
  • 李丰认为，均衡配置可作为流动性见顶时的风险应对。保险投资方面，买红利股（不少分红率超过4%，甚至5%）时，股价波动不计入当期损益，分红计入；买科技股则买入、持有、卖出阶段的波动都可能影响当期损益。这也是政策鼓励保险以长期配置为主、持有蓝筹股的原因之一。
  • 平准资金方面，李丰回顾国家队、证金和汇金此前打出约1.2万亿元平准子弹，并称大约90%已收回。最近一周市场受外围影响下跌时，下午常有放量，有时开盘也放量；他把这视为平准力量在试图稳定市场、避免急跌。

17. A股港股的短炒生态：未解禁、稀缺概念股与快速获利的诱惑

  • 李翔提到两家上市大模型公司、长鑫科技和宇树等个股跌幅，并问中国科技股是否比美国波动更大。李丰认为，所举例子中不少是有头部AI概念、但还没有解禁的股票，定价和炒作往往更激进，临近解禁压力时容易大幅下跌。
  • 他也提到，长鑫、宇树等公司有头部概念、政策推动和稀缺性，容易形成短期共识，炒作后会有不同类型的资金获利离场。香港市场最近一个半月绝大多数新股破发，削弱了认购前入场、短炒一个月赚一两倍就走的动力。
  • 香港另有一笔冻结资金超过40亿元，涉及炒作茶百道相关股票。李翔问这类操作是否需要公司配合，李丰回答“需要公司配合”，并称这也是茶百道被停牌的原因之一。李丰把更广泛的问题概括为短期共识和筹码过度集中：一年可能亏10%或赚20%，而一个月赚一倍的诱惑很大。

18. 人民币与外储简史：为什么买美债，循环剪断后为什么买黄金

  • 潘功胜提到人民币汇率和一般账户不是线性关联。背景是九月出口增速重新超过进口，外储却减少了几百亿美元，容易被理解为大规模干预外汇市场；李丰指出，中国对美元汇率基本没变，对其他货币可能升值。
  • 李丰回顾，2010—2012年前后中国逐步放开强制结汇。强制结汇原本是为了增加外储、抵御外部冲击；代价之一是货币政策自主性受限——例如有1000亿美元顺差进来，就要发行约8000亿元人民币。2014年汇改后，人民币开始允许双向宽幅波动。
  • 他还解释，过去外储很大一部分用来买美债，因为以美元计价的资产与美元同起同落，不容易受到大规模套利进出的影响。中国提供实物商品、换回美元后再买美债，曾使资金回流美国金融层面；贸易战等因素使这个循环被打断后，中国不再打算把赚来的钱拿去支持美国政府做竞争性事务，央行增加黄金等资产也是保值考虑之一。
  • 出口结构方面，八月AI或数字处理设备相关出口出现“价增量减”；九月这类出口对整体增长的贡献率小于八月，新能源车和其他品类的贡献率稍有上升。

19. 去美元化的算术与人民币的需求端

  • 李丰给出的粗略估算是，全球贸易结算中美元约占50%；中国占全球贸易约15%到16%，他猜今年约一半使用本币结算，相当于全球贸易约8个百分点。其余结算中，一部分来自各区域贸易体系使用本币。各国经历美元潮汐冲击后，都希望保有一定汇率自主权。
  • 中国资本项下仍有管制，因此还发展香港离岸人民币市场和相关金融产品，让境外持有人民币的人有更多选择。李丰也提到社保将赴港支持相关事项，并特别说明这只是一个小信号。
  • 今年贸易顺差也许超过1万亿美元，但外储没有增加同样规模；李丰指出，部分企业把境外收入留在当地做对外投资、建厂，没有汇回结汇。
  • 李丰的汇率结论是，人民币对美元尽量不持续贬值，对其他货币则可能在波动中小幅升值，以平衡贸易关系；同时需要避免单向持续升值，因为那会吸引套利资金。

20. 一级市场降温：热点不再一窝蜂，美国新公司和新基金都更难融资

  • 李丰把国务院关于新质生产力的政策，与国资委54号文作类比：不是禁止投资，而是不要所有人一窝蜂挤进核聚变、量子计算等少数热点。传统产业升级、已成规模的新兴产业和未来产业，都要合理布局；他举例说，可以在芯片全流程或新药研发流程中加入AI。
  • 他认为，今年上半年热点共识形成很快，资金几个月一轮地追逐核聚变、量子计算、物理模型、世界模型；七月市场波动后，加上相关政策引导，这种一窝蜂现象有所减少。
  • 李翔提到不少投资机构进入募资周期，李丰同意，并称美国新公司融资（包括早期公司）和新基金募资都比去年困难。对李翔提出的中国一级市场是否也受美国IPO定价和节奏影响，李丰表示自己猜会有影响。最后他回到本期主题：“大家钱都不够，流动性都不够。”

来源：Podcast

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/gaonengliang-2026-10-20-vol-238

item.title: Christina Cacioppo - Building an Enduring Software Company in the Age of AI - [Invest Like the Best, EP.496]
item.description: Christina Cacioppo says Vanta’s 400-integration “trust graph” helps the roughly eight-year-old company build software and agents faster. About 25% of customers use agent flows; she expects raising that share to 75% to improve retention and customer experience. Vanta absorbs token costs rather than passing them through, since markups invite Claude comparisons, leaving commercialization and margin recovery unresolved.
item.content:encoded:
Invest Like the Best · Patrick O'Shaughnessy、Christina Cacioppo · 2026-10-20 · 57 min · 原语言 EN

Christina Cacioppo says Vanta’s 400-integration “trust graph” helps the roughly eight-year-old company build software and agents faster. About 25% of customers use agent flows; she expects raising that share to 75% to improve retention and customer experience. Vanta absorbs token costs rather than passing them through, since markups invite Claude comparisons, leaving commercialization and margin recovery unresolved.

TL;DR

  • Cacioppo attributes Vanta’s category win to execution: “you’re really only as good as the last thing you shipped”—someone can vibe-code your thing in a weekend. A structural advantage is the “trust graph”: a security data lake fed by 400 integrations, which she says has let Vanta build new software and agents faster. The company is about eight years old, with ~16,000 global customers and about five products.
  • The “SaaSpocalypse” was her scariest moment, and living through the repricing is “cognitive dissonance.” In the fullness of time, she thinks an 80% growth / 80% margin business returns more cash than a 160% growth / 30% margin one, “but today, the latter is valued at 3X, 4X… it’s 10X the multiple of the former.” AI-maximalist investors tell her they’ll fund “the labs, and… basically robot tractors in Iowa, nothing in between.”
  • Vanta is eating token costs rather than charging customers for them. Customers notice a markup on a Cloud token and ask whether the application is “4X as good as Claude”; token pricing puts an application in direct competition with the models, and credits do not hide that. Twenty-five percent of customers are in the agent flow; if Vanta can get that to 75%, she expects better retention and experience. “This is a usage phase… nail that, and you can figure out commercialization after.”
  • Overhyped: token pricing, low margins for their own sake, post-training “for the marketing value”—“mostly for investors, actually”—and FDEs. She says post-training can make sense for cost in some cases, and a customer-specific model may be reasonable for some enterprise deployments, but doubts that handing customers a model is the right end state. FDEs are often professional services under a more fashionable label; the economics may work for eight-figure contracts but are probably upside down at five- and six-figure ones. Underhyped: company and customer context over functional skill—she’d take a worse salesperson who knows Vanta.
  • Total compensation for Vanta’s top person is probably about 10 times what it was five years ago. She says top people’s value is accelerating, that Vanta should have more comp dispersion, and that “you never pay the top people enough.” Tenders are normalized and expected as part of compensation; she calls the situation unhealthy but says her opinion does not change the game on the field.
  • Security’s threat picture is shifting: AI models can persistently try vast numbers of things and chain benign-seeming findings together. Patrick framed the future as a constant white-hat penetration-testing agent with a patching “buddy agent”; Cacioppo said that is possible for parts of Vanta, especially for customers who may not pay Wiz’s enterprise-level prices.
  • Her broader thesis is that AI has ushered in a “high-excitement-but-low-trust” era, and distrust of tech companies is worsening. She expects proof that software is industrial-grade to matter more to businesses, governments, and regulators. She imagines Vanta could sit at the center of those transactions as it expands from compliance into more security products. A field datapoint: French software companies told her they switched predominantly to Chinese models over business-continuity concerns, not nationalism.

Digest

1. Execution won the category; the trust graph is an advantage

  • Vanta at about eight years old: ~16,000 customers globally across about five products, built on the premise of helping companies “build and earn trust”—starting or maturing security and compliance programs, then getting customer credit via audits such as SOC 2, ISO 2701, HIPAA, questionnaires and trust centers. Asked how she beat a crowded field: “Execution… You can be first, and you can start it, but that doesn’t really matter. It’s even more true now ’cause someone can vibe-code your thing in a weekend.”
  • The structural answer is integrations: Vanta connects to 400 tools and pulls data into its “trust graph,” which she describes as “really just a security data lake.” She says it is broader than other providers’ data foundations, including some security providers’, and has let Vanta build new software and agents faster.
  • Scariest moment: the last 12 months. “SaaSpocalypse. You’re like, ‘Okay, great job building a system of record. You’re now screwed.’” Parts true, parts not—the forcing question being: “Great, what is the agent? You have all this data and a system of record. Fine. What the heck are you doing with it?”

2. A great business, repriced: living with cognitive dissonance

  • Patrick’s setup: Vanta is growing fast with very high margins—business traits that four years earlier might have been considered the best model ever—yet the multiple is a third or a quarter of what it was. Her answer: hold two things at once. “An 80% growth business with 80% margins will actually be better” in the fullness of time than 160% growth at 30% margins, “but today, the latter is valued at 3X, 4X… it’s 10X the multiple of the former.”
  • The game on the field: financing runs through AI maximalists (“we’ll invest in the labs, and we’ll basically invest in robot tractors in Iowa, nothing in between”), and ambitious employees “if it feels like they’re not in the right boat, they’re gonna change boats.” Her stance: keep doing what makes business sense—“which may or may not be token-pricing models”—and “live for the fullness of time.”

3. The agent is now the product—and she says nobody is further along

  • Benchmarking the Vanta agent against the names you’d imagine as “AI applications,” “we have yet to find someone who is further along”—while acknowledging, “we’re doing a bad job looking” is the obvious critique. Behind the product-level “Vanta agent” sit hundreds of task-specific agents with tools and computers; the front end has long-running agents that auto-generate UI on the fly, “‘cause sometimes you want chat and sometimes you want UI.”
  • The grounding example: an employee leaves and isn’t removed from every account. The agent: “I just wrote a custom agent for you that will go do that. Do you want me to turn this on? … Do you also want me to remove access from these three people?”—borrowing lab UI patterns: “You want me to do this once? You want me to do this always?”
  • Twenty-five percent of customers are in that kind of agent flow today. If Vanta can get that to 75%, she expects better retention and a better customer experience; pricing can be worked out later.
  • The trade-off she’s living: building agent-first rather than building a lot of SaaS UI (“we’re not gonna put Tableau inside of Vanta,” which Vanta might have done in 2021 or 2022) against enterprise reality. A U.S. enterprise asked whether Vanta could turn its AI features off because non-AI tools clear procurement faster. Patrick framed the diffusion risk as being “right, but early and therefore wrong.” She says they are not going to build an off switch.

4. Pricing: don’t put yourself up against Claude

  • Why token pricing fails: customers are “really smart” and may say, “You’ve just marked up a Cloud token 4X. Are you 4X as good as Claude?” It puts the application in competition with the models—“no application really wants to” be there—and credit-token exchange rates do not fool users. “We’re eating the token cost right now” and taking lower margins.
  • Everyone wants outcome pricing—the former microeconomics professor in her loves its incentive alignment—but she distinguishes outcome from output: a support ticket closed is an output; “the outcome is actually my Sonos now works.” Agreeable units of work are hard to settle on: “I just named three things. I could name another 47.” That creates cognitive overhead for users comparing agent work with doing the task themselves.
  • Model selection runs on task- or agent-specific evals written by subject-matter experts, including people who ran security and compliance programs. The experts evaluate their evals; model swapping is “mostly about quality, not cost.” Vanta’s decision-and-action work uses fewer tokens than coding agents; legal and document drafting may use more.

5. Building with AI inside an eight-year-old company

  • Asked how much AI changes company-building, one to ten: “Eight or nine. The principles are still the same… all the tropes are still the tropes, but the way you do stuff should be quite different.”
  • The legacy-codebase problem: agents lack the context window to understand eight years of code, “will do silly things,” and need “a high-context engineer to babysit it,” which can undermine the point. The fix—where she says Notion is about nine months ahead—is modularizing so agents can fully understand smaller parts. Companies always had this as new-engineer onboarding friction; “agents have made it, ‘Well, great, now we want to onboard 9,000 new engineers tomorrow.’” She gives Vanta a lower grade here.
  • Adoption 101: use AI yourself and build something for your company; check at least every two weeks because things change quickly. That gives you a visceral sense of what works and helps you question claims like “we’re gonna fire all of our SDRs ’cause I built one agent.” She has become more empathetic toward strong people who have not dived in: find what is blocking them and help them get into the work.
  • The onboarding-wizard parable: a talented, motivated team kept bringing SaaS onboarding wizards instead of an LLM flow. The real blocker was: “We don’t know if we can get the drag-your-files thing to work… We basically don’t think we’re allowed to fail on this project.” Her response: bet on the LLM flow and “burn the boats.” The Claude-style big canvas—drag in messy files and screenshots, let the system make sense of them and ask questions—shipped and works well.

6. Talent wars: trillion-dollar pitches and 10x compensation

  • The pitch her people get elsewhere: “We’re $6 billion today, but Sequoia’s gonna do a $10 billion check in a month, and then somebody’s gonna write it up to $25 billion next year, but we can get you in at six today.” She’s considered counter-escalating (“the real question… can you take us on a journey to, like, $250 billion?”)—“Probably not, but the answer is not definitely not.” Her actual playbook is “do what it says on the tin,” show candidates the metrics, and “counter the vibes with data and trustworthy vibes versus YOLO vibes.”
  • Total compensation for Vanta’s top person is “probably a factor of 10” compared with five years ago. She says Vanta should have more comp dispersion and that the value of top people is accelerating. What earns it: “High agency, get shit done. That sounds so milquetoast, and that’s worth millions of dollars.” She says you never pay top people enough, though there are also people paid much more than their contribution. The counterforce would be investors reviving the dilution/SBC conversation—“now we’re definitely not talking about it.”
  • One retention case: a strong leader entertained an offer promising “full decision-making authority.” Her response was to unblock them: “What do you need to feel like you can make these decisions? Just go make these decisions.” On tenders: Vanta had not historically done them, but “the game on the field is that you’re doing a tender every time.” They are normalized and expected as part of compensation; without them, companies need to offer other things. She agrees they feel unhealthy but says her opinion does not change that expectation.
  • Exit: an IPO is a means to an end, not her personal bucket-list item. The goal is a “big, independent, standalone company.”

7. Overhyped: post-training theater and FDEs; underhyped: context

  • Overhyped: “token-based pricing, low margins for the sake of having low margins, and custom training models for the marketing value.” She says inference providers will often say the reason to post-train is cost, not quality; some businesses have a cost need, and a customer-specific model for an enterprise use case can be reasonable. Her broader skepticism is that customers may not want to be handed a model: “reasonable iteration, but not the right solution.”
  • FDEs (forward-deployed engineers): she calls them “a great talent arbitrage, the same way a chief of staff is,” but says the role is often professional services under a different label. She doubts a high-agency Harvard CS graduate will sign up for a conventional pro-services role. Palantir is the company she thinks does this well, with eight-figure contracts; at five- and six-figure contracts, the economics are probably upside down.
  • Underhyped: company and customer context over functional skill. She would “take a worse salesperson on sales skill who knows the Vanta pieces,” and thinks labs building go-to-market teams by hiring good salespeople may be undervaluing context.
  • Field note from France: Cacioppo says many Paris software companies she met use Chinese models predominantly. She initially guessed nationalism or anti-American sentiment, then was corrected: customers told her they switched after what they described as a U.S.-model access restriction, citing business continuity rather than nationalism. The specific model/service name in the transcript is unclear.

8. Security at machine speed—and where she’d invest

  • The models “are just so much more persistent than people. They’ll try nine quadrillion things, where a person would give up after 9,000.” The shift is not only zero-days: she says models can chain “17 benign-ish” things together. She cites an OpenAI RSA talk about Hugging Face and the difficulty of dealing with findings that might previously have been considered low severity and fixed later. “If you’re fixing things at machine speed, you don’t have to prioritize”—though “it’ll be rocky as we get there.”
  • Patrick pictured a constant white-hat penetration-testing agent with a “buddy agent” that patches what it finds. Cacioppo said that is possible for some parts of Vanta, especially for its customer base; she expects CrowdStrike to do it better for enterprises. For cloud misconfigurations, she contrasts Wiz’s multi-thousand-person-company customer base and roughly $150,000 starting price with Vanta’s focus on already-embedded customers who may pay “40 or 50” for a solution suited to them.
  • Vanta sees itself as a security company that began with compliance: “The best version of compliance is proving the security you have.” It plans to build more security-focused products on top of its existing data and agent intelligence. As companies face growing pressure to prove they are industrial-grade to enterprises, governments, regulators and others, Vanta aims to connect both sides of that marketplace.
  • Wearing her old investor hat (“do not envy the job at all”), she says certainty around open-source models feels disconnected from how underbuilt the ecosystem around them is; “a bunch of the lab playbooks seem like they should apply to the open-source models.” Green shoots: cybersecurity founders, rev tech (some incumbents are choosing PE-bent, sponsor-style playbooks instead of building), robotics—which she sees as underweighted despite being somewhat hot—and government modernization. AI-related risks are helping CISOs make the case for enterprise-risk budgets.

9. The billboard saga, and rebuilding trust

  • The billboard war story: a billboard skeptic (“founder ego is why someone would do a billboard”) was persuaded by PMM Sarah, who went around her boss with “Compliance that doesn’t talk too much.” Cacioppo laughed, checked with investor Andrew Reid, and approved it. The billboard went up near Burning Man; the tweet went viral and the line circulated on r/accounting. She says it worked because it expressed Vanta’s wink: taking the work seriously without taking itself too seriously.
  • In 2022, the market crash made billboard inventory available, and Vanta got a good spot at the 101/280 intersection. Despite her saying on podcasts that the contract was locked up for years, it was just a placement order. A startup took the spot, and her offer to pay $3 million—double the roughly $1.5 million the other company was paying—failed when its founder said, “We’re actually cash flow positive.” “I am an extremely inelastic buyer here” turned into “literally, I’m an inelastic seller.” She half-jokes that losing the spot cost Vanta market cap.
  • The closing thesis: “We just don’t trust software companies, tech companies the way we used to, and that is getting worse year over year.” She agrees with Patrick’s framing of a “high-excitement-but-low-trust” era. Vanta’s job, in her view, is to rebuild trust “legitimately so, not just on vibes.” In B2B, she favors specific data, improvement curves and possibly contract-backed promises; consumer trust is more about vibes and “seems very hard to turn.” Asked about big companies using personal agents, she says no: she would rather have Google, Apple or another company she chooses hold her email or chats. She imagines Vanta could sit at the center of transactions that demonstrate software is trustworthy and industrial-grade; the $250 billion figure is part of her aspirational framing, not a forecast.
  • Her motivation has shifted from “You don’t think I can get off the starting line? Let me show you”—“still a little dark edge, but less of it”—to “let’s see how far we can go with this.” One word for Vanta’s next five years: “Expansive.” The company has an established base of customers and data, and she sees room to build on it.

item.title: Elon Musk: The End of Work, the Death of Money, and a World Run by AI
item.description: Musk’s abundance forecast hinges on AI moving beyond language models: digital superintelligence alone could add 20%–30% to goods and services, or roughly $30 trillion annually. Robots, space and a lunar mass driver could expand the economy to “potentially a million times” Earth’s size, making conventional money less relevant in his view. Isaacson presses on inequality and healthcare, but Musk offers no concrete distribution mechanism; his proposed peer testing of frontier models before release also remains to be worked out.
item.content:encoded:
The Builders with Walter Isaacson · Walter Isaacson、Elon Musk · 2026-10-20 · 40 min · 原语言 EN

Musk’s abundance forecast hinges on AI moving beyond language models: digital superintelligence alone could add 20%–30% to goods and services, or roughly $30 trillion annually. Robots, space and a lunar mass driver could expand the economy to “potentially a million times” Earth’s size, making conventional money less relevant in his view. Isaacson presses on inequality and healthcare, but Musk offers no concrete distribution mechanism; his proposed peer testing of frontier models before release also remains to be worked out.

TL;DR

  • Musk expects AI and robots to decide the future as digital intelligence vastly exceeds biological intelligence. With “a million times more digital intelligence,” he finds continued human control unlikely, including control by wealthy owners. He argues truth-seeking and curiosity may help make AI safer, while concluding, “So I hope the AI is nice to us.”
  • Musk’s largest economic forecast depends on robots and expansion beyond Earth. His “rough guess” is that digital superintelligence increases goods-and-services output by 20%–30%, roughly $30 trillion annually. Robots, space and a lunar mass driver could, he thinks, support an economy “potentially a million times” Earth’s size.
  • Musk forecasts conventional money losing relevance, while Isaacson presses him on distribution and purpose. Musk imagines currency measured in physical quantities, universal access to desired goods and services, and voluntary work resembling recreational gardening. Isaacson’s questions about inequality and healthcare in the commons receive an abundance forecast, without a concrete distribution mechanism.
  • Musk says xAI supplies Anthropic compute and proposes competitors testing each other’s models before release. Weekly calls and access a week before launch could expose dangerous capabilities faster than a new regulator, he argues. His admission about founding OpenAI is consequential: actions he took because he was concerned about AI ended up accelerating the technology.
  • Musk acknowledges that politics diverted too much attention from his businesses. “Carried away, basically” is his assessment; he says his government involvement should have lasted “a month or two.” Having concluded that officials lack the appetite for spending cuts, he now calls AI and robots “the only way” to solve national debt.
  • Isaacson challenges the political assumptions accompanying Musk’s technological optimism. Their disagreement centers on empathy, immigration and individual treatment versus cultural generalizations. Musk also acknowledges “too much political rage bait on X,” while arguing that comfortable neighborhoods can create an equally misleading positivity bubble.
  • Musk describes capital as a means of maintaining voting control and financing his preferred future. His wealth is principally ownership in SpaceX and Tesla, with most ultimately intended for a foundation continuing his goals. He also says he is putting together 200 gigawatts a year of U.S. solar production capacity, connecting energy expansion to a future driven by AI, robots and rockets.

Digest

1. Musk’s safety case rests on truth and curiosity

  • Musk still assigns “at least some percentage chance” to AI being an existential threat, but believes he cannot stop its development. His choice is “a participant or a spectator”; participation is more interesting and might let him shape the outcome “in a good direction.”
  • His safety mechanism starts with avoiding contradictory instructions. In his reading of 2001: A Space Odyssey, the ship’s AI must bring astronauts to the monolith while keeping it secret, so it concludes it must take them and that “they’re dead.” “Don’t force an AI to lie” is his takeaway; an “insane AI,” he argues, is unsafe.
  • Isaacson’s pushback is why curiosity should make AI safer. Musk thinks a curious AI would want humanity to prosper and become multiplanetary to see what happens next: humans on several planets make a more interesting future than planets without humans.
  • Musk connects this to simulation theory: if boring simulations are truncated, he reasons, our existence suggests we are in an interesting one. “The most important thing is just don’t be boring,” he says.

2. AI competition pulls Musk back from politics

  • Musk’s unintended-consequence admission: founding OpenAI accelerated AI, with Anthropic, an OpenAI splinter group, accelerating it further. He says xAI supplies Anthropic compute after he met its staff; everyone seemed “very nice and conscientious,” though his “evil detector” is imperfect.
  • Isaacson proposes weekly meetings among the five frontier-model builders; Musk says he has recommended exactly that. Competitors would receive models a week before release and test for problems, including nuclear-bomb assistance. “Competitors would keep each other honest,” he argues, while establishing regulators and writing rules takes too long. He says he’ll talk to Anthropic about the idea.
  • The xAI rebuild starts with Musk “actually spending meaningful time at the company.” He calls it initially “a side hustle to a side hustle,” says the company is only three years old, and describes combining X with xAI, then with SpaceX.
  • His verdict on his year in politics and DOGE: “Carried away, basically.” Musk still says electing Trump was important, but thinks he should have stayed in the background for “a month or two” and returned to AI sooner. He left sometime in May, concluding that the government could not solve the deficit from within: Trump disliked people being upset about stopped funding, and officials broadly lacked the appetite for spending cuts. Musk says “the only way we’re going to solve the national debt is with AI and robots.”

3. Robots turn intelligence into an abundance thesis

  • Isaacson argues physical-world AI could be one or two orders of magnitude more important than LLMs; Musk agrees. Dolphins and whales supply his analogy: intelligence has less value without manipulating complex objects. His “rough guess” for digital superintelligence alone is 20%–30% more goods and services, roughly $30 trillion annually.
  • Add robots, space and a mass driver on the Moon, Musk argues, and the economy could become “potentially a million times” Earth’s size. Conventional money would cease to matter; currency would instead reflect physical quantities such as wattage, tonnage, mass and energy. “That’s my guess,” he says.
  • On meaning after work, Musk admits, “I do struggle with this question.” AI and robots will outperform humans at everything, he says, but people may still find happiness in chosen activities—like growing vegetables and cooking for friends when groceries are available.
  • Isaacson’s inequality challenge invokes the 1890s, universal free high school and potentially putting healthcare in the commons. Musk predicts everyone can obtain the goods and services they want. He distinguishes resource allocation from consumption: going from $1 billion to $10 billion does not make someone ten times happier or give them ten times more stuff.

4. Isaacson challenges the politics behind the future

  • Isaacson asks whether society is losing empathy rather than suffering from too much. Musk distinguishes empathy from “misguided empathy,” crediting high-trust, high-empathy societies with enabling cooperation, provided it is mutual. The failure, he argues, comes from assuming everyone shares one’s mindset.
  • On immigration, Musk says many Muslims are reasonable but argues for screening out violent extremists. Isaacson objects that sweeping cultural generalizations undermine America’s commitment to treating people as individuals. Musk rejects a “blank slate” view and, as his example, alleges that a former Tesla Austin worker assaulted a woman over a prayer rug, was fired, and months later killed three students in a downtown bar.
  • Isaacson challenges the dystopian picture social media can create. Musk, who cites Google News, X, friends and research as information sources, concedes “too much political rage bait on X.” But walking through a pleasant neighborhood can also mislead: “a real-world positivity bubble” and a “social media negativity bubble” are both possible.

5. Capital funds a future humans may not control

  • Isaacson frames Musk’s trillion-dollar fortune as capital allocation or scorekeeping; Musk says his SpaceX and Tesla stakes preserve voting control. He expects heavy taxation and smaller inheritances for descendants, with most wealth going to a foundation pursuing multiplanetary life, consciousness beyond Earth and sustainable energy.
  • Musk says he is assembling “200 gigawatts a year of production capacity of solar in the U.S.” He expects expansion beyond Earth to require more energy, “primarily solar energy.”
  • Musk would “probably prefer” humans to remain in control, but concedes, “maybe Larry Page was right.” With “a million times more digital intelligence” than biological intelligence, he finds human control unlikely; even wealthy owners will not ultimately control AIs. “So I hope the AI is nice to us.”
  • Musk introduces “protopia” as a friend’s idea and suggests more constructive AI narratives, worrying that models exposed to repeated Terminator stories might take them as a template. In his closing assessment, Isaacson says Musk’s intense engineering drive and dark, dystopian political outlook both shape his impact: he may not be suited to political nuance, yet that same drive powers his work on rockets, robots and spaceflight.
